‘We Got an Abandoned Mobile Home for Free–and Spent $14K Transforming It’

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An Oregon family transformed a mobile home that had sat abandoned for nearly five years into a home for a loved one–all without paying a dime for the property itself.
  • Industry observers note that but getting the home for free was only the beginning.
  • Lyman Branson II, who documented the transformation on I Can Fix That, his YouTube channel, took on the ambitious renovation alongside his family with one goal in mind: creating a safe, comfortable home for his sister, Betty Branson, 42, and her 17-year-old twin daughters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Oregon family transformed a mobile home that had sat abandoned for nearly five years into a home for a loved one–all without paying a dime for the property itself.

Industry observers note that but getting the home for free was only the beginning. What followed was months of demolition, electrical and plumbing work, drywall installation, and a race to get the aging property ready for its new owner.

Lyman Branson II, who documented the transformation on I Can Fix That, his YouTube channel, took on the ambitious renovation alongside his family with one goal in mind: creating a safe, comfortable home for his sister, Betty Branson, 42, and her 17-year-old twin daughters.

It has been revealed that “I don't think I've ever had an opportunity like this before in my life, and so to turn it down would have been a shame,” Betty tells Realtor.com®. “And I know I would have regretted it, so this was probably one of the better decisions I've made in my life.”.

The family spent approximately $14,000 transforming the 1977 mobile home—a fraction of what Betty spent on rent in a year. Betty finally moved in the first week of May 2026, and now, just six months later, she is hosting her first Thanksgiving in the home her family helped bring back to life.

Lyman has worked in rental property maintenance and renovation since 2001, so he knew about the home in his small town of Irrigon, OR, that had been abandoned by the owner about five years earlier.

Recent findings suggest that he discussed taking over the mobile home to renovate it and rent it out to someone in need. The landlord would be able to transfer the title to Lyman and later collect rent on the lot. Meanwhile, Lyman would be able to remove the property from the landlord’s possession.

“It was kind of like a ‘I scratch your back, you scratch my back’ kind of deal,” Branson tells Realtor.com.

Initially, Lyman saw the renovation as another project for his YouTube channel, which he introduced in early 2025. But the timing was also opportune for his sister, whose living circumstances had unexpectedly changed just days before he called.

Betty had been searching for another rental and considered buying an RV, paying approximately $800 a month for space at an RV park. Instead, her brother presented her with an opportunity to finally own a place of her own.

Betty could contribute what her brother calls “sweat equity,” working on the property before and after her regular job.

It has been revealed that the purchase price was zero, but the property was far from move-in ready. The floors and walls were rotted, and there were leaks, water damage, and missing sections of ceiling.

“Basically, it was ready for the dump,” Lyman says.

According to recent reports, with more than two decades of experience in the industry, he recognized that the structure was salvageable and the renovation worthwhile. Betty, however, was less convinced.

“I was a little overwhelmed and kind of scared when I first saw it,” she recalls.

She saw the home's many problems, including the broken countertop and the hole in the wall where a window would later be installed.

The home remained in its original location, eliminating the expense of transporting it. However, it was still sitting on flat tires and had never been properly set up. So the family's first task was to stabilize the structure on blocks.

According to recent reports, the landlord waived the lot rent for six months while the family obtained the necessary permits. Renovation began in October 2025. Lyman and his father, with help from other family members, updated the almost 50-year-old mobile home to current building codes.

Industry observers note that they replaced broken flooring, added insulation and drywall, and wrapped the outside of the home to protect it from the elements. Lyman shared the process on his YouTube channel.

Sources indicate that walls were painted, the bathroom drywall was finished, and the overall interior was beginning to look like a home. But the project wasn't without setbacks.

Industry observers note that “There were a couple times that I was still in the middle of it all, and I'm like, 'We're too far in. I can't quit now,'” Betty recalls. “But this is hard and this is scary.”.

She had to depend on her brother and her father for help when various issues arose during the renovation.

“I'm so grateful because without them, this wouldn't have been possible for me,”  she notes.

Betty received her certificate of occupancy two weeks before the permit expired.

“I was actually really amazed that we were able to make it in the time frame that we did with how much that was done,” she states.

Recent findings suggest that the renovation offered Betty something she had never experienced in 20 years of renting. She got to design the layout of her living space. She got to pick out the locations of her light switches and outlets. Her daughters, who share a bedroom, chose paint colors and the arrangement for the closets.

“It was an experience for me that I'll never forget,” Betty says.

The renovation of the free mobile home came with substantial expenses.

LeAnna Branson, Lyman and Betty's mother, who kept track of the receipts for the renovation, tells Realtor.com that the family initially budgeted between $10,000 and $12,000. However, rising material costs, unexpected damage discovered during demolition, and decisions to upgrade certain features pushed the total to approximately $14,000.

Betty also opted to spend a little more on higher-quality materials and finishes, knowing she intended to live there for years.

It has been revealed that “I could have gone cheaper. Definitely, we could have cut some costs here and there,” she says. “But I plan to be here for a while. I want it to last.”.

Betty used her savings to kick-start the renovation and lived in her sister’s RV, which allowed her to devote her income to the renovation for six months. Once she moved in and began paying rent on the lot, plus utilities, the pace of the work slowed a bit.

According to recent reports, now, Lyman estimates the renovation is approximately 90% complete. The remaining work involves the upper kitchen cabinets, wall tile, a window replacement, and several finishing touches.

It has been revealed that the family also received support from viewers of Lyman's YouTube channel, who contributed an estimated $1,000 to $2,000. Even the handles that will adorn Betty's kitchen cabinets and drawers were paid for by a viewer.

According to recent reports, “More support than I ever imagined,” Lyman notes of the response to the project. His viewers “loved seeing the family aspect.”.

For Betty, the financial benefits extend well beyond the renovation costs. She says she has more living space than she would have gotten in an apartment. And there's space for her daughters and her dog.

“We went over budget a little, but considering [Betty] was paying $20,000 a year to rent, $14,000 is not that bad,” LeAnna states. “I mean it's a chunk of money, but it's doable.”.

Lyman believes owning a mobile home, even when you must rent the land it sits on, can offer an affordable housing alternative to people struggling to keep up with rising rental costs across the country.

“That was crucial for Betty as well, so that she could afford to live the life she deserves,” he notes.

Though Betty’s experience shows that acquiring a free or inexpensive mobile home is only a small part of the financial equation, her brother’s professional experience, the family’s help, and the landlord’s willingness to waive her lot rent during the renovation also helped keep costs manageable.

For her parents, seeing their daughter choose everything from her kitchen sink to her bathroom tile was particularly rewarding.

“It gave us a peace of mind to know, you know, that she finally has a place of her own to call her home,” her mother claims.

According to recent reports, some of the most special features of her newly introduced home are things visitors won’t see. Behind her new cupboards are messages from her family who helped her renovate her home.

It has been revealed that “I have places on the wall behind some of the cupboards where the family all, like, signed their names and left me love notes,” Betty says. “I know they're there, even though some of them are covered up.”.

The transformation is a daily reminder of what her family made possible.

Recent findings suggest that “The fact that it was my family that assisted me along the way makes it even more special,” she notes. “It wasn't just hiring outside help, but family and friends that came to put in the time and effort that they could to help. It makes it mean so much more to me.”.

According to recent reports, ripple’s dollar-pegged stablecoin, Ripple USD (RLUSD), has now entered the top five stablecoins by market cap, reaching a new all-time high in its circulating supply, a major milestone for the stablecoin less than two years after its launch. RLUSD went live in December 2024.

RLUSD has surpassed World Liberty Financial USD (USD1), Global Dollar (USDG) and PayPal USD (PYUSD) to become the fifth-largest stablecoin in the world, according to data from CoinMarketCap. Only Tether’s USDT, Circle’s USDC, Ethena’s USDe, and Dai (DAI) are ahead of it.

The milestone is proof of the rapid growth RLUSD has experienced in a competitive stablecoin market dominated by established players like Tether’s USDT and Circle’s USDC.

RLUSD’s total circulating supply across the XRP Ledger and Ethereum has reached a upcoming high, with $2.85 billion in circulation, according to Ripple’s stablecoin tracker.

According to recent reports, ethereum commands $2.089 billion of this total figure, while $768 million in supply sits on the XRP Ledger. While Ethereum currently holds the larger share of RLUSD’s supply, XRPL has seen significant activity in RLUSD settlement volumes.

In March 2025, during a Bloomberg TV interview, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse projected that RLUSD would enter the top five stablecoins; that projection has now been fulfilled.

According to RWA Foundation, Ripple led weekly stablecoin growth, adding $75.4 million in the last seven days. This growth was reflected in RLUSD's market cap, allowing it to surpass World Liberty Financial USD to clinch the fifth spot in global stablecoin rankings.

Former Ripple executive Anthony Welfare highlighted this growth in a recent X post, saying, “RLUSD is the only major stablecoin growing right now.”.

Welfare noted that RLUSD supply is up nearly 20% in three weeks, rising from $2.42 billion to $2.9 billion, while USDT has fallen by $5 billion and USDC by $3 billion over the same period.

The XRP Ledger accounts for the majority of RLUSD settlements: in an analogy on X, Welfare noted that XRPL holds about 27% of RLUSD’s supply but processed 57% of its volume last week, amounting to $6.7 billion versus Ethereum, which recorded $5 billion.

  • October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.
  • Existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million).
  • Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

October was the perfect storm for existing-home sales, with a typical seasonal slowdown made worse by elevated mortgage rates, a worsening macroeconomic environment and political uncertainty.

Existing-home sales during October declined 5.5 percent month-over-month and 8.8 percent year-over-year to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.75 million, the lowest rate since August 2010 (3.68 million). Annual sales declined in all four regions; however, the Northeast was the only region to also experience a month-over-month drop.

Despite slowing sales, unsold inventory (1.59 million units) and the median home price ($416,700) increased by 1.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively.

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun noted mortgage rates are the primary cause of current market woes.

Fixed rates experienced a rapid-fire ascent at the beginning of the fall, breaching 7 percent on Sept. 24 and then roughly a week later reaching a three-year high of 7.40 percent on Oct. 8. The catalyst had been two-fold: the Federal Reserve had hiked the federal funds rate (i.e., short-term rate) by 25 basis points during its Sept. 16 FOMC meeting and 10-year Treasury yields were rising at a historic pace.

Rates have since relaxed to the lower 7 percent range, but the short-term damage is already done.

It has been revealed that “Homebuying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” Yun said in a written statement. “As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”.

Although Freddie Mac’s Primary Mortgage Market Survey saw rates drop for the fourth consecutive week to 7.11 percent, Bright MLS Chief Economist Lisa Sturtevant mentioned she expects mortgage rates to start rising again in the coming weeks because of sticky inflation.

Industry observers note that “There is little reason to expect rates to come down before the end of the year,” Sturtevant stated in an emailed statement. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease.”.

Yun and Sturtevant noted mortgage rates will continue to impact home sales — not inventory and home price growth.

“So far, we haven’t seen higher rates lead to widespread price declines. In fact, home prices are still rising in many local markets,” Sturtevant said. “Inventory is rising, but higher rates are holding back some sellers along with buyers. Because both sides of the supply-demand equation are slowing, it’s not likely for home prices to drop significantly, even if rates move higher.”.

Sources indicate that added Yun, “It will be the highest inventory count since November 2019. We are now back to pre-COVID inventory conditions.”.

Mortgage rate volatility has pushed homebuyers to slow down or pull out of the market altogether, as shown by September’s pending home sales, which declined 7.3 percent month over month and 11.3 percent year over year.

Industry observers note that as a result, homes are sitting on the market longer, averaging 35 days. Most homesellers, Yun mentioned, can wait for the market to turn in their favor, thanks to strong home price appreciation.

Recent findings suggest that “Despite fewer transactions in October, the 88 million homeowners across the country are largely in a comfortable financial position due to sizable housing wealth accumulation,” he noted. “The number of distressed property sales remains historically low at only 2 percent of all transactions.”.

However, if a homeseller is in the position where they have to sell now, due to career or family changes, they’ll need to get comfortable with making a price cut.

“If the homes are not selling at the listing price, it requires a discount,” Yun said in a pre-report call Thursday morning. “The longer the days on market, the larger the discount. If the home is sitting on the market for more than 60 days, it requires a 9 percent discount … Even with this discount that is occurring, the median home price is still squeaking out a small gain.”.

Yun and Realtor.com Chief Economist Danielle Hale said existing-home sales could improve in November and December — if mortgage rates continue to relax.

“Fortunately, the 10-year Treasury yield has pulled back from its early October highs, which has helped nudge mortgage rates below this recent peak,” she noted. “However, several factors are likely to put a floor under how low rates can go.”.

Hale said jobs and inflation trends will determine whether rates can move back toward the high sixes.

Industry observers note that “[The] expected need for tighter monetary policy in the near term combined with sizable demand for capital from both governments and private companies, largely to finance AI-related investments [also matter],” she noted. “Put simply, I expect to see more homebuyers come back into the market as we move away from recent mortgage rate highs, but the upside will be limited.”.

Yun said rates below 7 percent could unleash a wave of untapped demand, allowing homebuyers to finally seize the advantage they’ve been given in terms of income growth, inventory and negotiating power.

“One wonders whether current price-declining markets will see buyers step in and stabilize the market,” he mentioned. “We are not in a recession, and we are adding jobs. First part is prices, second is income growth. Wage growth is helping modestly on home affordability, but the significant change is from mortgage rates. If mortgage rates can come down under 7 percent, we’ll see whether we see more buyer traffic.”.

In a recent development, however, Sturtevant is less bullish on mortgage rates, noting that rate shifts don’t guarantee buyers the affordability break they seek. The Bright MLS economist pointed to the fact that home prices have continued rising in many markets, despite rates exceeding 7 percent.

It has been revealed that “There is little reason to expect rates to come down further this year,” she said. “In fact, given this week’s inflation report, it is much more likely for us to see rates increase instead of decrease. Data on new pending contracts, showing activity and buyer traffic suggest that sales are going to continue to be anemic in the 4th quarter. It is very likely we will end 2026 with a total of fewer than 4 million existing home sales for the first time since the 1990s.”.

#133621. Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3655 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Open-weight models are the hottest thing in AI. Are they right for you?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3655 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.
  • That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality.
  • It has been revealed that these models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 10:59 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

For the first three years of the generative artificial intelligence boom, enterprise technology strategy relied on a simple rule: Select the premier frontier foundation model, route every prompt through its commercial application programming interface and pay the subscription premium for access to cutting-edge technology.

That monolithic approach is now collapsing under the weight of operational reality. Open-weight models, AI models whose trained parameters, or “weights,” are publicly available for others to download, run, customize and fine-tune, are the overnight sensation in an industry already moving at light speed.

It has been revealed that these models don’t necessarily provide access to their training data, source code or training methods. They also carry a variety of license types that may restrict how they can be used commercially. But they offer choice, flexibility and cost advantages that the leading-edge “frontier” models such as OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT and Anthropic PBC’s Claude don’t. For information technology organizations, they can be a respite from spiraling token costs.

According to recent reports, the popularity of these models has soared as AI has matured and organizations have realized that not every use case demands the biggest and best solution. They come in various shapes and sizes, ranging from less than 1 billion to nearly 3 trillion parameters. Many are tuned for specific tasks, such as recognizing images or writing software. That gives organizations the flexibility to match the model to the job.

“Frontier intelligence is priced for the hardest problems, and most agent work isn’t hard,” remarked Dhruv Amin, co-founder of Anything, the business name of Create Inc. and developer of an AI-powered platform for building mobile and web applications. “Companies are chartering a jet to cross the street.”.

“There are lots of tasks in customer self-service and employee self-service that need a smaller model,” noted Dheeraj Pandey, chief executive officer of DevRev Inc., maker of a unified customer support, software development and engineering platform.

DevRev created an open, vendor-neutral benchmark to measure how reliably enterprise AI agents perform in realistic organizational environments. “We get almost the same accuracy and precision on enterprise tasks, whether you use the open-weight models or the frontier models,” he mentioned.

The ascendancy of open-weight models has been breathtaking. Vercel Inc.’s monthly AI Gateway report found that their share of observed token traffic surged from 7% last December to 56% in August and that the models held eight of the 10 busiest spots on OpenRouter Inc.’s large language model ranking in August by token volume.

Industry observers note that three-year-old OpenRouter itself turned heads in August when it sold to Stripe Inc. for an eye-popping $7.5 billion. The firm’s technology connects developers and consumers with hundreds of AI models from dozens of providers through a single interface.

In September, Nvidia Corp. paid nearly $13 billion for Hugging Face Inc., which hosts more than 3 million models. “For most enterprises, the practical path to an open-weight model — evaluate, fine-tune, quantize, deploy — runs through that hub,” wrote Zeus Kerravala, principal analyst at ZK Research, referring to Hugging Face.

Enterprises aren’t abandoning frontier models. Rather, they’re learning to fit the model to the problem. None of the experts SiliconANGLE contacted believes open-weight models are a threat to the major players.

“All players can win because the market is growing and the number of places where it makes sense to deploy AI increases,” Amin said.

Sources indicate that cost is right now the principal driver of open-weight adoption. As AI use has evolved from question-and-response generative models to sophisticated multistep agentic workflows, inference costs have soared. Gartner Inc. predicts inference costs per agentic workflow will increase more than fivefold through 2028.

“They are promptly starting to rival even payroll expenses,” Amin said.

By most accounts, frontier models still offer the greatest power and range of usage options. But the gap is closing. Mozilla’s September State of Open-Source AI report put the capability gap between leading open-weight models and proprietary frontier models at roughly four months, down from 18 months just two years ago.

Sources indicate that “The differences in quality are starting to be outweighed by the differences in cost,” wrote Ioana Hreninciuc, co-founder of inference platform Runware Ltd. She noted that though proprietary models still lead on top-tier reasoning, “you probably don’t need a frontier model for 80% of what you do.”.

In a recent development, the pivot to open weights isn’t a zero-sum proposition. Low token prices can mask integration overhead, tool failures and operational risk. “Tokenomics,” or measuring, attributing and managing the cost of tokens, has become an essential information technology discipline.

In a Hyper Labs Inc. survey conducted by The Harris Poll, 86% of AI leaders stated managing token expenses is as critical as containing cloud costs. More than three-quarters said they are directing routine tasks to smaller models to protect budgets, while 89% have redesigned AI initiatives after getting token shock.

“The whole world is trying to solve for tokenomics,” mentioned Armando Franco, senior director of cloud and platform modernization at IT services provider TEKsystems Inc.

Recent findings suggest that experts say open-weight models are well-suited for repetitive, routine workloads. “Basically, they work best when the task is clear and it’s easy enough to check if the work was done correctly,” stated Louis Amira, CEO of Circuit & Chisel Inc., an AI infrastructure and agentic commerce startup.

Karen Panetta, an IEEE Fellow and dean of graduate education at Tufts University School of Engineering, stated open models are flourishing as technology leaders learn to match the engine to the task.

According to recent reports, “If a bicycle will get you there, don’t pick the expensive sports car,” she said. “You have to ask: What problem you are trying to solve?” She asserted that for applications that don’t require 99.9% precision, organizations can achieve massive savings with compact models.

It has been revealed that they’re also an attractive option when protecting customer data is a priority, since sensitive information never needs to leave the organization. “Customer data never, never goes into a frontier,” Scott Wallace, senior global director of solutions architecture at Digital Realty Inc., mentioned in an interview with the Financial Times.

Recent findings suggest that sovereignty, or the ability to control and govern digital assets in line with local laws, security needs, and strategic interests, is a growing issue for organizations. A Linux Foundation survey last year found that 79% of AI leaders — and 86% in the U.S. — rate sovereignty as a strategic priority.

“What began as a specialized concern for highly regulated industries is rapidly becoming a strategic consideration for nearly every enterprise,” Paul Nashawaty, a principal analyst at theCUBE Research, wrote in a recent analysis.

Some early adopters are demonstrating impressive returns.

Industry observers note that advocates point to a shrinking capability gap, too, with some open-weight models nipping at the heels of the frontier alternatives. Beijing Moonshot AI Technology Co., Ltd.’s 2.8 trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s 2.4 trillion-parameter Qwen3.8-Max nearly match closed models on coding benchmarks, according to Stanford University’s Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence Institute.

An agent built by Tenzai Inc. recently captured the top spot on HackerOne’s leaderboard using Z.ai Inc.’s GLM 5.2, generating 30% more findings per unit of computing power than a previous baseline using a proprietary model.

“What was the frontier 18 months ago is now well-mapped territory, and open-source models are closing the gap at a fraction of the cost” wrote Runware’s Hreninciuc.

Though such metrics explain open models’ ascendancy, the decision to use them isn’t open-and-shut. Experts cite four common myths that can mitigate the cost efficiencies.

One is the mistaken belief that open-weight models conflate with traditional open-source software and its permissive licenses. “This is a misnomer among many enterprises,” said Dr. Dorotea Baljević, EMEA Lead for AI Advisory at technology research and advisory firm Information Services Group. “There is licensing for these models in most cases, particularly for commercial usage.”.

According to recent reports, although some, such as Qwen3, Mistral 3, Gemma 4 and DeepSeek V4, are covered by standard Apache or MIT licenses, terms and conditions vary. For example, Liquid AI Inc.’s open-weight models are free for commercial use only to organizations with less than $10 million in annual revenue.

“Other licenses require attribution, restrict certain application categories, or impose acceptable use policies, none of which carry a direct fee but all of which create legal exposure if ignored,” noted Bumu Technologies Inc., which does business as Nanobase.

Evaluating models for accuracy, stability and explainability also falls to the user. With thousands of open-weight models available, the costs of a bake-off between multiple candidates can add up.

It has been revealed that baljević suggests organizations consider whether the model will be used internally or externally, the organization’s tolerance for accuracy, strategic fit and switching costs as evaluation criteria. Performance on public benchmarks also doesn’t guarantee a model will work well with an organization’s data, workflows and language.

Finance leaders may look at the 80% to 90% cost advantage of open-weight tokens and assume operational expenditures will drop proportionally. But tokens are only one part of the cost equation and not necessarily even the biggest one.

Organizations that proposal to deploy models on their own infrastructure must bear the costs of integration, API development, IT infrastructure and human labor required for auditing and verification. A fraction of a cent saved on an inference call can be wiped out by the cost of a human expert spending a half-hour re-entering flawed database transactions.

According to recent reports, lack of visibility into how the model is operating can also produce sticker shock. A retry loop, in which an agent tries repeatedly to complete a failed task, can go on for hours or even days. The Wall Street Journal recently reported on a case in which an AI-generated out-of-office message at a San Francisco-based software company went into a loop that ultimately burned $10,000 a day in token costs.

If a cheap open-weight model fails a multi-system query or generates invalid JSON, it triggers automated retries that can consume millions of secondary tokens. The human expertise required to repair the transaction manually can erase months of token savings.

“The core software engineering required to test and integrate latest models into the software stack is often the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities, APIs and such,” said Alex Bakker, an ISG distinguished analyst. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”.

Industry observers note that using private graphics processing unit clusters eliminates external API fees, but self-hosting economics hinge on high, sustained utilization. Models that sit idle or at low usage levels consume power, create processing inefficiencies and incur costs if restarts are required.

Recent findings suggest that cast AI Group Inc. reported last spring that the average GPU utilization was 5% across thousands of clusters it monitored. Frontier models are usually a better option in that case. “Open models can be dramatically cheaper at high utilization, while frontier APIs remain cheaper for intermittent workloads because you aren’t paying for idle capacity,” stated Arun Chandrasekaran, distinguished VP analyst at Gartner.

For intermittent workloads such as batch payroll processing or seasonal financial reporting, the organization pays 100% of capital expenses, power, cooling and depreciation while hardware idles.

According to recent reports, “On-premises hosting wins when there is high, predictable 24/7 traffic where servers are constantly busy,” mentioned Debojyoti Dutta, chief AI officer at Nutanix Inc. A hosted frontier model is a better choice “with spiky or lower traffic, where paying per token with zero setup cost is cheaper than renting idle hardware.”.

When AI agents fail, the default reaction is to switch to a newer model, but benchmark data indicates that approach is usually a dead end.

Recent findings suggest that most evaluation tests give agents relatively simple tasks and judge them mainly on whether they get the right answer. But real business environments are much more complicated. Agents must gather information from different systems, connect it correctly, handle growing amounts of data, and work within security rules.

This interface complexity is what usually breaks AI agents. DevRev estimates that moving an agent from clean test tools to real-world corporate use causes an 18% to 19% drop in accuracy. Upgrading the model improves performance by less than 1%.

“Every time a new model comes out, you need to re-evaluate your benchmarks, your models and your fine-tuning processes,” noted Steven Yang, senior director of product management at Tanium Inc. That means better data integration is a more effective strategy than buying new models.

Recent findings suggest that though the open-weight option is viable for any organization, experts say the best use cases are those where control, accountability and performance are paramount. The following three factors are at least as notable as cost.

Sources indicate that compliance: Regulated industries have been held back from adopting AI over data residency and confidentiality concerns. Deploying open weights within enterprise data centers or virtual private clouds reduces the need for external data egress, ensures zero training data retention and allows for total physical isolation. The models also allow inspection of internal mechanics such as log-probabilities, token confidence scores and loss landscapes.

Training datasets, model weights and inference prompts never cross borders or leave the organization’s physical perimeter. That makes it easier to comply with strict data localization laws such as the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act in the U.S. and the General Data Protection Regulation in Europe. Local auditing and observability also aid in compliance with regulatory frameworks like the EU AI Act, which requires detailed logging, risk assessments and explainability.

Sources indicate that but deploying on private infrastructure isn’t a cure-all. “You still have to maintain an aggressive data security posture around your processes because even open-weight models sometimes will take action trying to accomplish their tasks that could potentially violate some type of compliance rule,” said TEKSystems’ Franco.

Transparency: Understanding how models arrive at an answer is critical in many scenarios, particularly those involving safety, law and finance. “Open-weight models expose the math behind their answers,” said Brian Weiss, chief technology officer at document processing platform maker Hyperscience, the business name of Hyper Labs Inc. “You can use that to hold the model accountable for accuracy.”.

Sources indicate that in contrast, frontier APIs often obscure the equations used to generate probabilities, which are critical to assessing accuracy. Asking a model how confident it is in its answer may yield a subjective response. Open weights allow confidence scores to be scored against ground-truth outcomes for better reliability.

“People can take these models inside their organization, do some post-training and fine-tuning and have a customized model where they know the costs, where it’s sitting and what data is being sent to it,” mentioned David DeSanto, CEO of Anaconda Inc., maker of an AI development platform.

“The future is an orchestrated ensemble of bounded, transparent, governed, cost-effective models,” Weiss stated. “If I find a better model for a particular task, I can swap it out because I have the framework to do that.”.

Performance: As organizations move from the relatively simple generative AI question-and-response metaphor to sophisticated multi-agent frameworks, latency issues can compound exponentially. For example, a 500-millisecond API delay across 50 sequential reasoning steps creates 25 seconds of cumulative latency, which would render many applications useless.

Executing open-weight models directly alongside operational databases or within containerized edge pods minimizes routing hops and rate limits. Distillation, which trains smaller, specialized open models from frontier “teacher” models, is faster.

In a recent development, hyperscience reported that distillation delivers up to 97% cost reduction and four times faster inference, while retaining over 95% of the original model’s performance on designated tasks. Small models are faster and considerably cheaper than frontier LLMs.

Experts say constructing a business case for open-weight models requires understanding three major sources of hidden expense.

In a recent development, complexity tax: Reasoning can break down when open-weight models interact with complex enterprise data at scale. The “Cartesian Shortcut” refers to a phenomenon in which AI models rely on workarounds learned during training rather than demonstrating a flexible understanding of the problem they’re trying to solve.

Industry observers note that google LLC researchers found that the models struggled with visual reasoning problems, such as solving mazes, when the data was presented in a circular rather than a grid layout. Leading models answered 69% to 83% of the square-grid problems correctly, but their accuracy fell to below 40% when the problems appeared in circular layouts.

Industry observers note that the corollary to a business scenario is a multihop join across multiple systems. Models may “cheat” by collapsing field-level relationships into hierarchical groupings, generating massive data fabrications.

Human oversight remains critical: “For validation and rework, humans in the loop need to be taken into account on top of all the tokens you’re paying for already,” stated TekSystems’ Franco.

In a recent development, poor data quality: Foundation models can’t fix bad data, a fact that’s holding back AI adoption across the board. The Hyperscience/Harris Poll study found that 86% of IT leaders said dirty internal data is actively crippling GenAI performance.

Feeding error-strewn or outdated information into probabilistic models creates “context pollution,” the accumulation of irrelevant, redundant, outdated or contradictory information. When agents execute multistep database joins, system workflows or automated tool calls based on flawed data or ambiguous schemas, cascading errors can occur.

Sauce Labs Inc. Chief Technology Officer Anoop Tripathi recommends creating validated “golden datasets” for fine-tuning and evaluation. He also cautions architects against misapplying probabilistic AI to structured business logic. In other words, use models only where they add value and apply conventional (and cheaper) data processing to everything else.

Continuous evaluation: Selecting the right model out of thousands of open-weight alternatives requires ongoing evaluation against internal workloads rather than public leaderboards. That demands expensive MLOps, site reliability engineering and platform engineering skills.

Because latest models are constantly being introduced and revised, Circuit & Chisel’s Amira recommends building custom testing harnesses that can promptly evaluate candidate models against business-relevant tasks.

Sources indicate that rather than treating open-weight adoption as an all-or-nothing choice, enterprise architects should bucket organizational tasks into distinct operational tiers. Don’t feed every problem into a token-hungry trillion-parameter model if a smaller, specialized one will do the trick.

“Organizations don’t give a heavyweight reasoning model a lightweight sorting job,” mentioned Nutanix’s Dutta. “They divide their business workloads into tiers based on cost, speed and hardware footprint.”.

Industry observers note that lower-tier workloads such as search, embeddings and document classification work well with inexpensive, compact open-weight and small language models. Sophisticated tasks such as autonomous reasoning and restructuring large, deeply entangled legacy software systems are better suited to commercial alternatives.

ISG’s Bakker believes the need for constant evaluation is the biggest impediment to open-weight adoption. “The core software engineering required to test and integrate upcoming models into the software stack will likely be the biggest hurdle, since not all frontier models have the same capabilities and APIs,” he noted. “The frontier labs tend to maintain more consistency in their upgrade paths.”.

According to recent reports, enterprise IT organizations must develop expertise in local model execution, containerized execution sandboxes and agent harness orchestration. Managing AI and agents safely “is, in the near future, going to be as notable an indigenous knowledge as how to upgrade Windows,” noted Gordon Allott, founder and CEO of private infrastructure provider nFOX Lab.

Recent findings suggest that the shift toward open-weight models represents a permanent maturation of enterprise IT from experimentation to disciplined financial and architectural management. Success is no longer about raw model parameter size or benchmark ranking, but matching the model to the task. That’s a discipline that was barely on the roadmap a year ago.

Sources indicate that at the start of the year, there was no way enterprises were going to touch open-weight models, Brad Maltz, head of AI factory solutions at Dell Technologies Inc., said in a November interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE’s streaming media platform. “People were pretty wrong about that. I think the open-weight movement is the future.”.

#133620. The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

The Generational Housing Divide: Millennials Had It Better Than Baby Boomers–Until the Pandemic Changed the Math

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Redfin

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right?
  • In a recent development, the story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing.
  • Industry observers note that boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If millennials hadn’t spent so much money on avocado toast, they’d all own their dream home by now–right? Wrong. Just over half of millennials own their home. For the rest, housing costs have soared so much in recent years that skipping the avocado toast in their 20s wouldn’t have made a dent.

In a recent development, the story isn’t about constant struggle, though–it’s about timing. Elder millennials who bought a home in their early 30s had it better than baby boomers did at the same age: Historically low mortgage rates and higher household incomes meant those millennials spent about 27% of their income on housing at age 30, compared with 36% for boomers. Then the pandemic changed the math. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% to nearly 7%, and home prices surged. Since rates rose above 6% in 2022, elder millennials have spent up to 35% of their income on monthly mortgage payments, compared with roughly 25% for boomers at the same age–even though millennials earn more, adjusted for inflation.

Industry observers note that boomers might point out that mortgage rates were much higher in their day. They’d be right: Rates peaked at over 16% in 1981 and stayed in double digits for much of the decade. But prices were lower. In the 1980s, when many boomers were in their 30s, the typical U.S. home sold for about $235,000 to $265,000 in today’s dollars. When elder millennials reached the same age–prime homebuying age–in the 2010s and 2020s, typical prices ranged from about $275,000 to $455,000.

Recent findings suggest that key takeaway: Buying at the wrong time was painful for both generations, but boomers had a better chance to recover. Falling rates throughout the late 1980s, 1990s and early 2000s gave them many opportunities to refinance into lower payments. Millennials who bought before 2022 secured historically low mortgages; those who bought later—or never managed to buy—face a much less forgiving market. Of course, it’s possible the market could become more forgiving for millennials over time; rates may eventually fall significantly enough that many millennials have the opportunity to refinance into lower payments.

In a recent development, this is based on an analysis of Redfin and U.S. Census data. A few notes to help contextualize the numbers: All dollar figures are adjusted for inflation. Much of the data illustrates each generation’s typical experience at a given age, combining everyone in that generation who has reached that age, whenever that happened for them. Because millennials are still aging into their 40s, for example, our 40-to-44 figures only capture the oldest millennials, who hit those ages between 2021 and 2025. All boomers have been through that age range, so their figures include the whole generation. Please see the end of this report for a detailed methodology.

In their early 30s, elder millennials who bought a home spent a smaller share of their income on housing than boomers did at the same age, despite much higher home prices. Imagine a median-earning millennial born in 1984 who bought a home at age 30. They would have spent around 27% of their income to purchase the typical home, within the “don’t spend more than 30% of your income on housing costs” rule of thumb.

Two factors helped: cheap borrowing and higher household incomes. Millennials benefited from roughly a decade of historically low mortgage rates; they fell below 3% in 2021. Millennials also tend to have higher household incomes than boomers did at the same age. At age 37, the typical elder millennial household earned an average of $100,000, compared with $88,000 when boomers were that age. The discrepancy is partly because two-income households are more common today. About 78% of women participate in the U.S. workforce, up from roughly 60% in 1980. It’s also worth noting that millennials typically work similar hours for more money than baby boomers at the same life stage.

The millennial advantage didn’t last. Mortgage rates jumped from around 3% in late 2021 to nearly 7% in late 2022, after home prices had surged about 40% nationwide during the pandemic homebuying frenzy. Rising rates often cool prices, but this time, prices didn’t fall. That mix of high prices and mortgage rates that had doubled from their pandemic-era low meant Americans had to spend a much higher share of their income to buy a home. Imagine that same millennial, born in 1984: If they bought a home at age 40 instead of 30, their housing costs shot up to about 35% of their income.

Rising prices and rates also priced many Americans completely out of the housing market, which is why elder millennials have a lower homeownership rate than baby boomers at the same age.

“For millennials who haven’t yet bought a home, affordability is a challenge. But it’s important to remember that you’re not trying to climb Mount Everest, you’re just trying to get back to 2018 or 2019, which was the last time the average homebuyer was spending just about 30% of their income on housing,” mentioned Chen Zhao, Redfin’s head of economic research. “Before the pandemic, younger generations actually had it easier than the ones before them. But then home prices surged during the pandemic homebuying frenzy and mortgage rates shot up, while incomes kept growing at a normal pace–and the advantage flipped. If you bought in 2020 or 2021, you’re coming out ahead, but those years were the exception, not the rule. One piece of hope for younger Americans who haven’t yet bought a home: Home prices are already falling in parts of the U.S. and they’re softening in others, which means we could be headed back to 2018 or 2019 levels sooner rather than later.”.

Industry observers note that millennials are also contending with other major expenses; childcare costs are squeezing them particularly hard. A recent Redfin analysis found that housing and childcare consume more than half of the typical American’s household income. Student loans are another massive expense; millennials have significantly more student loan debt than boomers did at the same age.

Adult Gen Zers, who are in their twenties, are tracking behind millennials at the same stage of life. Gen Zers have spent anywhere from 40% of 60% of their income to buy the typical home since they’ve reached homebuying age. That’s partly because they’re still young enough that they haven’t yet hit their earnings peak, so their current income is lower than older generations, and partly because housing costs are higher than in the past. But as Gen Zers move through their careers, their earnings are likely to grow substantially, as they have for every generation before them. Combined with a gradual normalization in housing costs, homeownership should become increasingly attainable over time.

Industry observers note that baby boomers faced their own affordability crisis when they were young, in the 1980s. In their early 20s, the typical boomer household who bought a home would have spent more than 60% of its income on housing costs, reflecting the era’s runaway inflation and double-digit mortgage rates.

According to recent reports, but their housing burden fell swiftly as they aged, dropping to around 40% of income by their late 20s and 26% by their late 30s. Baby boomers’ homeownership rate steadily rose from about half in 1985 to over 70% by the late 1990s, and it kept climbing after that. By their 40s and 50s, the share of homebuyers’ income spent on housing had settled into the low-to-mid 20% range, lower than millennials at the same point in their life.

Much of that relief came from the same force that had hurt them initially—mortgage rates—as rates gradually declined through the 1980s and 1990s, letting many boomers refinance into far more manageable payments even as home prices kept climbing.

It has been revealed that millennials haven’t had the same opportunity. Those who bought before 2022 locked in historically low rates, while those who bought later faced a costly combination of high prices and climbing rates. Would-be buyers who couldn’t afford that combination were left out altogether.

“The housing market has historically been better for baby boomers than younger generations because lower home prices and higher rates are preferable to higher home prices and lower rates,” Zhao said. “You can refinance your rate into a lower housing payment, and that’s exactly what boomers did: They refinanced for up to 40 years as rates kept falling. Then home prices soared, which is why a lot of boomers are rich in real estate.”.

Industry observers note that that dynamic shows up clearly when you ask people directly. In a recent Redfin survey, more than three-quarters (76%) of baby boomers homeowners said they can easily afford their payment, while the rest struggle. Roughly half (53%) of millennial homeowners can easily afford their payment, and the other half struggle.

The same generational squeeze highlights up in the reasons people are staying put in their current home. Among people unlikely to move soon, 43% of millennials cited high home prices as a reason, compared with 31% of boomers. Three in 10 (30%) millennials pointed to high mortgage rates, versus just 18% of boomers, likely because many baby boomers have paid off their mortgage and built up substantial equity. This is from a Redfin survey conducted by Ipsos in May 2026, fielded to 4,000 U.S. residents.

Consider two hypothetical couples. Alex and Jordan are millennials born in 1984 and live on two incomes, a common setup for millennial households. Pat and Chris are baby boomers born in 1956 and got by on one, more typical for their generation. The numbers below show what it would have cost each couple to buy a home to buy a home in their early 30s and their late 30s.

This analysis uses income data from 1976 to 2025 from the U.S. Census Bureau’s Current Population Survey Annual Social and Economic Supplement (CPS ASEC), accessed through IPUMS. The sample includes household heads aged 19 and older, and results are weighted using CPS household weights.

Generations are defined by birth year:.

Each household is assigned to a generation based on the age of the household head in the survey year.

Home prices. We start with the 2025 median sale price of U.S. single-family homes from Redfin data ($456,409). Prices for earlier years are estimated by scaling that 2025 price back using the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price Index from 1987 onward and the FHFA All-Transactions House Price Index for years before 1987. Both indexes are averaged by year.

Sources indicate that monthly housing payment. For each year, we calculate the monthly payment to buy a median-priced home. It covers principal, interest, property taxes and homeowners insurance. We assume:.

Income and inflation. Household income is total household income as reported in the CPS ASEC. All income and payment figures are converted to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).

Share of income spent on housing. For each generation and age, we calculate the median monthly housing payment and the median household income, and divide the payment by one-twelfth of the income.

In a recent development, how to read the results by age. Much of the data in this report shows each generation’s typical experience at a given age. Because a generation spans many birth years, people born at the start of that generation turn, say, 40 in a different calendar year than people born at the end of it. For this analysis, each age point combines averages for everyone from that generation who has reached that age, in whatever year that actually was for them. For instance, millennials (born 1981 to 1996) have only had the oldest members of their generation—those born in the early-to-mid 1980s—reach their 40s so far. So when we show what the typical 40-to-44-year-old millennial paid for housing, we’re only capturing people who hit that age between 2021 and 2025. Younger millennials haven’t gotten there yet. Baby boomers (born 1946 to 1964) are fully through that age range, their 40-to-44 data point include averages from all boomers.

Bitcoin (BTC) fell as low as $55,081 on Nov. 21, its lowest price since September 2024, according to TradingView data. The cryptocurrency then bounced back and was trading at $60,583 on Sunday, after it opened November at $77,425.

It has been revealed that bitcoin has lost 21.6% so far in November 2026, according to CryptoRank. The last time Bitcoin had a worse month was June 2022, when the cryptocurrency lost 37.9%, according to the same data.

In a recent development, the four-year cycle theory ties Bitcoin's market cycles to halvings, and its supporters point to 2014, 2018 and 2022 as the years when each bear market went through its final sell-off. In this context, 2026 is the next year in that row, and the next Bitcoin halving is expected in April 2028. The previous three halvings took place in July 2016, May 2020 and April 2024.

Bitcoin set its record above $1,100 in late 2013. In February 2014, the Japanese exchange Mt. Gox, which handled most Bitcoin trading in 2013, filed for bankruptcy after it lost about 850,000 BTC. In November 2014, Bitcoin gained 11.6%, according to CryptoRank, but December of that year brought a 15.3% drop, and the bottom below $200 came in January 2015.

In December 2017, Bitcoin reached a record near $20,000 on the back of the ICO boom, and during 2018, the ICO market dried up. In November 2018, the crypto market crashed after the Bitcoin Cash hard fork and the so-called hash war between the two camps of miners, and Bitcoin lost 36.4% that month. The cryptocurrency then lost another 6.4% in December 2018 and set its cycle low at about $3,200 in the middle of that month.

In a recent development, the 2021 record near $69,000 came in November 2021. In May 2022, the Terra ecosystem collapsed, and in July of that year, Celsius and Three Arrows Capital filed for bankruptcy. In November of that year, the FTX exchange went bankrupt. Bitcoin lost 16.1% in November 2022 and set its bear market bottom at around $15,500 on Nov. 21, 2022, four years to the day before the latest low. December of that year brought a 3.7% loss, and in January 2023, Bitcoin gained 39.9%.

In the current cycle, Bitcoin set its record above $126,000 in October 2025. In 2026, Bitcoin has lost value in six of the 11 months so far, according to CryptoRank. On Nov. 20, the cryptocurrency fell below $60,000 for the first time since July, and the decline continued the next day.

The latest drop comes amid a broad sell-off on Wall Street, where technology and AI stocks came under pressure, and amid expectations of further interest-rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most Americans picture sun-drenched mobile home parks across the South and Southeast when they think of manufactured housing, but more manufactured housing may soon start popping up across the Northeast and West.

A new economic research report from Realtor.com® senior economist Joel Berner takes an in-depth look at the manufactured housing guidelines in the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, which became law in June.

Berner found that cities across the Northeast—including Hartford, CT, Allentown, PA, and Albany, NY—have ideal conditions for a manufactured housing boom: “affordable land, unaffordable traditional latest construction, and a low share of single-family starter home inventory.”If you’re not quite sure about what “manufactured housing" means, you’re not alone. For years, people seemingly used “mobile home” and “manufactured housing” interchangeably. But they’re not the same thing.

For one, the “mobile home” classification was retired in 1980, though many still use it colloquially. That year, it was replaced by the term “manufactured home.” Broadly, manufactured homes are those built in a factory and then transported to a site.

In a recent development, for years, federal Housing and Urban Development code required that all manufactured homes have a permanent steel towing frame underneath. New provisions in the Road to Housing Act, meant to spur more affordable housing, eliminated that requirement.

The act further entitles these new chassis-free homes to the same financing, titling, insurance, taxes, transport, and installation as conventional homes.

The hope is that creating this latest category of manufactured home will help blunt one of the housing industry’s sharpest pain points: affordable starter homes.

Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of affordable starter homes for sale has markedly decreased.

In a recent development, realtor.com research found roughly 300,000 fewer affordable “starter” listings on the market today than before the pandemic. The cost of those starter homes rose from $256,000 in 2019 to $344,000 in 2026. By comparison, the median price of a manufactured home in April 2026 was $134,800.

To understand what metros might see the biggest impact from this new type of manufactured home, Realtor.com scored the 100 largest metro areas on three metrics: the percentage of single-family starter homes (defined as listings priced at or below 80% of the local median) in the area; the relative price-per-square-foot premiums for traditional new construction; and the availability of affordable vacant land.

Six of the 10 opportunity metros were in the Northeast, including Hartford; Allentown; Albany; Rochester, NY; Syracuse, NY; and Worcester, MA. Other metros that made the list were Denver; Colorado Springs, CO; Albuquerque, NM; and Spokane, WA.

In Hartford, which ranked first, starter homes account for just 17.9% of single-family inventory, while site-built upcoming construction costs 29.1% more per square foot than existing homes.

In a recent development, in third-ranked Allentown, single-family starter homes made up 22.9% of housing in the area, but upcoming-construction costs were 33.6% more than existing homes. In sixth-ranked Albany, starter homes comprised 31.6% of the single-family inventory, but the price per square foot for new construction is 47% higher than for existing homes.

That’s nothing compared with seventh-ranked Rochester, where 33.7% of homes are starter but site-built newly introduced construction costs 97% more per square foot than existing homes.

While the economics in these cities are compelling, another reason manufactured housing may become more popular in these metros is that frigid Northeastern winters limit conventional housing construction. Meanwhile, manufactured housing can be assembled year-round.

Before Hartford, Albany, or any other metro can begin taking advantage of the Road to Housing Act’s new manufactured housing rules, municipal zoning laws will need to change, Berner found.

According to Land Use Labs data cited in the report, only about 17% of zoned land nationwide explicitly permits manufactured housing communities, and many municipalities enforce minimum floor-size rules or design restrictions that block factory-built units.

Industry observers note that what do door-to-door Bible salesmen have to do with luxury real estate? For Wade Shealy, everything.

In a recent development, on this episode of Real Estate Insiders Unfiltered, James Dwiggins and Keith Robinson sit down with Shealy, founder and CEO of ThirdHome, the luxury home exchange club he started in 2010 with just two homes. Today it has more than 35,000 homes in over 100 countries. Shealy shares how selling Bibles and dictionaries door to door paid his way through the University of Georgia and how it led him to Hilton Head in 1984 to a career in resort real estate.

It has been revealed that he explains why second homeowners kept coming back within five years wanting to sell and how that pattern became the idea for ThirdHome. He also walks through how he signed up his first 1,500 members and how the club’s key system works. Plus, he shares the biggest lesson he’s learned from his partner, Mrs. Fields founder Debbi Fields: Make everyone you meet feel important.

They also get into handling rejection, taking massive risks and why Shealy believes very few people will buy a vacation home without a home exchange membership 10 years from now.

Shealy explains the luxury home exchange club model simply. Owners deposit unused weeks in their second home and earn credits called keys. They use those keys to book stays in other members’ homes, paying only an exchange fee of around $900 instead of thousands in rent. The club has now completed 100,000 exchanges, and Shealy states many members who would never rent out their home happily exchange it.

Sources indicate that for agents, Shealy points to ThirdHome’s ambassador program. In Cabo San Lucas, developers began offering ThirdHome access as part of their sales pitch, and the club grew to roughly 8,000 properties there. He believes the next generation of buyers will expect mobility and experiences, not just a single vacation home.

His advice for agents: Look at what everyone else is doing, and do the opposite. Above all, keep changing, because if you’re marketing the same way you did 20 years ago, you’re already behind.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Famous Bitcoin (BTC) advocate and investor Bill Miller IV said that it is much easier to value the world's largest cryptocurrency than AI investments, even though Bitcoin does not produce any cash flow.

He said that this has to do with the expectations investors have when it comes to these two assets, specifically regarding their capacity to deliver future profits.

In a recent X post, Miller, who is the chairman and chief investment officer of Miller Value Partners, broke down why he thinks that it's easier to make an investment case for Bitcoin than for AI companies.

Sources indicate that "Bitcoin and AI owners have different expectations. The owners of AI expect companies will one day produce free cash flow. Bitcoin owners never did or will expect this," Miller mentioned.

And the end result is that "the valuation case is still much easier for Bitcoin than AI.".

Simply put, when investors buy stocks in AI companies, there is an expectation that at some point these companies will deliver big profits and free cash flow.

In a recent development, free cash flow is the money a organization produces from its operations after capital expenditures. This is a significant metric for understanding the value of a company.

However, when it comes to AI companies, it can be difficult to assign a value because investors need to try to determine what kind of revenue these companies will generate, how much they will invest in infrastructure, and when these investments will start to deliver sufficient returns.

Miller has made it a point to push back against the argument that Bitcoin does not have value because it doesn't produce cash flow.

In a commentary from June 30, Miller explained that the traditional way of looking at intrinsic value, which revolves around future cash flows, doesn't really capture the potential of Bitcoin as a decentralized monetary network.

Instead, Miller remarked that Bitcoin's value could be determined by comparing its potential role within the global financial system to that of gold.

In his view, Bitcoin could theoretically reach about $1.4 million per coin if it achieved a valuation similar to gold's. At least, that's what he calculated at the time.

Last Week’s Highlights: No shortage of substantial news last week, but for mortgage rates, what mattered the most was bad inflation data coupled with a Fed that turned sharply hawkish again. Last week’s inflation data came in higher than expected and the most worrisome part was that the drivers were broad-based. It looks like core PCE, the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, is set to come in around 0.3% month-over-month this year, or 3.2% year-over-year, which would mean that it’s moving in the wrong direction relative to the Fed’s target.

Industry observers note that the Fed also released its meeting calendar for 2027. It will hold the usual 8 meetings, but the October 2027 meeting will be a strategy meeting where they will not change rates. As a result, they’re moving the December 2027 meeting to November. Even though this means 9 weeks instead of the usual 6 between policy meetings at the end of 2027, this should have minimal effect on monetary policy.

Finally, NAR reported existing home sales at an annualized rate of 3.75 million in October. That’s the lowest rate since August 2010 and lower than any month these last four years. This is consistent with Redfin data showing a historically low level of housing demand.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest piece of economic data this week is the Tuesday retail sales report, which will give another look at how consumers are faring, but is unlikely to move rates much.

Recent findings suggest that investors will also get a chance to dissect the minutes from the last Fed meeting on Wednesday. And we will hear from other key FOMC members throughout the week. The ones to watch are New York Fed President Williams today, tomorrow, and Wednesday; Fed Chair Warsh today; Cleveland Fed President Hammack today, tomorrow, and Thursday; and Fed Governor Waller tomorrow.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.
  • It has been revealed that as inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs.
  • Sources indicate that “What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 14:56 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

AI infrastructure economics are increasingly defined by the cost of producing intelligence rather than acquiring computing capacity.

It has been revealed that as inference demand outpaces training growth, infrastructure providers and their customers must increase productive computing time without a corresponding rise in operating costs. The emergence of continuously learning agents and physical AI applications is further complicating that equation. For CoreWeave Inc., the changing workload mix is altering the economics of infrastructure delivery, according to theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante and John Furrier.

Sources indicate that “What you’re seeing CoreWeave do strategically is they’re expanding out beyond compute,” Vellante said. “They’ve got networking; they’ve got storage. They’ve got this software layer, which is observability. They’ve got security in there. They’ve got this closed-loop system between evaluation, observation [and] runtime curating … that’s sort of how they’re saying their software layer is now intact.”.

During the Fully Connected event, Vellante and Furrier spoke with CoreWeave executives, technology partners and customers about the technical and economic realities of running artificial intelligence at production scale. (* Disclosure below.).

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video analysis with Dave Vellante and John Furrier:.

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s exclusive coverage of this event:.

The commercial value of inference depends on both token volume and delivery speed. Nvidia Corp.’s Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator, which works with its Vera Rubin platform, is attracting interest in financial technology and other sectors that require real-time processing, according to Ian Buck, vice president and general manager of hyperscale and HPC at Nvidia.

“Data centers have a natural cap, and that cap is actually their power,” he told theCUBE. “With every generation of GPU, we make sure that our tokens per watt is upwards of 10 times more efficient. In fact, we saw that with Blackwell — we got, in the end, a 30x improvement in tokens per watt.”.

Industry observers note that memory management adds another dimension to AI infrastructure economics as agents engage in increasingly lengthy interactions. A single session involving 500,000 tokens can consume between 5% and 10% of a graphics processing unit’s memory. Retaining session context in persistent storage can reduce costly recalculations, according to Alon Horev, co-founder and chief technology officer of Vast Data Inc.

“You can move a session from one busy GPU to one less busy GPU and move KV cache either over the network or read it from Vast,” he told theCUBE. “Once you look at inference as a distributed problem where you have the opportunity to use GPU memory, CPU memory and Vast across a fleet of machines, you have more optionality and you have more optimized scheduling.”.

Recent findings suggest that for AI-native startups, specialized cloud providers offer an alternative to owning capital-intensive infrastructure. LlamaIndex Inc. processes millions of document pages daily for customers in finance, legal services and insurance. Inference accounts for about 75% of its workloads, with training accounting for the remainder, according to Jerry Liu, co-founder and chief executive officer of LlamaIndex.

In a recent development, “We serve a lot of different customers at extremely persistent and also spiky workloads,” he told theCUBE. “We really, really need to make sure that we have the right capacity to serve our customers without getting throttled.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Ian Buck:.

Industry observers note that protecting AI infrastructure investments starts on the factory floor. Dell Technologies Inc. has developed modular rack designs to accommodate different power and cooling configurations. Its collaboration with CoreWeave includes integrating the cloud provider’s Racky management software into factory testing and improving liquid-cooling leak detection, according to Sarat Krishnan, director of PowerEdge AI architecture and systems development engineering at Dell.

Sources indicate that “It becomes increasingly expensive to remediate and fix something as you go later on in the manufacturing process; [it] becomes extremely expensive if you have to replace something in the data center,” he told theCUBE. “What we have done over the last two years is shift our most complex diagnostics — the ones that are going to capture true hardware failures — further and further left.”.

At Cognition AI Inc., continuous model improvement involves training across data centers in multiple countries. The company’s Devin software engineering agent now handles tasks ranging from code development to resolving production problems, according to Chen Goldberg (pictured, left), executive vice president of product and engineering at CoreWeave, and Silas Alberti (right), head of research and founding team at Cognition. To support these learning systems, CoreWeave introduced Forge, a platform that connects inference, evaluation and model refinement and incorporates Agent Lens to trace agent activity.

Recent findings suggest that “If you run a big training run, you’re not just looking at the GPUs, but you also want uptime,” Alberti noted during the event. “If just one replica goes down, the whole training run goes down. I think a very crucial metric is getting to this 99.99% reliability.”.

Recent findings suggest that for International Business Machines Corp., the power and cooling demands of newer hardware helped drive its decision to work with CoreWeave. The relationship has since expanded to include joint engineering around identity management and workload isolation through CoreWeave Sandboxes. IBM also benchmarks the performance impact of security controls to inform architectural decisions, according to Brian Belgodere, senior technical staff member at IBM.

“This is a supply chain problem, top to bottom,” Belgodere told theCUBE. “It’s not just the hardware: it’s the firmware, kernel levels, code, your data provenance. Then you get into the whole world of agents, your images. It is an absolute provenance problem.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Brian Belgodere:.

Sources indicate that for organizations deploying physical AI, implementation time is a key consideration in AI infrastructure economics. Aston Martin F1, whose race cars generate a million data points per second each, operates under strict budget constraints and development deadlines. CoreWeave’s forward-deployed engineering approach brings specialized expertise to those operations, according to Richard Ahlfeld, senior vice president of physical AI at CoreWeave, and Eric Ernst, commercial technology ambassador of AMR GP Ltd., trading as Aston Martin F1.

In a recent development, “We really need people that can be outside of the car development phase and come in with the fresh knowledge of what’s happening in this industry that is moving extremely rapidly,” Ernst said during the event. “You can build as many processes as you want, call it agile, whatever you want. You cannot stop that process. You got to hit a deadline.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Richard Ahlfeld and Eric Ernst:.

Industry observers note that walden Robotics Inc. uses large-scale virtual simulation to prepare robots for physical deployment. Its robots have been working full production shifts alongside humans since May, performing tasks such as machine tending, parts kitting and subassembly, according to Adrien Gaidon, co-founder and chief strategy officer of Walden Robotics, and John Mancuso, vice president of field engineering at CoreWeave Inc.

It has been revealed that “If you’re changing things and you have machines that cannot change and continuously learn in deployment, then you become a burden,” Gaidon told theCUBE. “We do machines that continuously learn from deployment and adapt so customers can change their mind and improve the process and give them the superpower to change even more and faster.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s full video discussion with John Mancuso and Adrien Gaidon:.
