  • Recent findings suggest that essentially, the proposal allows hiding which transactions customers have been looking up, which is a potential deanonymization vector.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

In a recent development, on Zcash Community Forum, a fresh grant application has emerged which is aimed at making Zcash even more private on iPhone-based wallets. The author seeks a $25,000 grant in order to implement a private way of retrieving encrypted transaction memos.

Recent findings suggest that essentially, the proposal allows hiding which transactions customers have been looking up, which is a potential deanonymization vector. Considering how Zcash placese itself on the market, revealing any kind of external information is a step which might shorten the distance between a random transaction and a specific user.

In a recent development, the proposal itself won't touch the network or the blockchain behind it as is. It's an improvement of an SDK (Software Development Kit) that will allow developers to use tools that can help make Zcash more privacy-resilient.

According to recent reports, zcash transactions today contain encrypted data called memos. Various wallets read those memos in order to receive information about the transaction. The message itself stays encrypted, so is retrieved data, however, the query itself is not protected by any means which enables potential tracing.

Even when using Tor, the transaction ID stay out in the open and can be read by anyone.

With the integration of private information retrieval into SDK, hiding the query itself wil be easier, messages would be decrypted locally and wallets themselves will verify the returned information.

The first tests have already shown promising results. During testing in an iOS Simulator, the modified SDK managed to retrieve a 512-byte memo through an encrypted query, without revealing the transaction ID to the wallet server.

The developer expects the implementation of the proposal by January 30, 2027, with testing on physical iPhones and a public SDK release planned for the final stage.

However, the proposal is still seeking funding, and its actual adoption will depend on individual wallet developers.

A former professional athlete on selling real estate to other athletes

  • Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While it’s easy to get starstruck when working for an athlete or other high-profile client, Yohann Sangaré, an agent with eXp’s sports and entertainment division, discourages it. “You come as a problem solver, not a fan,” he said.

Sangaré, a French former professional basketball player who played for 16 years across Europe, sometimes avoids reading up too much about his athlete clients’ accomplishments in their prospective sports so that he can focus on the task at hand: Finding them the right home and advising them on large investments.

According to recent reports, sangaré came to the U.S. when he was hired to work for Tony Parker, his former teammate, in San Antonio, Texas; he started as a financial advisor for professional athletes. During COVID, he moved into real estate, specializing in finding homes for athletes instead.

Sangaré explains that the pros tend to make a lot of money for a short period of time, and for that reason they’re usually interested in buying investment properties (often right after they’ve found homes for themselves and their family members). A big part of their real estate agents’ job, then, is to keep their eyes on investment properties with the potential for strong returns.

Athletes have specific needs. “As a rookie, they’re just starting out, and they may not want to buy,” Sangaré told Taylor Anderson at eXpcon in Salt Lake City last month. Depending on the length of the contract, a rental might be a better idea. “There are times you tell people now’s not the right time to buy. If they feel you’re working in their best interests, they will trust you,” said Sangaré, who is part of eXp’s relatively latest sports and entertainment division (which several brokerages offer).

You have to be patient when working with athletes, he mentioned, since their situations are tied to ever-changing contracts; of course, players can be traded, and have to move rapidly. You also have to be prepared to wait and work with them as they grow in their careers.

Recent findings suggest that what you don’t have to be: A major follower of their particular sports. Sangaré admits that as a European, he doesn’t know much about football or baseball, but that doesn’t stop him from working with athletes in those sports. Sometimes not being starstruck helps him work with a more level head, he stated.

According to recent reports, but you do need to know the nuances of sports contracts. For example, some leagues, like the NBA, offer several-year guarantees, while others, like the NFL, don’t; housing options will vary based on those.

In a recent development, often the connection to an athlete client comes through their financial advisor or sports agent, Sangaré said. “The sports agent is always talking to the player, and he’ll know to reach out to you when someone gets traded,” he said.

It has been revealed that but that can be a long road. Sangaré stated it can take anywhere from five months to two years from starting a relationship with a sports agent to seeing any traction with a player, but you want to start that relationship early since once their clients do start to get traded, they’ll undoubtedly be approached by many other real estate agents. One practical tip he gives is going to the NBA Summer League in Las Vegas and taking agents out for coffee or lunch. “You have to be present where they’re present,” he said.

In a recent development, and when you do get connected to the client, make sure you don’t start with a sales pitch. “You can’t try to sell them something right away,” Sangaré mentioned; instead, you want to counsel them on how they can protect themselves and what they really need to know when buying a home — whether as an investment property or to live in.

  • Industry observers note that the refinance index increased 1% from the previous week and was 51% lower than the same week one year ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mortgage applications increased 6.1% from one week earlier, according to data from the Mortgage Bankers Association’s (MBA) weekly mortgage applications survey for the week ending November 20, 2026.

On an unadjusted basis, the Index increased 3% compared with the previous week.

Industry observers note that the refinance index increased 1% from the previous week and was 51% lower than the same week one year ago. The seasonally adjusted purchase index increased 10% from one week earlier. The unadjusted purchase index increased 5% compared with the previous week and was 16% lower than the same week one year ago.

According to recent reports, “Mortgage rates moved higher, with the 30-year fixed rate rising to 7.38%, its highest level in five weeks. While mortgage rates increased slightly on a weekly average basis, rates declined over the course of the week, which likely spurred purchase application activity,” said Joel Kan, CMB, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist. “Purchase applications reached their strongest weekly pace since September but remained well behind last year’s pace.”.

Sources indicate that kan added that a larger share of borrowers gravitated to ARM loans. The ARM share of activity accounted for 11.5% of applications, the highest share in more than a year, Kan noted.

“At 6.39%, the ARM mortgage rate was nearly a full percentage lower than the 30-year fixed rate last week. Refinance activity was flat over the week with conventional applications showing a small increase while VA refinances dropped more than 11%,” he remarked.

The refinance share of mortgage activity decreased to 40.1% of total applications from 41.1% the previous week. The adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) share of activity increased to 11.5% of total applications.

By product, the Federal Housing Administration (FHA) share of total applications decreased to 15.9% from 16.1% the week prior. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) share decreased to 12.4% from 12.8% the week prior. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) share of total applications remained unchanged at 0.5% from the week prior.

The average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with conforming loan balances ($832,750 or less) increased to 7.38% from 7.35%. Meanwhile, the average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages with jumbo loan balances decreased to 7.29% from 7.31%.

Industry observers note that the average contract interest rate for 30-year fixed-rate mortgages backed by the FHA decreased to 7.05% from 7.06% while rates for 15-year fixed-rate mortgages increased to 6.79% from 6.64%. The average contract interest rate for 5/1 ARMs slightly increased to 6.39% from 6.38%.

Xactus’s Mortgage Intent Index — which analyzes aggregated, anonymized credit-pull activity across the Xactus Intelligent Verification Platform — increased week-over-week to a reading of 97.8.

“Mortgage intent edged up approximately 2.2% week over week,” mentioned Thomas Lloyd, chief strategy officer at Xactus. “The uptick follows last week’s Veterans Day-suppressed reading, suggesting underlying borrower demand remains present even in a challenging rate environment.”.

Lloyd continued, “Early readings from the Daily Xactus Mortgage Intent Index offer some cautious optimism heading into Thanksgiving week — Monday’s reading of 65.9 reflects expected seasonal softness, but the year-over-year gap of approximately 16.5% is a notable improvement from the roughly 25% deficit seen in recent weeks.”.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the firm’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith remarked on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

According to recent reports, petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

Sources indicate that we’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

Owners cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it debuted publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of customers. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:00 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

In a recent development, elon Musk’s Space Exploration Technologies Corp. today received approval from the U.S. Federal Communications Commission to deploy up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to operate as data centers in orbit.

In a recent development, issued by the FCC’s Space Bureau under delegated authority, the order is described by the agency as “the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space.”.

It has been revealed that “By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr noted. “This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home.”.

Replying to Carr on X, Musk wrote that Starmind “will be a great asset to America and the world.”.

Sources indicate that under the terms of the approval, the Starmind satellites are to sit in six orbital shells, or altitude bands, between 500 and 1,002 kilometers, below the 2,000-kilometer ceiling in SpaceX’s original application. Most communications will run over optical links to other satellites, including those in the Starlink network. The license itself covers a backup Ka-band radio system for emergency telemetry, tracking and command.

It has been revealed that the approval does come with conditions. SpaceX’s orbital debris strategy was found to comply with the agency’s rules only for satellites below 600 kilometers, and four of the six shells sit above that line. Before deploying anything higher, SpaceX is required to file a modification application containing a final debris plan.

A request from the firm to retire some of those higher satellites into disposal orbits around Earth or the sun, rather than having them re-enter the atmosphere within five years, was deferred for lack of information.

Recent findings suggest that to keep the authorization, SpaceX has to have its first Starmind satellite in operation by Nov. 25, 2033. The schedule then calls for 100,000 satellites by 2035, 500,000 by 2038 and the full 1 million by 2040. Missing any of the deadlines would void the license.

Petitions to deny the application from Amazon.com Inc.’s Amazon Leo satellite business, Viasat Inc. and the American Astronomical Society were all rejected. In a March filing, Amazon had described the initiative as “a lofty ambition rather than a real plan.”.

In a recent development, according to the bureau, nothing in the FCC’s rules limits how many satellites a single constellation can include. Astronomers’ concerns about the satellites’ brightness in infrared were ruled to fall outside the scope of a radio license.

Industry observers note that spaceX first applied for the system in January, shortly before it acquired Musk’s artificial intelligence tech giant xAI Corp. Orbital data centers then featured in SpaceX’s pitch to investors ahead of its record initial public offering in June. Built around a space-optimized version of Nvidia Corp.’s Vera Rubin NVL72 rack-scale system, the first-generation Starmind satellite, known as AI1, could reach orbit as early as the third quarter of next year, according to Musk.

The competitors Carr referred to include Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin LLC, which applied in March for Project Sunrise, a planned network of up to 51,600 data center satellites. Starcloud Inc., a startup developing AI data centers in orbit, raised $250 million at a $2.3 billion valuation in August.

Shares of SpaceX closed up 1.3% today.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Inman ↗ Open Full Page

Sometimes the most valuable data is the house nobody bought

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (829 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Inman

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no.
  • According to recent reports, when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds.
  • But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Want to price more precisely? Canceled listing data in the MLS can reveal where buyers said no. Learn three steps to add failed listings to your next CMA.

According to recent reports, when agents sit down to price a listing, we know the drill: Pull the solds. Look at what’s coming soon, active and pending. Adjust for condition, location, square footage and amenities. Figure out where our house fits.

But there’s another category of data sitting right there in the MLS that we frequently overlook: the houses nobody bought.

Recent findings suggest that expired. Canceled. Withdrawn. Earlier in my career, I looked at these failed listings all the time. Then the market changed. When inventory became tight, and buyers were competing for homes, digging through failed listings often wasn’t necessary to determine where a property would sell.

Now the market is shifting again; pricing must be more precise, and I’m sharpening my approach by bringing an old tool back into my pricing process.

A sold comp tells us where a buyer stated yes, but a failed listing can help us figure out where buyers said no. And in a buyer-favored market, that’s valuable information.

According to recent reports, imagine you’re pricing a home, and the recent comparable sales range from $600,000 to $625,000. Then you expand your search.

It has been revealed that suddenly, you know considerably more than the sold comps alone told you. Other sellers have already tested the upper limits of pricing, and buyers responded. It’s essentially a series of pricing experiments someone else conducted for you — and they paid the carrying costs.

In a recent development, one of the most interesting things buried in MLS history is the pricing journey. A property might show a final list price of $649,000 and an eventual sale of $630,000. Dig deeper, and you may discover this:.

$725,000 → $699,000 → $675,000 → canceled → relisted at $649,000 → sold for $630,000.

Industry observers note that that’s a different story. The sale tells us what one buyer eventually paid. The listing history tells us buyers had previously rejected that house at $725,000, $699,000 and $675,000.

It also illustrates something sellers don’t always understand: Getting to the right price eventually isn’t necessarily the same as pricing correctly from the beginning. After months of market exposure and multiple reductions, buyers may stop asking, “Could this be the house?” They start asking, “What’s wrong with it?”.

It has been revealed that when I find a comparable property that sat for 90 days without selling, I want to know what did sell during those same 90 days. Sometimes we blame the market when the market was functioning just fine. Buyers were buying houses. They simply weren’t buying that one.

In a recent development, maybe they chose the renovated house at $640,000. Maybe they paid $650,000 for the better lot. They may have even paid more for another property because it offered something the failed listing didn’t. That’s useful information when you’re sitting across from a seller who believes buyers just need more time to appreciate their home.

If buyers repeatedly toured the property and purchased competing homes instead, the market may already have delivered its opinion.

Industry observers note that this is where agents have to resist oversimplifying the data. An expired listing isn’t automatic proof that a house was overpriced, and a canceled listing certainly isn’t either.

Listings fail for all sorts of reasons. Sellers change their minds. Job transfers fall through. Repairs surface. Agents get fired. Sometimes a seller receives a perfectly acceptable offer and decides not to move.

According to recent reports, so, investigate. Call the previous agent. I might simply say:.

“I’m pricing a similar property and noticed yours was on the market last year. Is there anything you can tell me about the activity or why the seller decided not to continue?”.

It has been revealed that twenty-seven showings and no offers tell me something. Two showings in four months tells me something different.

There’s one more number worth considering: the cost of the pricing journey.

Find a house that started high, sat, reduced, expired, relisted and eventually sold. Then compare it with similar homes that entered the market closer to where buyers were actually buying.

Sellers often view aspirational pricing as a no-risk strategy: “We can always come down.” Technically, that’s true. But time isn’t free, and neither is market perception.

The next time you’re preparing a CMA in a shifting or buyer-favored market:.

We’re very good at studying success in real estate. But as pricing gets harder, I’ve found myself returning to an old habit: studying the failures, too. Sold listings tell us where buyers have been willing to say yes. Sometimes the house nobody bought is the one that tells us exactly where they started saying no.

Roxanne Hale is the associate broker of the Art House Team, brokered by RealtySouth in Birmingham, Alabama. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really major step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

According to recent reports, for the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

It has been revealed that nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles noted.

Boles stated the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”.

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”.

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “notable step toward undersea superiority.”.

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson mentioned in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”.

Next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

The maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The manufacturer is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The firm has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

Darryl Davis Seminars Inc.’s multi-million dollar federal trademark infringement lawsuit against Epique Realty, which accuses the virtual brokerage of unlawfully using the POWER AGENT® brand in its nationwide operations, is headed to court next week.

Sources indicate that during the first week of December, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Upcoming York will hold a hearing on a motion for a preliminary injunction filed by Darryl Davis and his firm that would bar Epique Realty, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, from using the POWER AGENT trademark.

Recent findings suggest that originally filed in late June, the lawsuit alleges that Houston-based Epique Realty adopted the POWER AGENT name and “built an entire brand architecture around it” despite being put on notice and asked to stop, according to the announcement. In addition to Epique Realty, the lawsuit also lists Joshua Miller, Janice Delcid, Christopher Miller, XYZ Corps 1-10 and John and Jane Does 1-10 as defendants.

Darryl Davis Seminars says it has used the POWER AGENT mark continuously since 1993 through The POWER Program, which it describes as the real estate industry’s oldest and longest-running agent training and coaching platform.

Sources indicate that “POWER AGENT® has been our name since 1993, and both it and THE POWER PROGRAM® are registered trademarks,” Davis told HousingWire. “The law expects a trademark owner to protect its marks. We have for decades, and we will keep doing so. Because the matter is pending, I will let our court filings speak to the rest.”.

In October, Epique filed a counterclaim asking for a ruling from the court that Davis’s trademark registrations of Power Agent programs do not give his firm exclusive rights to the word “power” and that this does not give Davis or his manufacturer the rights to a family of “Power” trademarks. Epique is also asking the court to force Davis and his firm to prove likely confusing for each expression of “Power” Epique was accused of. Epique is also seeking rulings from the court that its current uses of PowerFlex and PowerCon, do not infringe on Davis’s trademarks and that it is not liable “merely because an independently controlled agent or third party used POWER-formative wording.”.

Industry observers note that epique emphasized in the filing that its agents are independent contractors and that the firm does not hold passwords for agents’ personal social media accounts in order to edit or delete content, nor does it review agents’ social media posts or websites before they are published. This contradicts Davis’s complaint, which alleges that the brokerage’s independent contractor agreement requires agents to submit marketing or advertising posts for approval prior to publication. Additionally, the company said that under state law in Texas, where Epique is headquartered, the firm is only responsible for ensuring that advertising content produced by agents complies with state rules.

In a filing earlier this month, Davis largely denied Epique’s counterclaims, namely that he is trying to trademark the word “Power” by itself and he and his firm rejected Epique’s request that the court declares that Darryl Davis Seminars does not own the word “power” exclusively and that it does not have an across-the-board monopoly over trademarks containing the word. Throughout the filing, Davis maintained that Epique infringed on his firm’s trademarks and he asked the court to reject Epique’s counter claims.

Sources indicate that this news was first reported by Inman. Epique Realty did not immediately returned HousingWire’s request for comment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Donald Keene Center, a Columbia University institute, had Digital Silk rebuild its site as a mobile-friendly archive in English and Japanese.

According to recent reports, UPCOMING YORK, Nov. 26, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Donald Keene Center of Japanese Culture at Columbia University has launched a new bilingual website with Digital Silk. The site turns more than 30 years of lectures, events and programs into an archive that students and the public can browse on any device.

According to recent reports, the project addresses a problem shared by many university centers, museums and libraries. Their history is often their strongest proof of authority, yet it sits on aging websites where few people can find it.

A Legacy Hidden on a Desktop-Era SiteThe Center was named for Donald Keene, the late Columbia scholar and translator of Japanese literature. For more than three decades, it has hosted lectures, book talks, symposia and programs such as the Sen Lectures and a translation prize.

According to recent reports, that record had piled up on a website built for desktop browsing, with no clear way to explore it. On a phone, the site was difficult to use. The old site also reinforced a narrow reputation. The public mainly saw the Center as a literary institution, while much of its programming reached into film, the arts and culture.

In a recent development, letting the Scholarship LeadDigital Silk started with little more than a logo, Columbia's brand guidelines and a request for a conservative academic look. Rather than add visual effects, the team let the scholarship lead. The design uses a clear editorial hierarchy and a few quiet video moments, so the site reads as scholarly but not cold.

The site is now organized around how visitors explore: About, Programs, Events and Lectures, the Archive and News. Major programs, including the Sen Lectures, the translation prize and Columbia student support, each have a dedicated home. Visitors can filter events by lectures, book talks, workshops and symposia.

Digital Silk migrated more than 30 years of historical material into a dedicated archive of lectures, events and translated works. Consistent page templates for programs, lectures, events and resources let the Center present its film and arts programming as clearly as its literary work.

The Japanese version is a full site, not a translated summary. Typography and layouts were designed for both scripts, and language signals tell search engines which version to show each audience. Contact and newsletter forms give the Center a direct line to its audience, and search optimization on the main pages prepares the site for future discoverability.

"Academic institutions often assume a modern website means more motion and more marketing. For the Keene Center, it meant the opposite," said Ana Margarida Meira, VP at Digital Silk. "Thirty years of lectures was the most persuasive thing they had. The work was to make that record easy to find, in both languages, for a team of essentially one person.".

Full report available at https://www.digitalsilk.com/press/how-digital-silk-rebuilt-the-website-for-columbia-universitys-japanese-culture-center/.

For other university centers and cultural nonprofits, the project serves as a reminder that before a redesign adds latest features, it should make existing scholarship visible, organized and readable on a phone.

Explore Digital Silk's university website design services for academic centers, departments and libraries.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.
  • The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing.
  • In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Connecticut is the latest state to help first responders reach their homeownership goals with assistance for down payments and closing costs.

The “First Responders’ Time to Own” program gives state and local police officers, full-time and volunteer firefighters and emergency medical service personnel $25,000 in forgivable assistance through the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority (CHFA) and the Connecticut Department of Housing. To qualify, first responders must have completed two years of service and purchase a primary residence within the community they serve.

In addition to down payment and closing cost help, the program gives applicants a 0.125 percentage point interest rate reduction on their CHFA first mortgage.

“Connecticut’s police officers, firefighters and EMS personnel dedicate themselves to protecting our families and communities, and we want to make sure they have the opportunity to build their own futures here,” Governor Ned Lamont said in a prepared statement on Tuesday. “By helping reduce one of the biggest barriers to buying a home, we’re investing in the people who serve our state and the communities that depend on them.”.

The program is part of Public Act 26-12, a state bill that aims to increase the number of first responders with a number of incentives, including college tuition reimbursement and improved labor protections.

“The people who protect and serve our communities should be able to afford to live in those communities, and this program with help them do it,” Comptroller Sean Scanlon said in a written statement. “Helping the people who put their lives on the line for us every day buy their first home is literally the least we can do, and I’m proud to have worked with Governor Lamont and legislature to make this a reality.”.

It has been revealed that seven other states also have down payment assistance programs for first responders. Florida, Nevada, Georgia and South Carolina provide flat amounts, ranging from $10,000 to $35,000. Texas, Maryland and Ohio’s programs are percentage-based and offer assistance ranging from 2.5 percent to 5 percent of the purchase price.

The terms of each program vary. Most states forgive the assistance after five to seven years, but Nevada requires homebuyers to repay the funds within 30 years. And like Connecticut, Ohio also offers a 0.25 percent mortgage rate discount.

“Homeownership offers more than a place to live. It creates stability, strengthens connections to community and provides an opportunity to build wealth over time,” CHFA CEO and Executive Director Nandini Natarajan mentioned in an announcement. “Through First Responders’ Time to Own, we’re helping the people who answer the call for our communities take an important step toward achieving their own homeownership goals.”.

First responders often fall through the cracks of housing assistance programs because they don’t earn enough to afford market-rate housing but earn too much to qualify for federal housing vouchers.

Recent findings suggest that inman explored this dilemma last September in a feature on workforce housing in resort towns like Jackson Hole, Vail and Tahoe. These towns can’t operate without first responders and other essential workers in the hospitality and retail sectors. However, rental and for-sale home prices have far outpaced what these workers earn, forcing them to commute long distances from more affordable towns or take on second and third jobs to survive.

The solution for some of these towns has been investing in workforce housing, which caps prices for households that earn between 60 percent and 120 percent of their area’s AMI. Most workforce housing is rent-only, but some states are extending the programs to include for-sale properties.

Sources indicate that “I think the fact that workforce housing can be necessary or is a thing in the first place is really an indictment of the state of housing affordability in the country today,” Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel remarked. “I think it’s important to ground any conversation about workforce and affordable housing in that reality. It’s a market failure and a policy failure that someone could be a doctor, a teacher or another kind of professional and cannot afford to pay the market rent or own a home outright.”.

Windermere Principal Economist Jeff Tucker said workforce housing isn’t a panacea for affordability and works within an ecosystem of other housing and economic policies, such as upzoning, to create a more equitable market.

Tucker’s comments came a month after the Senate introduced the ROAD to Housing Act of 2025, and three months before the House introduced the Housing for the 21st Century Act. The bills were eventually combined into the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed in June.

Recent findings suggest that “A broad package of necessary reforms to make more housing construction possible in much of the country is a really key component of a long-term solution to the housing affordability challenges we face,” Tucker said. “Our current housing shortage took years to develop. So it’ll take years to build our way out of it.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.
  • Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with substantial financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.
  • For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with substantial financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The organization started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

According to recent reports, beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

Sources indicate that for Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond firm agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Recent findings suggest that listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

Industry observers note that the five-year-old manufacturer was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei mentioned Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he stated.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the organization.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

Industry observers note that what’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has mentioned it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will patch the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As demand for major crypto assets has increased, Ethereum remains on hold amid growing market fear and uncertainty, while exchange activities across the broad crypto market are showing a bearish trend.

While Ethereum remains one of the most affected cryptocurrencies during the prolonged crypto market volatility, the latest data from the crypto analytics platform CryptoQuant shows a massive slowdown in its exchange outflows.

Amid growing market fear, Ethereum outflows from Binance over the last month have hit a historic low as investors continue to move fewer ETH tokens away from the world’s largest crypto exchange, Binance.

The data shows that about 3.58 million ETH have been withdrawn from Binance over the last 30 days, marking an all-time low in Ethereum outflows on the exchange.

Further data shows that the decline has come as Ethereum continues to struggle to stabilize its price and continues to weaken, trading around the $1,700 mark.

It is vital to note that the decline in exchange outflows is expected, considering the growing market weakness and negative shift in investor sentiment over the period.

However, the metric has drawn different attention from market participants, given expectations that the massive security breach Binance suffered should trigger large withdrawals from the exchange.

Although blockchain trackers recently identified multiple large Ethereum withdrawals by the Binance hacker, it appears that the moves did not materialize into increased Ethereum outflows.

Apart from the attackers' withdrawals, it appears that Ethereum holders on the exchange did not respond to the attack in the conventional way, as security incidents like this often make investors more cautious and wary about keeping their assets on the exchange.

While this typically prompts them to transfer the assets into private wallets where they have greater control, it appears that Ethereum holders remained comfortable with keeping their funds on the exchange.

Breaking: BOXABL financial filing demonstrates cash burn and scaling risk

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

💡 Key Takeaways
  • [Editor’s note: HousingWire TBD author Dan Oppenheim contributed financial analysis and insight for this report.].
  • Factory-built housing’s promise of a not-so-distant brighter future has always been compelling.
  • Forever, it seems, it has carried an “always within five years” sense of inevitability, stuck in limbo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: HousingWire TBD author Dan Oppenheim contributed financial analysis and insight for this report.].

Factory-built housing’s promise of a not-so-distant brighter future has always been compelling.

Forever, it seems, it has carried an “always within five years” sense of inevitability, stuck in limbo. Build homes faster, with less waste, fewer labor constraints, greater consistency, in conditioned indoor offsite space, and at costs low enough to bend asking-price curves toward households priced out of homeownership.

It has been revealed that the arrival of housing’s future, however, seems caught in the unforgiving calculus of time and space’s infinite divisibility. Progress happens and promises soar, but the ultimate goal of powering United States home development and construction with modern manufacturing going concerns keeps falling short, trapped in an echo chamber of not-exactly-here and not-quite-yet.

Sources indicate that the rub has always been turning the promise of housing’s future into a business that can reliably produce homes, deliver them to customers, cover its costs, and generate enough cash to keep doing it. Many homebuilding business leaders who’ve tried a lot of things and kept doing what works are apt to think of all that as homebuilding’s never-ending siren’s song, one that, should it emerge, should be dispelled as a wishful-thinking distraction.

BOXABL, the Las Vegas-based modular housing manufacturer that completed its Nasdaq listing in July, now faces that test amid mounting difficulties, including self-inflicted ones.

Its November 16, 2026, quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission provides data to address questions that experienced homebuilding executives have long raised about factory-based housing ventures and that they have expressed about BOXABLE.

Sources indicate that can a manufacturer achieve sufficient production volume to absorb fixed costs? Can it coordinate factory output with site readiness, permitting, installation, and customer financing? And can it sustain those operations when capital is expensive, construction inputs remain inflation-pressured, and affordability-constrained homebuyers are wavering for any of half a dozen good reasons?

BOXABL’s filing shows progress in generating orders. It also shows that the company’s operating model still falls far short of demonstrating the economic soundness, scalability, and durability required to sustain a residential construction business. The company’s options have not disappeared, but they have narrowed, and time is quickly passing. Management has less room and less time to demonstrate the business’s financial sustainability.

Recent findings suggest that BOXABL’s Form 10-Q, filed on November 16 for the quarter ended September 30, reports $14 million in unrestricted cash, down from $29 million at year-end 2025. During the most recent quarter, the company used $6 million in cash for operations, down from $8.4 million in the third quarter of 2025. This translates to a cash burn rate of about $2 million per month, so the $14 million of unrestricted cash on hand as of the end of Q3 represents seven months of operations.

That metric doesn’t precisely forecast when BOXABL might run out of cash. Instead, it demonstrates the relationship between available resources and BOXABL’s most recent cash-burn rate.

In Note 4 of the filing, the organization states: “Substantial doubt about the Company’s ability to continue as a going concern exists.”.

It has been revealed that is the disclosure a prediction of failure? Technically and officially, no. Management identifies continued cost controls, accelerated Casita deliveries and sales, and additional equity financing as measures intended to address the uncertainty. There’s no ambiguity that those measures must deliver results even as the company continues to consume cash.

BOXABL reported 209 net orders for Casitas in Q3, bringing its total for the first nine months to 362 net orders. As of September 30, the company had 679 Casitas in backlog, representing approximately $45 million in potential revenue. Those figures indicate customer interest but raise what are arguably the most notable questions for BOXABL – how legitimate the orders are, how much of the backlog will convert to revenue, and when that conversion will occur.

The point is that while most homebuilders count a signed contract as an order only after the customer has satisfied mortgage qualification, BOXABL notes that 85 Casitas in the backlog (and recorded as an order during a recent quarter) are pending feasibility studies to assess whether the customer’s site can support installation.

In a recent development, in addition, another 311 units in the backlog were associated with orders that were one to two years old, raising questions about whether they will convert to revenue. Together, these 396 units, the 85 units that still require feasibility assessment, and the 311 older orders represent 58% of the firm’s reported backlog of 679 units.

That disconnect is not merely a scheduling matter. Backlog becomes financially meaningful only when orders reliably convert to completed sales. For BOXABL, that conversion process remains insufficiently demonstrated, likely raising investor doubts about the authenticity of the orders and the cleanliness of the backlog.

During the first nine months of 2026, BOXABL generated $2.629 million in revenue, up from $588,000 a year earlier. It delivered 36 Casitas, compared with eight in the prior-year period. However, cost of goods sold totaled $13.78 million, resulting in a gross loss of $11.15 million.

It has been revealed that approximately $10 million of those costs were inventory valuation adjustments and allowances for slow-moving or obsolete inventory. These accounting charges should not be mistaken for the direct manufacturing cost of the 36 delivered units. Nevertheless, they reflect the economic consequences of producing and carrying inventory that would not generate sufficient revenue.

Looking at BOXABL’s production costs, excluding obsolete inventory, inventory adjustments, scrapped inventory, warranty expense, and allocations such as stock-based compensation expense, the company reported a cost of Casitas sold of $2.075 million for the first nine months of the year, compared with $2.629 million in revenue, leaving an adjusted gross profit of approximately $550,000.

Sources indicate that however, when assessing BOXABL’s ability to produce Casitas at a profit, it’s difficult to ignore the message and significance of the largest component of the inventory charge, $7.4 million, which represented an adjustment to reduce the carrying value of the inventory to its realizable value. Although that charge affects more inventory than was sold in the first nine months of 2026, it is unclear whether BOXABL’s newly produced inventory would sell at or above its cost of production.

It has been revealed that BOXABL is not currently scaled – from a management perspective – for this low level of volume and revenue. Its $2.629 million in revenue for the first nine months of 2026 was dwarfed by $15.553 million in operating expenses, which included general and administrative expenses, sales and marketing, and research and development. BOXABL has developed a product and a manufacturing system.

By any measure, however, its reported results have not yet demonstrated that the system can operate at volumes and margins sufficient to sustain it.

It has been revealed that perhaps the most revealing figures concern inventory. At September 30, BOXABL reported $17.645 million in inventory for 388 units, including 198 finished Casitas and 190 work-in-process units. While this inventory balance may not sound like much, it represents 6.7x the revenue generated during the first nine months of 2026. That $17.645 million of inventory is also after adjustments (write-downs), as the cost to produce the inventory was $10 million higher.

It has been revealed that management explains that significant finished inventory remains on hand because customer sites are not ready for delivery and installation. Delays stem from feasibility studies, permitting, land preparation, and other deployment requirements. That disclosure addresses a problem that residential construction executives understand.

In a recent development, manufacturing a housing unit is only one part of delivering a completed home. Factory efficiencies cannot eliminate the complexities of land preparation, local regulations, logistics, installation, and customer financing.

According to recent reports, when manufacturing and delivery schedules diverge, capital remains tied up in products that cannot yet generate revenue. Inventory must be stored, managed, and sometimes modified to meet changing specifications. BOXABL’s filing reports that approximately $7.1 million of finished goods was reclassified as work in process in 2025 to accommodate modifications for California’s modular housing requirements.

None of this establishes that the manufacturing approach cannot work. It highlights that the economic benefits of industrialized construction must be measured across the entire housing delivery process, not merely the time or labor required to assemble a unit in a factory.

It has been revealed that notably, BOXABL announced that on October 27th, it signed a contract to sell 20 Casitas to Kaw Gaming, Inc., a Native American tribe in Oklahoma, and just yesterday issued a press release saying that shipment of those orders began last week, with more shipping this week. If that short timeline from order to shipment indicates that it is shipping finished inventory, that would certainly be a positive sign for deliveries, cash flow, and inventory management.

BOXABL’s July Nasdaq listing provided access to public equity markets but not the large infusion of unrestricted operating cash the manufacturer likely hoped for. After shareholder redemptions, the business combination generated approximately $47.2 million in gross trust proceeds. About $31.1 million was allocated to obligations under an equity prepaid forward transaction, and additional closing costs reduced the net increase in unrestricted cash to approximately $6.5 million.

According to recent reports, the tech giant established an at-the-market stock (ATM) offering program on September 25th, authorizing up to $100 million in equity sales. As of November 6, the company had generated about $646,000 in gross proceeds from the stock issuance. Notably, the program was initiated in late September, when the stock traded just under $4 per share.

The tech giant issued very little equity in the six weeks after initiating the program (when the stock was at a higher price, relative to the November 24th closing price of $0.95), but some of this likely reflects restrictions on issuance during the quiet period before reporting results for the quarter.

Management believes that existing cash, product sales, forward-transaction proceeds, and future equity sales can fund operations for the next 12 months. The company also reported approximately $2.7 million in additional forward-transaction receipts from October 1 to November 6. Given recent trends, it appears unlikely that the company will become cash flow positive from operations in the near term. In addition, with the stock now trading below $1 per share, issuing equity at this level would not generate significant capital and would send a worrisome signal about the company’s liquidity.

Sources indicate that those resources provide some financial flexibility, but the gap between authorization to raise capital and actually securing it remains significant. BOXABL can continue cutting costs, seek additional financing or strategic partners, focus on markets with more favorable delivery conditions, and prioritize converting finished inventory into revenue.

It has been revealed that each alternative involves trade-offs. Cutting expenses preserves cash but can constrain efforts to accelerate deliveries. Slowing production reduces near-term spending but weakens overhead absorption. Raising equity extends the operating runway but may dilute existing shareholders. Narrowing the tech giant’s product or geographic focus could improve execution while postponing the scale central to its original economic proposition.

These are not necessarily signs of an inevitable endpoint. They are choices facing a capital-dependent manufacturer whose commercial progress has not yet matched the resources needed to sustain operations. The longer that gap persists, the more difficult it becomes to preserve every element of the company’s original ambitions.

It has been revealed that experienced homebuilding leaders approach industrialized construction ventures with both interest and skepticism, for good reason. They recognize the efficiency potential of factory production. They also know that housing profitability depends on capital allocation, customer demand, regulatory compliance, construction execution, and cash conversion.

Those disciplines become more demanding when borrowing costs remain elevated, input costs are under pressure, and homebuyers demand concessions to overcome affordability constraints.

Recent findings suggest that BOXABL’s financial challenges do not invalidate industrialized construction. Different approaches to modular production, panelization, and off-site manufacturing entail distinct capital requirements and operating models.

But its latest disclosures illustrate how difficult it can be to translate manufacturing innovation into a financially sustainable housing enterprise. The next several quarters will show whether BOXABL can accelerate deliveries, reduce inventory exposure, improve manufacturing margins, and secure sufficient liquidity without further constraining its flexibility.

The manufacturer has made some progress in slowing its cash outflow, and those improvements deserve recognition. It also continues to operate at a substantial loss, consuming considerably more cash than its products generate and depending on financial and operational improvements that remain uncertain.

Sources indicate that BOXABL’s challenge is no longer primarily to persuade investors and customers that industrialized housing could transform residential construction. It is to demonstrate, through completed deliveries, disciplined working-capital management, and eventually positive cash flow, that its approach can sustain a business.

In a recent development, the company’s recent hiring may indicate that it’s doing all it can to deliver on this. Since September 15th, the company has hired Larry King as Chief Financial Officer, Heather Clayton as Chief Accounting Officer, Josef Elimlich to oversee sales strategy and the structure and performance of the sales organization, and Antonio Gonzalez as director of home delivery. While the company likely should have had the right people in these roles some time ago, the hires may indicate that it recognizes its challenges and is working to resolve them.

In homebuilding, being built for difficult conditions means more than having a promising product or innovative manufacturing process. It means having an operating model that can produce, deliver, and earn its way forward when capital is expensive, buyers are cautious, and the market offers little forgiveness for execution problems.

That’s a standard BOXABL, founded in 2017 and boasting having raised more than $230 million from more than 50,000 investors, now must meet. Otherwise, it will join scores of prior valiant, promising, deeply-funded ventures that got caught in the echo chamber of not-exactly-here and not-quite-yet.

  • Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 24, 2026 at 9:53 am.

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid swiftly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Recent findings suggest that underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he noted.

It has been revealed that he founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

Recent findings suggest that “I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

Recent findings suggest that for Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

Recent findings suggest that “I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he said. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

In a recent development, after graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

According to recent reports, “I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd remarked. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

According to recent reports, he wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who noted the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he noted, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd mentioned, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion firm Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

According to recent reports, A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

Sources indicate that while the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The manufacturer landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Recent findings suggest that team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd said he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Industry observers note that endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd stated there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

Sources indicate that the manufacturer now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

Breaking: So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.
  • Recent findings suggest that nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn.
  • Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a massive decision to make in the next few weeks: take the manufacturer’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.

Recent findings suggest that nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a massive decision to make in the next few weeks: take the manufacturer’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman declared the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The tech giant expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

According to recent reports, microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

According to recent reports, all of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in upcoming hires.

Sources indicate that the worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the company decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a tech giant right now?

Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

Industry observers note that one of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

In a recent development, but it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one company.

It has been revealed that hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more notable than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

The jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

According to recent reports, AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI firm today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Industry observers note that hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual firm. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software company.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.

Software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

Sources indicate that the true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue rapidly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

The bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

Industry observers note that one venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

There are three fundraising paths.

According to recent reports, 1) Think VERY major, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a company that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

In a recent development, 3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

There are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

It has been revealed that whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Significant Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a latest role, a company of their own or a year with their family.

#133556. Breaking: How real estate agents handle proof of funds and disclosures
