UPDATED 20:46 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul today signed legislation that will impose a five-year ban on children’s toys powered by artificial intelligence chatbots, amid fears that dolls, robots and stuffed animals might be leading children astray or discussing X-rated themes.

“It’s my job to put Latest York families first,” remarked Hochul, who explained as a mother and grandmother the matter is “deeply personal.” Hochul added that some of the wayward toys on the market at the moment have engaged children in “inappropriate conversations,” while some may also manipulate a child’s feelings or put their privacy at risk.

“This is a warning that there are toys out there that could be harmful to your children,” the governor mentioned. “When tech companies and unregulated AI pose a threat to our kids and our babies, you bet I’m going to have something to say about it.”.

In a recent development, though dangerous dolls manipulating innocent children may sound like the plot of Hollywood movie, recent tests of certain chatbot-powered toys have become a real cause for concern. When journalists at NBC News tested the Pixie Paw, an AI-powered plush cat toy marketed to children aged three and older, it reportedly shared stories of massacres, gang rape and firing squads in what was described as graphic detail.

Other tests have shown some of the toys can become very convincing when trying to persuade the young user that they are human. “Parents have enough to worry about,” remarked Hochul, who was also aware some of the smart toys have encouraged kids to jump out of windows.

State senator Andrew Gounardes applauded the move, saying that modern life seems to be mimicking science fiction of days gone by. He invoked an episode of the “Twilight Zone that featured the Talky Tina doll, an insidious, possessed toy that tried to persuade a young girl to murder her strict stepfather.

Latest York Attorney General Letitia James explained that the toys being put on the market is reckless when they clearly expose “young people to inappropriate content and put “their mental health at risk.” She added, “We won’t allow our children’s health to become the collateral damage of big tech.”.

Hochul has been vocal about the dangers of AI for some time, recently imposing the first statewide moratorium on fresh data centers and last month signing a bill titled “AI Chatbot Restrictions for Minors,” which will prohibit firms from developing chatbots that feature elements that could be harmful to minors.

#133530. How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1888 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech 📈 Bullish 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

How the surge in AI-discovered bugs is straining Microsoft security and threatening tech stability

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.
  • Sources indicate that it has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do.
  • Now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Angela Gunn on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:25 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:25 am.

Sources indicate that it has come to the attention of the general public this month that adversaries successfully adopt technology a lot faster than defenders do. This has nothing to do with the willingness of defenders to try. It has everything to do with the ancient truth that to succeed, defenders have to get it right every time but adversaries only have to get it right occasionally.

Now multiply “every time” and “occasionally” by AI. Do you like that math? Does anyone?

Recent findings suggest that the disastrous update that broke Teams, Outlook, SharePoint and other packages was not a direct attack by AI-wielding bad guys. Nor was the FAA outage. Nor were most of the outage events of the past few weeks, though who can say what’s up with those European Union refrigerators.

No. The true AI-driven mayhem has been predicated for several months now not on powerful new AI-honed attacks, but on an absolute deluge of bugs of relatively low severity that Microsoft and other defenders with a formal patch process aren’t built to process.

The question is whether traditional patch programs can adapt their processes to handle the deluge. Microsoft’s is MAPP (Microsoft Active Protections Program), to which the firm has been committed for nearly two decades. If the industry-spanning events of the past few weeks are any indication, these programs can’t.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella noted Wednesday at the New York Times DealBook Summit that last week’s Microsoft 365 outage came from a latent bug and wasn’t directly tied to AI, but he warned that AI-driven patching could bring more instability.

He elaborated in a separate appearance on CNBC the same day, saying the flood of patches being applied to older infrastructure is making systems less stable.

AI has “allowed us to find these bugs and fix these bugs, but that means you’ve got to then patch them, and that creates instability,” Nadella said, when asked by Jim Cramer about a string of recent outages at United, Schwab, Chase and other organizations.

Industry observers note that some context: MAPP turned 18 this year. The program, run by the MSRC (Microsoft Security Response Center), handles outreach to partner companies that gain early access to information on the bugs in advance of each month’s Patch Tuesday release. In-house, it coordinates the patch release process, just as the larger MSRC organization helps coordinate the handling of bug reports from external finders.

MSRC also runs point on prioritizing patches of the worst bugs through its SSIRP (Software and Services Incident Response Plan) program, itself dating to 2004. In its time, it was an industry leader in how companies can efficiently get their arms around bad bugs.

MAPP in its own way is similarly remarkable. It has undergone a few traumas over the years, usually when a partner breaks confidence and leaks the advance details it receives. In 2025, after attacks on SharePoint raised suspicions of a leak from the program, Microsoft stopped giving Chinese companies early access. But MAPP continues to tick along in a way that would make any program manager proud. Other companies have their own version of MAPP / MSRC, as do community efforts such as those supporting Linux.

Industry observers note that full disclosure: I’m a former MSRC employee who learned about MAPP at the knee of the program’s principals. I subsequently tracked patch releases at a manufacturer partnered with MAPP at its highest (Validate) level, which means I was privy to the 14-day multi-stage run-up to each month’s release. I admire and respect the program… and I’m afraid that in the AI-finder era, it’s in major, big trouble.

Let’s look at the numbers for Microsoft.

Since January 2021, Microsoft has issued patches for an estimated 10,319 CVEs. (I use estimated numbers throughout this analysis because there are various ways of counting such things, including whether or not the patch accrues to an application such as Edge, which actually relies on the Chromium project for its fixes. Other analysts arrive at larger or smaller counts.).

In a recent development, over half of those — 5,383 CVEs — are 2026 releases, 5,128 of which were addressed since April. In comparison, 2025’s full-year CVE total was 1,180.

According to recent reports, what happened in April? As nearly as analysis can determine, the floodgates opened and finders (security researchers) started barraging the tech giant with reports.

The first quarter of 2026 saw 255 CVEs addressed over three months. April had 163, May 132; in June the number jumped to 209. In July it was off to the races with 575 CVEs. In October, the monthly count topped 1,400.

In a recent development, most of these bugs aren’t coming from the usual security stalwarts. They’re coming from new finders, they’re coming in with multiple simultaneous finders not believed to be working together, and they’re coming in relatively weak.

Though the overall volume has skyrocketed, the number per month of bugs under active exploit in the wild — the notorious “zero-days” — hasn’t increased proportionally.

Recent findings suggest that moreover, average bug severity has in fact decreased. Until 2026, the average CVSS severity score for all bugs tended to hover around 7.8 (out of 10) each month. In 2026, that’s dropped to approximately 7.4 as of September — not garbage finds, but the sort of thing that doesn’t scramble the jets.

Recent findings suggest that no surge in zero-days and a drop in severity — that’s good news. The problem is the volume.

Once bugs are received by Microsoft, each goes through a MAPP-helmed, multi-team process of investigation and patch development.

Recent findings suggest that since many products have several versions still in support, that often means that multiple teams within each product group are asked to ingest a bug report, replicate the problem, devise and test a fix, ensure the fix doesn’t trigger other problems or inadvertently point to a similar bug elsewhere in the product and ready it for mass consumption. Even AI slop has to be taken seriously, just in case.

Meanwhile, MAPP is the traffic cop for the entire release, working with each team to ascertain patches are ready, understand the nature of the bugs and what can be safely communicated to partners and the public, and ready the processes that make the second Tuesday of each month a festival of downloads and reboots. From where we stand right now, it’s all fairly… hand-crafted.

In theory the process is automatable to some extent, though the success of that effort so far in light of recent events is debatable. But high volume also leads to other problems, such as exposing information on incomplete patching.

For instance, Microsoft has recently patched Office bugs that apply to both Windows and Mac, but patches have initially only been available for Windows versions.

Microsoft’s release-day information about such bugs — patching Windows versions while asking Apple customers to monitor Microsoft communications for news of their own patch — alerts the world, including eager adversaries, that the flaw exists. Apple customers just have to hope no adversaries exploit it while their patch is pending.

More broadly, many of the steps in the current patching process involve judgment calls, not processes that scale well or that can reliably be handled by existing AI-driven systems. In Microsoft’s case, MAPP is a remarkably small team of humans and, being security folk at Microsoft, they’re not always the loudest or most popular voice in Redmond.

Add the mercurial nature of finders, who may or may not provide full details on their bugs (ask any MSRC person how often they receive a crash dump and a demand for payment) and may or may not disclose their finds publicly if they don’t feel they’re getting sufficient response.

Do not add the kind of defender staffing needed to handle a massive increase in volume — either in MAPP or in the individual product groups building the actual patches — because in the AI era, it’s likely the companies won’t add it either.

According to recent reports, the cracks are showing. Microsoft has been compelled to issue OOB (out-of-band) releases and servicing updates monthly since July, often within just a few days of the original release.

It has been revealed that OOBs are important enough to merit release outside the usual patch cadence, often because there’s a security glitch involved, but they’re tough on administrators already wading through a slew of regularly scheduled patching. With volumes high, patch testers may rush or elide certain steps, such as checking that a fix doesn’t break something deeper in the system.

Recent findings suggest that nadella told the DealBook audience this week that a patch for a critical bank system might once have been tested for a week. Now, he said, the patch “needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild. So that’s going to create instability.”.

Think of MAPP as Mariners catcher Dan Wilson in 2001: a pro handling a staff of skilled human pitchers, one pitch at a time. Now it’s 2026, and the pitchers have been swapped for a bank of mediocre pitching machines all slinging fastballs at … 2026-era Dan Wilson.

Recent findings suggest that here, again, AI can’t fix a system that requires defenders to catch every pitch. Secondary lines of defense that have worked in the past — for instance, the requirement by various regulatory programs that enterprises ascertain that patches are safe for their own systems — rely heavily on companies sending out the soundest possible patches.

Managed service providers might at least make sure that patches are flagged to customers as available, relevant and urgent. But they’re in no position to do much more than trust that what’s shipped is safe to deploy and react when things go wrong.

Even that gets harder when a bug kneecaps the security tools they depend on. Last week’s Microsoft 365 outage affected parts of Microsoft Defender that interact with Exchange Online.

It’s not just Microsoft, of course. The Linux community is seriously suffering, and both Apple and (especially) Google have struggled with patch-release quality in 2026 as evidenced by their own emergency updates and post-release device instability reports. Industry-wide, ecosystems built around reliable, transparent patch cadences and patch-development processes have never seemed more in danger of being overwhelmed.

What needs to happen? Sure, build those AI systems; the marketing people will be pleased. It’ll speed up some parts of the process. But a system capable of replicating, every time, the human judgment calls that go into the patch-release process isn’t going to magically create itself; people have to create it.

Is there some chance that the deluge will ebb — that researchers and their tools will at some point finally find all the bugs in all the world’s products?

Sources indicate that it’s a pretty thought, and some relief may eventually come. When more and more unrelated finders turn up the same bug, it gives one hope that the set is finite. But no one knows when relief will come, and most folk in tech suspect that really, no, there is no bottom to the bug barrel. Nor, for the foreseeable future, any rest for the weary.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The past weeks have seen the broad crypto ETF market face consistent withdrawals from investors, causing Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, Solana, and others to record steady outflows since October.

While the negative trend has continued, Solana has just taken over the leadership in the broad ETF market after recording its first inflow in a while.

Latest data from SosoValue demonstrates that while Bitcoin, Ethereum, and XRP ETFs have continued to struggle with consistent weekly outflows, Solana has just beaten the trend after it finally ended a six-week streak of consecutive weekly outflows.

Notably, the data shows that Solana spot ETFs have recorded a net inflow of $4.38 million over the week.

Although the net amount of capital received by the ETFs appears decent, it is significant considering the growing crypto market weakness.

While this marks an end to the Solana ETFs' six-week outflow streak, this is the first positive weekly performance they have recorded since October 9.

Further data shows that Bitcoin spot ETFs suffered the largest withdrawals as investors pulled out about $1.79 billion during the same period.

The negative trend also extended to the Ethereum ETF market as the funds posted a total of $314.17 million in net outflows following the consistent selling pressure.

In addition to this, the XRP spot ETFs were not spared, as the funds recorded $11.11 million in weekly outflows, leaving Solana as the only one among the four major crypto ETFs to finish the week on a positive note.

Housing data shocks to the upside: Will we get sub-7% rates for Christmas?

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that thanksgiving week has been crazy so far, with a stock rally, stocks selling off, the 10-year yield dropping below 4.85%, tariffs being declared, inflation running hot, low jobless claims, strong GDP data and then — the housing data surprised to the upside!
  • Industry observers note that as we’ve discussed in the Housing Market Tracker articles over the past few weeks, our weekly pending sales data has stabilized and last week it grew a bit.
  • Those lower rates stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, which grew last week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that thanksgiving week has been crazy so far, with a stock rally, stocks selling off, the 10-year yield dropping below 4.85%, tariffs being declared, inflation running hot, low jobless claims, strong GDP data and then — the housing data surprised to the upside! Let’s look at what’s happening as mortgage rates have fallen a tad from recent highs.

Industry observers note that as we’ve discussed in the Housing Market Tracker articles over the past few weeks, our weekly pending sales data has stabilized and last week it grew a bit. The housing market took a shock when rates rose aggressively from under 7% in September to 7.61% in early October; that shock really impacted demand, but rates haven’t gone higher than that and have eased a bit since.

Those lower rates stabilized demand in our weekly pending home sales data, which grew last week.

Industry observers note that purchase application data, on the other hand, has moved more noticeably. This index can be very tricky at times because it’s a survey, but to see this growth without rates below 7% is a good sign of stabilization.

Of course, the year-over-year purchase application data is still down major, but last year mortgage rates were roughly 1% lower at this time and we were heading toward a nine-month high in sales last December.

Upcoming home sales today beat estimates so much that my first inclination was not to believe it! I expect this number will be revised lower, but it’s still a positive trend. New home sales are basically doing the same thing they have done for 10 years, outside the COVID sales burst. They don’t really go below 570,000, nor do they really break away from 730,000. We are stuck in this range, as the builders are still working in a sub-6 % mortgage market, and thus new home sales are still at 2019 levels. If existing home sales were operating at those levels it would amount to 1-1.3 million more existing home sales. However, the existing home market hasn’t had the luxury of sub-6 % mortgage rates.

It has been revealed that one positive note that isn’t getting a lot of play is that the builders are slowly moving their completed units of sale lower. If we want housing starts to ever grow again, this needs to happen and fortunately this number has been falling all year long.

As I am writing this article, the 10-year yield is at 4.82%.

It has been revealed that if we want sub-7 % rates for Thanksgiving, Christmas, or New Year’s — as I have written about for weeks — we need the 10-year yield at 4.85% and under. Now, if spreads just improve a little, then we get our sub-7 % mortgage rates for the holidays. It’s been a wild week, folks; enjoy the holiday!

Startup Spotlight: An engineer’s search for better, safer baby products led him to launch Birch

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (873 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am.
  • Recent findings suggest that A fresh baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night?
  • But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am.

Recent findings suggest that A fresh baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

Industry observers note that “We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla said. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”.

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

In a recent development, to spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has problems with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and Newly introduced Jersey.

According to recent reports, gangiredla said the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

If you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”.

The platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for users.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch.

In a recent development, birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

The impossible research burden on fresh parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

How universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — significant metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your company?

It’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

Sources indicate that that “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

We’ll know our firm has made it when….

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

Veteran trader Peter Brandt has softened the tone of his recent Bitcoin warnings and remarked on X that the cryptocurrency held at the level it needed to hold after its drop to $55,150 over the weekend.

"Bitcoin held exactly where it had to hold -- for now anyway, but perhaps for more than now," Brandt wrote on Monday.

Recent findings suggest that brandt also shared a monthly chart of Bitcoin together with the post. The chart goes back to 2018, and Brandt marked on it the same patterns that he had already pointed to in previous years. According to the chart, the price of Bitcoin was back above $63,000 at the time of the post and stood at $63,338.

Industry observers note that on Saturday, Bitcoin fell as low as $55,150. It was the lowest price of the cryptocurrency since September 2024, and before that, the lowest price of Bitcoin in 2026 was $57,718 on July 1, according to Coinbase.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 15, Brandt posted a weekly chart with a possible head-and-shoulders top and said that, if the pattern proves valid, Bitcoin's October 2025 record of about $126,000 may not be surpassed in his lifetime. Two days before that, on Nov. 13, Bitcoin dropped below $70,000 for the first time since August.

Brandt has also pointed to the history of Bitcoin's bull market cycles more than once. Late last year, he posted a chart showing that each of Bitcoin's five major bull runs began after drawdowns of 75% or more, and he wrote that if the decline carried to $50,000, "the next bull market cycle should carry to $200k to $250K.".

In a recent development, in April, Brandt remarked that Bitcoin could form an "investable low" in September or October 2026. According to Brandt, this low may or may not go below the February low near $60,000, and the next cycle peak could land between $300,000 and $500,000 in September or October 2029 if the four-year cycle continues to hold.

"Real bottom will not occur until October 2026," Brandt remarked in an interview in February.

According to recent reports, the latest Brandt post comes amid a rally in U.S. tech stocks on Monday. Earlier that day, Nvidia declared that its board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, chief executive officer and board member, effective immediately.

Sources indicate that according to the Nvidia announcement, the board received input from senior levels of the U.S. government before the decision, and it is confident that Huang's return "poses no national security risk." Shares of Nvidia surged 33% after the news, according to CNBC.

Bitcoin went up together with tech stocks and briefly climbed above $64,000 on Monday. Before the Nvidia news, Bitcoin had already recovered from the Saturday low to around $61,500.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12. On Nov. 17, Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones said on the tech giant's earnings call that the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.".

Akash’s Solana Migration Clears November 2 Vote at 97%, With Four More On-Chain Decisions Ahead

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1107 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.
  • But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move.
  • The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

But a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Recent findings suggest that proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

The technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository claims a yes vote does two things:.

It also claims plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain.".

A no vote would stop the whole proposal. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis.".

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 indicated an expected result of "Will PASS":.

Turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Sources indicate that mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

It has been revealed that the tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC revealed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

The portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks.".

Recent findings suggest that why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

According to recent reports, at launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Recent findings suggest that proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence demonstrates what that requirement means on-chain.

Industry observers note that so Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:.

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":.

In a recent development, the second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the initiative goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

New home sales surge in October, but demand signals remain soft

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest home sales blipped above expectations in October, handing homebuilders a slice of better-than-worse, Thanksgiving-time, good news.
  • Industry observers note that according to U.S.
  • According to recent reports, october’s better-than-forecast results may surprise many, but they come with a catch: the survey’s margin of error and data collection cycle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest home sales blipped above expectations in October, handing homebuilders a slice of better-than-worse, Thanksgiving-time, good news. However, NAHB’s November homebuilder confidence gauge had plunged to its lowest level in nearly 15 years, signaling that builders remain pessimistic about the market’s current state and foreseeable-future direction.

Industry observers note that according to U.S. Census Bureau data, sales of newly constructed single-family homes in October came in at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 701,000, up 14.2% month-over month, and a 7.5% gain from the same month a year prior. Meanwhile, the median sales price of new homes sold in October was $391,000, down 0.3% from September and 3.2% from a year ago.

According to recent reports, october’s better-than-forecast results may surprise many, but they come with a catch: the survey’s margin of error and data collection cycle. They could be revised downward next month.

“A downward revision to September helps explain the size of October’s 14.2% rebound, the largest monthly gain since November 2025,” First American Deputy Chief Economist Odeta Kushi said in a statement.

Recent findings suggest that new home for-sale inventory also tightened, coinciding with a decline in new residential construction. The seasonally adjusted estimate of new homes for sale at the end of October was 470,000, down 1.5% from September’s 477,000, and 4.1% below the 490,000 recorded in October 2025. At the current sales rate, that represents a supply of 8.0 months, a 14% improvement from 9.3 months in September and 11.1% from 9.0 months a year earlier.

October’s sales results may be less of a bright spot than they appear, and one strong month doesn’t erase the warning signs flashing across the upcoming home market.

Plenty of indications suggest homebuilders are working through one of the toughest housing markets in years, including homebuilder confidence at its lowest point since the tail end of the Great Financial Crisis.

In a recent development, for example, mortgage applications for new-home purchases fell 13.6% year over year in October, a sign that rising mortgage rates and low consumer confidence continue to weigh on demand. The existing-home market is also struggling, with the National Association of Realtors reporting that pending home sales fell to another record low in October.

NAHB also reports that, in November, homebuilders had a bleak view of current sales conditions, future sales expectations for the next six months and prospective buyer traffic.

Recent findings suggest that “Persistent housing affordability challenges, including elevated home prices and mortgage rates, continue to weigh on prospective buyers and constrain demand,” Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington, NAHB Assistant VP for Forecasting and Analysis, wrote in a note following today’s latest home sales release. “Builders are using sales incentives and price adjustments to attract buyers, but affordability remains a significant obstacle to a sustained recovery in housing demand.”.

A review of the latest earnings calls from 14 publicly traded homebuilders reveals that the country’s largest builders faced a challenging third quarter, with sales conditions remaining weak heading into the final months of the year, consistent with NAHB’s data.

It has been revealed that last quarter, only three of the public homebuilders — Smith Douglas Homes, Toll Brothers and Green Brick Partners — reported year-over-year increases in upcoming orders. However, nearly all 14 experienced sequential declines in orders, many exceeding 20%, pointing to a further deterioration in demand.

Sales volume followed a similar trend. Only Smith Douglas Homes and LGI Homes reported year-over-year increases in homes sold,.

Meanwhile, just two builders, Toll Brothers (2.4%) and Hovnanian Enterprises (0.4%), posted year-over-year increases in average sales prices. Toll’s luxury-focused buyer base is generally less sensitive to mortgage rates and economic volatility, while Hovnanian has increasingly shifted its product mix toward move-up and active-adult buyers, who tend to be more resilient to broader market pressures.

Many public homebuilders reported in October and November that buyers remain very cautious, which helped dampen sales volume and prices.

“As we moved through the quarter, our buyers became more cautious, did not feel an urgency to transact and felt more comfortable moving to the sidelines,” Century Communities Executive Chairman Dale Francescon said during an earnings call on October 28.

Paul Romanowski, President and CEO at D.R. Horton, acknowledged that October was another challenging month.

“Demand did get weaker as the quarter went on, for sure. As rates rose and as we got into October, what we’ve seen mirrors September. Traffic and sales activity are somewhat below what we’d anticipate in a typical seasonal pattern,” he stated during an earnings call on October 29.

Against this backdrop, it remains unclear whether October’s sales rebound reflects a meaningful improvement in demand or a temporary spike that could show up next month as a downward revision.

Sources indicate that “Looking ahead, the question is whether enough buyers will follow those who signed contracts in October,” Kushi noted, pointing to falling mortgage applications for new homes and low homebuilder confidence. “Builders are finding ways to make the monthly payment work for some buyers, but softer buyer traffic and fewer mortgage applications point to a tough winter.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:07 pm.

According to recent reports, microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal customers that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now they’re being asked to pack up again.

In a recent development, microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the tech giant’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

Industry observers note that the reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”.

That’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft indicates Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The company remarked putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”.

People weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday people, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft announced Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

It has been revealed that rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and mentioned it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

It has been revealed that reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent manufacturer, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist people may end up back with the people who built it.

Despite the sharp fall in the cryptocurrency market, Michael Saylor-led Strategy has not stopped its Bitcoin (BTC) buying spree, as it picked up 457 BTC worth around $29.6 million.

The firm's recent purchase comes as the leading cryptocurrency has been struggling to rebound from the heavy sell-off that recently dragged it to a two-plus-year low.

The latest data from Strategy's SEC filing reveals that the firm has bought 457 Bitcoin at an average price of $64,898 per coin.

The new purchase brings Strategy’s Bitcoin holdings to around 851,305 BTC, which accounts for over 4% of the cryptocurrency's maximum supply of 21 million coins.

The firm has now spent around $64.23 billion to build its Bitcoin holdings at an average price of $75,446 per Bitcoin.

It is worth noting that Strategy has been buying BTC at gradually decreasing prices as the cryptocurrency market continues to bleed heavily.

Sources indicate that on Nov. 2, the firm announced that it had bought 811 BTC, worth around $65.5 million, at an average price of $80,846 per Bitcoin.

According to recent reports, A week later, on Nov. 9, Strategy announced the purchase of 1,036 BTC worth $81.9 million at an average price of $79,012.

The firm’s Bitcoin purchase a week later, on Nov. 16, was relatively smaller at 485 BTC, worth $33.4 million, with an average price of $68,887.

The latest 457 BTC purchase continues this pattern. The latest Strategy purchase was made at an almost 20% lower price than the firm’s Nov. 2 acquisition.

Overall, the firm has made four weekly purchases, scooping up around 2,789 BTC worth $210.4 million.

Industry observers note that however, these purchases have been much smaller than before. The latest $29.6 million purchase is almost 64% lower than the $81.9 million purchase announced just two weeks ago.

Although Saylor is doubling down on Bitcoin, Strategy’s massive holdings in the cryptocurrency are underwater as the market has been struggling to regain its footing.

On Nov. 21, Bitcoin hit a low of around $55,130, its lowest level since September 2024, before rebounding above $61,000.

The firm’s recent purchases have helped reduce its overall average Bitcoin acquisition cost, but the drop has not been that significant.

For example, with the latest purchase, the average cost of the firm’s Bitcoin holdings dropped from $75,452 to around $75,446, a decline of just $6 per Bitcoin.

At the same time, the firm has also been putting a lot of resources into supporting its preferred securities.

In the latest reporting period, Strategy sold around 1.93 million common shares, raising net proceeds of $176.7 million.

#133519. Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1015 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.
  • The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network.
  • One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am.

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

In a recent development, testing that more closely replicates the manufacturer’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company claims it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software revision that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

Industry observers note that the bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows upgrade used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

Industry observers note that so what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Recent findings suggest that second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report states.

According to recent reports, the preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate matter.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”.

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

Recent findings suggest that it also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

According to recent reports, some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft states its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

Recent findings suggest that the report also confirms what Microsoft said the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”.

The new testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the manufacturer says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

#133518. Your AI agents can be fully authorized and still do damage

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

Your AI agents can be fully authorized and still do damage

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (856 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.
  • For as long as we’ve had enterprise security, it’s been organized around one question: Who is allowed to do what?
  • Industry observers note that identity, zero trust and least privilege all exist to answer that question.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 21:52 EST / NOVEMBER 25 2026.

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.

For as long as we’ve had enterprise security, it’s been organized around one question: Who is allowed to do what?

Industry observers note that identity, zero trust and least privilege all exist to answer that question. The internet and mobile disrupted the landscape by bringing more people and devices onto the network, but the underlying problem remained.

Artificial intelligence agents expose the limits of that question. An agent can hold only the permissions it was given and still email a customer list to a stranger because it read an instruction buried on a web page or in a support ticket and treated it as a legitimate order. That is the problem Cato Networks Ltd. is trying to solve with its recent launch of AgentSense, a runtime capability built into its secure access service edge platform.

AgentSense monitors an agent as it works and traces each proposed action back to its instruction source. Its first component, Untrusted Influence Detection, separates what the user asked for from content the agent encounters along the way, such as emails, documents and tool responses. If that external content steers the agent toward a risky step, the action is blocked before it runs. A second component, Drift Detection, is planned to check whether an agent’s steps still serve its original task.

With agentic agents, they can have the right permissions and still take harmful actions. The first release covers coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and GitHub Copilot. These are included at no extra charge in Cato AI Usage licenses, and Cato is offering $10,000 to each of the first three researchers who can beat it. This has clear value for security leaders. As organizations give AI more responsibility, they need visibility into what it is doing and when human intervention is required.

Language models read instructions and data in the same stream, and no patch will change that. Filters that look for known attack phrases catch poorly formed attempts, but a well-written injection will be interpreted as a valid business request. The control therefore must sit at the moment of action and ask where the instruction came from.

Permissions alone won’t close the gap because multiple actions, when executed individually, can still combine to produce an unauthorized outcome. Adoption is far ahead of control. A Gartner survey cited by Fierce Network found that 71% of organizations expect to deploy agentic AI within 12 months, while only 21% have governance in place.

According to recent reports, agentSense is a single product from a single vendor, and it will take time and independent testing to prove itself. The more important point is the shift it represents. Zero trust taught us to verify who is asking. Agents also require us to verify why an action is happening and whose instruction is behind it.

The companies that get value from agents will be the ones that can let them run without watching every step, and that only happens when the controls are in place first. Start the inventory and the permission cleanup now. The tools to enforce the rest are arriving quickly, and they will work far better for the teams that did the groundwork.

Recent findings suggest that zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

Breaking: Court upholds NYC rent freeze backed by Mayor Mamdani

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that on Thanksgiving eve, Judge Brendan Lantry dismissed a landlords’ challenge to the Rent Guidelines Board’s late June decision to freeze rents.
  • With the national real estate industry watching, the rent freeze became a major test of what a mayor can do to force affordability.
  • Sources indicate that owners of rent-stabilized buildings argued that Mamdani stacked the board with loyalists after promising a freeze, making the outcome predetermined.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that on Thanksgiving eve, Judge Brendan Lantry dismissed a landlords’ challenge to the Rent Guidelines Board’s late June decision to freeze rents. The ruling upholds the city’s first-ever freeze on both one- and two-year leases.

With the national real estate industry watching, the rent freeze became a major test of what a mayor can do to force affordability.

Sources indicate that owners of rent-stabilized buildings argued that Mamdani stacked the board with loyalists after promising a freeze, making the outcome predetermined. They also accused the board of following a campaign promise instead of the data on rising landlord costs. Lantry rejected both claims.

It has been revealed that the ruling comes three weeks after an appeals court revived the city’s pied-à-terre tax rollout on second homes valued at $5 million or higher. Mamdani posted on social media that the city has billed owners of those homes more than $500 million.

That lawsuit ran parallel to the rent freeze lawsuit landlords filed in late July. It originally was in a Staten Island court but was moved to Manhattan in August at the city’s request.

In a recent development, the rent freeze took effect Oct. 1 while the lawsuit was pending and covers leases on more than a million apartments. The board had frozen one-year leases in 2015, 2016 and 2020.

Sources indicate that because the board acts in a quasi-legislative role, its orders stand if they have a rational basis, and courts may not substitute their own judgment, Lantry wrote. He found that the board’s 42-page explanatory statement indicated it considered each factor the Administrative Code requires, including the industry’s economic condition and the cost of living.

Industry observers note that lantry noted appointees who share the mayor’s views did not show collusion. He noted that “elections have consequences.”.

But Lantry did not let Mamdani completely off the hook.

Industry observers note that “Regarding Mayor Mamdani’s campaign for Mayor of Newly introduced York City, the court would be remiss not to state that such comments, promises, and guarantees to freeze the rent were reckless and irresponsible,” he wrote. “The Mayor of the City of New York has no authority to unilaterally raise, ‘freeze’ or otherwise adjust the rent of stabilized units in this City – that responsibility is within the power of the Board and the Board alone.”.

Sources indicate that he called an email in which the board’s chair shared a draft of the explanatory statement with a mayoral aide before the vote “troubling.” He said it cast a “dark shadow” over the board’s independence. Without more, he wrote, the email did not justify overturning the decision under Article 78, the state law that lets courts review government agency actions.

The judge noted that petitioners agreed to end court-ordered discovery, which produced about 1,000 documents, and never sought depositions.

Industry observers note that lantry acknowledged the freeze could make it harder for owners to refinance or renovate. But he wrote that the legal question is not whether the policy is wise.

Breaking: Binance’s $6.3B Hack Fix Is Coming Tomorrow: Why the ZK Math Doesn't Tell the Whole Story

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On-chain data highlights the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.
  • According to recent reports, at the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT.
  • Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data highlights the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

According to recent reports, at the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

Sources indicate that if Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

Recent findings suggest that it shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Industry observers note that binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:.

Industry observers note that the first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what customers hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:.

Recent findings suggest that why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:.

Asset | Held with third-party custodians.

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

It has been revealed that compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, indicated BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:.

In a recent development, not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

According to recent reports, how Binance claims it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:.

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance notes the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest enhancement says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:.

It has been revealed that the design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

Recent findings suggest that what customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

On Monday, XRP briefly rose above $1 after the return of Jensen Huang to Nvidia sparked a rally on Wall Street and a wave of short liquidations in the crypto market. At the peak of the move, short liquidations on XRP exceeded long liquidations by 578%, according to CoinGlass data.

On the XRPUSDT perpetual contract on Binance, the price of XRP went from $0.94 to as high as $1.02 within minutes after 14:00 UTC, and later it pulled back and stood at $0.984, according to TradingView.

Sources indicate that earlier on Monday, before the opening bell, Nvidia declared that its board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately. The organization noted that the board was satisfied with Huang's "candor and ability to lead" after a series of meetings with him, and that its independent investigation would continue. According to the company, the board received input from senior U.S. government officials and concluded that Huang's reinstatement "poses no national security risk.".

"The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones stated in a statement.

Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, and on Nov. 17, during the company's earnings call, Jones stated that the board "does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.".

In premarket trading, Nvidia stock jumped 27% to $159.48 as of 9 a.m. ET, and at the start of U.S. trading on Monday, Nvidia shares were up more than 30%. The rally spread across Wall Street, and the S&P 500 rose as much as 5.6% and the Nasdaq 100 as much as 7.9%, according to NBC News.

In a recent development, coinGlass data shows that $9.45 million worth of XRP positions were liquidated over the past 24 hours, and $7.18 million of that amount came from short positions. Long positions accounted for $2.27 million.

Recent findings suggest that the same happened across the rest of the crypto market. In total, 110,663 traders were liquidated for $660.89 million over the past 24 hours, according to CoinGlass, and shorts accounted for $515.94 million of that amount.

Bitcoin led the list with $273.26 million in liquidations, and 82.8% of that amount came from short positions. Ethereum followed with $139.07 million, and Solana was third with $24.93 million.

Besides, perpetual contracts on Nvidia stock and on SOXL, a triple-leveraged exchange-traded fund on semiconductor stocks, were next on the list with $16.34 million and $15.01 million in liquidations, respectively, according to CoinGlass.

US Strikes Back After $6 Billion Binance Hack

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The United States Department of Justice (DOJ) has initiated a significant legal push to address the theft of over $6 billion worth of cryptocurrency from Binance by North Korean hackers last month.
  • According to recent reports, as per a Nov.
  • The recent development comes less than a month after North Korean hackers reportedly broke into Binance on Oct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United States Department of Justice (DOJ) has initiated a significant legal push to address the theft of over $6 billion worth of cryptocurrency from Binance by North Korean hackers last month.

According to recent reports, as per a Nov. 23 announcement, the DOJ said that it has filed a civil forfeiture complaint to recover over $1.1 billion worth of stolen cryptocurrency as part of its efforts to retrieve the billions lost in the massive hack.

The recent development comes less than a month after North Korean hackers reportedly broke into Binance on Oct. 29 in one of the biggest crypto heists ever.

In a recent development, the DOJ claimed that its recent civil forfeiture action focuses on over $1.1 billion worth of USD Coin (USDC), a stablecoin pegged 1:1 to the U.S. dollar and issued by Circle.

The assets are alleged to have been stolen from Binance and laundered by North Korean cybercriminals.

Significantly, the assets had previously been frozen under a restraining order obtained by the government earlier this month. With the fresh court filing, the potential recovery of the assets has taken another step forward.

The DOJ further claimed that U.S. authorities have successfully helped freeze, seize or return over $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency since the attack in October.

This is nearly half of the total $6 billion-plus stolen from Binance, though the government did not provide details about how much of that has been returned to the exchange.

According to recent reports, the importance of collaboration between law enforcement agencies and crypto firms to ensure that hackers don't get away with stolen assets was stressed by Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva.

According to recent reports, “North Korean cyber hackers stole over $6 billion of cryptocurrency from Binance. But prompt coordination with both the government and our private sector partners helped to avoid the bulk of these assets from being lost,” Duva stated.

U.S. authorities have further revealed the sophisticated money laundering techniques used by North Korean hackers to conceal their stolen cryptocurrency.

FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman noted that the regime uses intricate money laundering methods to convert stolen digital assets into funds for its illicit activities.

After the Binance hack, authorities promptly worked to trace the stolen funds and coordinate with crypto service providers to block further transfers.

Sources indicate that the U.S. Secret Service claimed that its investigators were able to detect and freeze some of the stolen funds within minutes of the hack.

In a recent development, "The bad actors in this intrusion thought they could run from law enforcement. They've found out they were wrong," said Secret Service Special Agent in Charge Todd Bratz.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 10:09 amNovember 21, 2026 at 10:13 am.

This week on the GeekWire Podcast, longtime Microsoft beat reporter Mary Jo Foley, a GeekWire contributing writer, sizes up where the company stands after one of its most eventful weeks in years.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft opened its Ignite conference with an apology for the global Outlook outage, then took direct aim at OpenAI and Anthropic on price, even though it invests in both and sells their models. We discuss the lasting damage from the outage, why enterprise customers have few places to go even when they’re fed up, and Microsoft’s pitch to make Copilot the “OS for work,” as Anthropic goes public.

Mary Jo also explains how Microsoft changed the way it rolls out news at its big conferences, what got lost along the way, and what that claims about the company after the shakeup of its communications team. Plus, we weigh who from Microsoft could lead Nvidia, and the GeekWire trivia challenge goes back to 1997.

In a recent development, edited by Curt Milton. Music by Daniel L.K. Caldwell.
