#133494. Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1390 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

Why businesses are embracing ‘good enough’ open-weight AI—and how geopolitics could get in the way

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the performance gap between open-weight and closed-weight models narrows, a growing number of businesses—from local start-ups to large multinationals—are turning to open-weight models for greater control, customization and cost efficiency.
  • “Frontier models at scale are incredibly expensive,” Damian Kim, the Asia-Pacific vice president of social media platform Pinterest, tells Fortune.
  • Sources indicate that anyone can download and customize the weights behind an open-weight model, which means firms can cut token costs while keeping tighter control of their data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the performance gap between open-weight and closed-weight models narrows, a growing number of businesses—from local start-ups to large multinationals—are turning to open-weight models for greater control, customization and cost efficiency.

“Frontier models at scale are incredibly expensive,” Damian Kim, the Asia-Pacific vice president of social media platform Pinterest, tells Fortune. “The cost to serve can be reduced dramatically when using an open-weight model versus a frontier model, where you’re at the whims of the API pricing.”.

Sources indicate that anyone can download and customize the weights behind an open-weight model, which means firms can cut token costs while keeping tighter control of their data. They’re also taking a growing share of AI traffic. In August, open-weight models ran the majority of traffic on Vercel’s AI gateway; 56% of tokens routed through the cloud platform went to open-weight models, up from 7% last year.

“Models are converging on similar performance for industry use: U.S. government evaluators put the best Chinese model about eight months behind the American frontier,” says Olaf Groth, a professor of practice at UC Berkeley’s Haas School of Business. “For most enterprise workloads, that is good enough.”.

It has been revealed that rather than paying for the most powerful model for every task, companies are turning to cheaper, customizable alternatives for routine work. But with Chinese developers behind many of the leading open-weight models, geopolitics may matter as much as cost or performance.

Before GPT-3.5 propelled AI to mainstream fame, most high-performing models were either small academic releases or commercial systems with restricted outside access. The first open-weight models originated in academic research, where sharing model weights to ensure reproducibility was standard practice.

Recent findings suggest that in 2019, OpenAI went against tradition by initially withholding the full 1.5-billion-parameter version of GPT-2, citing risks of misuse such as disinformation, impersonation and phishing. Most U.S. frontier labs, including Anthropic and OpenAI, keep the underlying parameters private, giving users access through apps or APIs rather than letting them download and run the models themselves.

In the early years of generative AI, most users preferred closed-weight models because they delivered performance that open-weight alternatives could not match. Yet in recent years, the improved capability and cost-efficiency of powerful Chinese models like Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3.1 Pro and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash has swung the pendulum back in favor of open-weight models.

“For the longest time, the idea has been that you can get the highest level of performance using closed-weight models, so many firms start off by using them,” says Hariharasudhan Saminathan, cofounder of Friday, a sovereign AI startup backed by global venture capital firm Antler. But now, “through distillation and other processes, open-weight models’ performance almost matches that of closed-weight models,” he says.

Sources indicate that “Many of our pipeline customers are now adopting open-weight models right off the bat,” he adds. “They’re not even touching the closed-weight ones.”.

Pinterest, for example, uses Alibaba’s open-weight Qwen models to power its online platform. “We’ve driven down our inference costs using post-trained open-weight models,” Kim explains. “They offer over 90% cost reduction.” (Many leading Chinese open-weight models activate only a subset of parameters per token, cutting compute and energy needed per request.).

Kim also cites the flexibility of these models as a draw. Last October, the firm released Pinterest Assistant: an AI-powered tool that pairs a customized Qwen multimodal LLM with the firm’s proprietary Taste Graph, to generate shopping recommendations for owners based on their individual aesthetic preferences.

“[With open-weight technology], we can create a specialized model that actually does what we need it to do very effectively, which is understanding visual information,” says Kim.

Rather than choosing one or the other, some firms are using a mix of open-weight and closed-weight AI models.

Eu Leong Oh, medical director at The Longevity Suite Asia, a Singapore-based wellness clinic, indicates he’s using Claude and Google’s Gemini to build the team’s in-house healthcare portal, but aims to pivot to open-weight models for daily use. “For things like prototyping, exploration and research, it’s still very useful to have a large-parameter, trained, closed-weight model,” Oh says.

He compares a top-tier frontier model to a Michelin-starred chef. “You’ll want a chef like Gordon Ramsay to decide the processes in your restaurant, but you don’t need him to do the cooking all the time,” he says. “Similarly, within companies, a lot of the heavy lifting and token budget will eventually be taken over by more cost effective open-weight models.”.

According to recent reports, token costs are also skyrocketing with the rise of agentic AI. An AI agent might consume five times more tokens than a chatbot interface, because it runs multi-step loops rather than a single task. Those increasing costs may push companies to adopt cheaper open-weight models on top of existing closed-weight ones.

According to recent reports, “Companies are becoming more cost-conscious about their AI deployment,” says Srividya Jandhyala, a professor of management at ESSEC Business School. “Not every task needs the power of a frontier model, and companies are recognizing that ‘good enough’ models work for a large variety of operations.”.

Yet a tech giant’s decision whether or not to use an open-weight model could come down to politics, rather than cost or technical ability. The leading open-weight models come from Chinese companies like DeepSeek, Alibaba, and z.AI; their growing usage in both U.S. and global business is worrying some in Washington about China’s growing influence over the technology.

“The American AI stack remains far stronger than China’s and we must continue to lead,” Representative John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), chair of the U.S. House’s Select Committee on China, wrote in a Sept. 23 statement.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 18, Reuters reported that the Trump administration was considering requiring U.S. firms to publicly disclose their use of Chinese AI models, in hopes of discouraging use of the technology without imposing fresh restrictions that might anger Beijing.

According to recent reports, in a Nov. 20 report, Moolenaar warned that American businesses were adopting inexpensive Chinese AI models. “Federal investigations, however, have found that major PRC developers used proxy networks and fraudulent accounts to harvest outputs from American frontier models and replicate their capabilities. While America is investing billions and racing to build ‘Super Intelligence,’ Beijing is using stolen intelligence to close the gap,” he wrote.

Cursor—whose Composer coding agent was built on Moonshot’s Kimi model—told Congress that it’s considering phasing out Chinese AI models due to “geopolitical risk,” CNBC reported.

It has been revealed that “For global companies, especially in Western markets, there is a trade-off between cheaper Chinese alternatives versus concerns about continued access,” explains Jandhyala of ESSEC. “If they think that future policies may force them to reduce their reliance on Chinese AI models, companies may pre-emptively start using U.S. open- or closed-weight models.”.

A handful of U.S. companies—including Thinking Machines, Reflection AI and Nvidia—are releasing open-weight models. Nvidia and its recently returned CEO, Jensen Huang, have also championed the technology. According to Reuters, Huang’s support for open-weight AI helped persuade Trump and Vice President JD Vance to push for his return.

The concern that Chinese models may come with hidden backdoors may be overstated, says Erik Cambria, a professor of AI at Singapore’s Nanyang Technological University (NTU).

It has been revealed that “Concerns about Chinese models should be distinguished between genuine technical security risks and geopolitical perceptions,” he says. “An open-weight model deployed locally, without transmitting sensitive data externally, presents a very different risk profile from a remotely hosted API, regardless of the model’s country of origin.”.

Recent findings suggest that still, geopolitical concerns may drive companies to diversify where they get their models from. “Europeans optimize for sovereignty and compliance,” indicates Groth of UC Berkeley. “In Asia and the Gulf, pragmatists hedge across both stacks and refuse to pick a side, unless they need models and applications which implicate national security.”.

In a recent development, for businesses, the goal may not be picking a winner in the AI race, but keeping their options open. “Businesses will combine models from different providers and select the most appropriate one for each workload,” says Cambria.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) community members have launched a new block explorer for Shibarium, the layer-2 network of the SHIB ecosystem, and Shiba Inu lead Shytoshi Kusama has remained silent on X since May.

According to recent reports, shiba Inu community veteran Mazrael declared the new explorer, scan.shibfun.app, in an X post. "Shibarium has a new block explorer," he wrote. According to Mazrael, the explorer was "built by the community, powered by ShibWatch, dressed in the Eternity Hub look.".

The launch comes as SHIB trades near its lowest levels in years. In November, the price of SHIB fell as low as $0.00000337, its lowest level since 2021, and on Nov. 22, the token traded at around $0.00000362, according to CoinMarketCap.

According to the post, owners can type a .shib name in the search bar and land on the wallet linked to it, and the explorer also shows newly introduced Shiboshis from Shibarium every day. For developers, Mazrael listed contract verification, read and write functions for contracts, the activity of ERC-4337 smart wallets, and a free API, which he described as "Etherscan-style too." Method names are decoded as well, and in Mazrael's words, there are "no more mystery 0x codes." The explorer also has a DApps page with Shibarium games and apps, and a button that adds Shibarium to a wallet in one click.

The work on the explorer is not finished yet. "Live blocks are complete now, and older history indexing," Mazrael wrote. On Tuesday, the explorer itself showed that 3% of Shibarium blocks had been indexed, and a notice on the site noted that some of the counts may be inaccurate. Mazrael added that the new explorer can be found on Shib.io under ShibWatch.

Recent findings suggest that shytoshi Kusama's last post or interaction on X dates back to May 13, 2026. In September, Kusama changed his X bio to "Polish" and his location to "Close," and he has not explained the meaning of either word. The official Shibarium account on X has not posted since July 13, 2026.

Still, Shibarium updates kept coming from community members. In October, Mazrael said that CreateX, a standard factory for deploying contracts at the same address on different chains, went live on Shibarium. According to Mazrael, all 12 Safe v1.4.1 contracts were deployed to their canonical addresses through the Safe Singleton Factory, and x402 went live too, so AI agents can now pay in SHIB, TREAT and wrapped BONE.

In September 2025, attackers exploited the Shibarium bridge and withdrew about $2.4 million worth of assets from it.

Sources indicate that according to Shibariumscan, Shibarium processed 546 transactions in a single day in late November, and on Oct. 31, the daily number of transactions on the network was 6,370. Since its launch in August 2023, Shibarium has processed more than 1.5 billion transactions in total.

In a recent development, at the same time, the number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million on Nov. 17, according to Etherscan.

#133491. Island is a latest screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (907 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Island is a latest screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A fresh startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time.
  • This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.
  • Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A fresh startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.

This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.

Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.

Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.

“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a major mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.

“So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”.

With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.

“A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj mentioned.

What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping customers meet their goals, the startup’s early data indicates. After early testing and an October launch, the team notes that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.

In a recent development, island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into consumers’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.

Sources indicate that the idea to encourage consumers to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.

Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.

According to recent reports, island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.

The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active people-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.

The app is right now free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The firm hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but looks to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am.
  • Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S.
  • Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith stated the president is “making an important point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 5:49 amNovember 23, 2026 at 6:01 am.

Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith offered a polite but pointed response to President Trump’s seemingly impromptu threat to tax U.S. companies that build data centers abroad: most of them have to be where their customers are.

Speaking on CBS News’ “Face the Nation” on Sunday morning, Smith stated the president is “making an important point,” and that there’s room to talk about keeping the training of the most advanced AI models in the U.S., much like the push to make more chips here.

But he mentioned most data centers run everyday cloud services, such as streaming video, video games and business software, and need to be close to the people using them.

“You can’t support Helsinki from Newly introduced Jersey any more than you can keep the lights on in Helsinki from an electricity power plant in New Jersey,” he said.

A tax on foreign data centers could have significant financial implications for Microsoft, which states it has more than 600 data centers in 34 countries.

Trump made the statement Friday at a White House press conference, saying companies would face a “tremendous tax” if they build data centers outside the U.S.

It has been revealed that his reason: “We’re not allowing data centers to go into other countries because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it.”.

.@POTUS: "Whoever wins SI, wins… We're not allowing data centers to go into other countries — because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen." pic.twitter.com/FiH1LfAQDu.

He gave no rate or timeline and acknowledged that he hadn’t told his own staff. “That’s a breaking story,” he mentioned. “I haven’t even said that to my people. But I’m telling them now — they’re here.”.

Trump had just returned from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Industry observers note that his one example was an unnamed tech giant that wants to build in Finland. Google revealed a €13 billion investment in Finland in September, covering data centers and clean energy projects. Margaret Brennan, host of the CBS program, remarked he might have meant a Chinese project.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who appeared earlier in the same CBS broadcast, mentioned he hadn’t spoken with the president about the proposal, but added that Trump is “very concerned that we don’t do a significant technology transfer offshore.”.

Smith also fielded questions on other topics in his “Face the Nation” appearance.

TikTok’s owner: Brennan asked about TikTok’s Chinese owner, ByteDance, which is in advanced talks to spend about $500 million more on Microsoft’s Azure cloud, mostly to use OpenAI’s models, The Information reported last week.

Sources indicate that rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., chair of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, remarked Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance, called it unacceptable for a Pentagon contractor, and asked the company for a briefing.

Smith noted that TikTok’s U.S. business is now a separate organization, and stated Microsoft expects to answer the committee’s questions on Capitol Hill.

White House ballroom: Microsoft committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom project, according to an internal donor list reported by the Washington Post. Brennan asked why, and whether Microsoft is worried about scrutiny from a Democratic-controlled Congress.

Smith noted Microsoft takes the same approach with every administration, regardless of party. “We partner where we can. We stand apart when we should,” he said.

He put the ballroom donation in the first category, and said the manufacturer “didn’t know, obviously,” that the project would involve tearing down the East Wing. In the second category, he pointed to lawsuits Microsoft has filed against the current administration, as it has against previous ones, to stand up for issues it considered key.

Outlook outage: Smith reiterated Microsoft’s apology for the Nov. 12 global Microsoft 365 and Outlook outage. He noted the outage wasn’t caused by AI or a cyberattack.

Speaking more broadly, he said much of the recent wave of tech failures can be seen as “AI ripple effects” — the result of AI making software bugs easier to find, which has companies racing to patch systems faster than they can test the fixes.

(GeekWire has covered that angle in depth, including the surge in AI-discovered bugs, Microsoft’s final outage report and Oren Etzioni’s column on the conspiracy theories.).

Smith said the patching race won’t be finished anytime soon. “The whole information infrastructure of the world is in effect being upgraded right now,” he said.

It has been revealed that this Saturday, November 28, is Small Business Saturday, the annual post-Thanksgiving tradition that urges holiday shoppers to buy from local, independent businesses. And Eva Longoria wants the people behind those businesses to feel supported all year long.

“I’ve always had so much respect for small business owners because I know firsthand what it takes to turn an idea into something real,” Longoria told Entrepreneur. “Being an entrepreneur can be incredibly rewarding, but it can also feel overwhelming when you’re making significant decisions and trying to figure things out on your own. That’s why I’m so passionate about supporting small businesses.”.

Recent findings suggest that the actress, entrepreneur and investor has partnered with Lenovo on Backing Every Business, a global initiative introduced this year to close the support gap facing small businesses. Founders can apply for grant funding, AI-enabled technology and one-to-one mentorship, including from Longoria herself.

“No two small businesses face the same challenges, and the best support starts with listening,” Emily Ketchen, SVP and CMO of Intelligent Devices Group & International Markets at Lenovo, told Entrepreneur.

At the heart of the initiative is Twinning, a mentorship program pairing small business owners across industries and borders. A newly introduced docuseries narrated by Longoria follows Twinning entrepreneurs as they tackle real business challenges together.

And then there’s Call Eva, which gave entrepreneurs a direct line to Longoria, Lenovo’s global ambassador. Founders left voice notes with their biggest business questions, and select callers get to speak with her directly.

“It’s been rewarding to be part of something that helps small business owners feel supported as they grow,” Longoria added.

Industry observers note that the stakes are major. The U.S. has 33.2 million small businesses that employ 61.6 million Americans and represent 43.5% of America’s GDP, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

It has been revealed that an analysis of 88 Call Eva submissions from eight countries revealed four overlapping themes. Here are the most common issues, and Longoria’s advice for overcoming them.

1. How to be seen. More than half asked about marketing and reaching new customers. Longoria’s advice: Lead with the story only your business can tell.

Sources indicate that “The tool that you have to use is storytelling,” she stated. “You’ve got to tell the story of the artisans and tell the story of the heritage behind these materials. I always think that cuts through the noise.”.

2. How to scale. Half asked about expanding without losing what makes them distinctive. Longoria urged starting focused and building on what works.

“I would think about one SKU, one target customer, one initial region, one retailer… Let’s see how that performs,” she noted.

3. How to lead and partner. One in five asked about juggling leadership and competing priorities. Longoria stressed finding collaborators whose audiences and values align.

According to recent reports, “Who are they trying to reach? What’s their demographic? How do you make this a win for that brand?” she said.

Sources indicate that 4. How to fund the future. About one in eight asked about raising capital. Her advice: Find investors who bring expertise and relationships, not just cash.

“You’re looking for a partner that adds value and not just in money,” she remarked. “I think one of the biggest mistakes you can make is partnering with the wrong investor.”.

Industry observers note that to see these lessons play out, watch the Backing Every Business Twinning docuseries on YouTube. Then, this Saturday, skip the big-box checkout line and support the shops, restaurants and makers in your neighborhood.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments.
  • Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn.
  • Sources indicate that zetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

Sources indicate that zetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

That detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no fresh mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain states nothing moves unless it passes.

In a recent development, if it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's fresh private AI app, ZetaLabs, releases alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a new whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

The snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Industry observers note that holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

On Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

That sequence is the strongest holder protection in the blueprint, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain says it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain says the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

Industry observers note that the biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange users depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

In a recent development, scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

On the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain says it will announce any change to the process in advance.

The vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

Recent findings suggest that if it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Recent findings suggest that taken together, this looks more like a retirement proposal for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As 81.5 million Americans travel at least 50 miles from home for Thanksgiving, conversations around the dinner table could present a rare opportunity for people to learn more about their aging loved ones. A newly introduced class of AI startups wants to help them preserve those conversations forever.

Charlie Greene, the cofounder and CEO of Remento, first learned about the importance of recording memories when his father, Don Greene, died during the hijacking of United Airlines Flight 93 on 9/11.

A 10-year-old boy at the time of the terrorist attack, which resulted in his father’s plane crashing in Shanksville, Penn., the now 34-year-old Greene mostly has a collection of old home videos to remember him by.

It has been revealed that so when his mother Claudette, 74, was diagnosed with stage-three lung cancer, he promptly acted to record her memories. With the intention of conducting an oral history interview, Greene searched “questions to ask a parent,” which Google morbidly autocompleted with “before they die.”.

When he started asking her the questions like “How did you get to elementary school as a kid,” she lit up, surprised he was interested at all.

“The thing that blew me away about that experience was how unmorbid it felt,” he mentioned.

Claudette is in remission, but her battle with cancer still left Greene “unhealthily fixated” on the idea of how to best preserve loved ones’ memories. In October 2023, he debuted Remento, which sends older “storytellers” a weekly text or email reminder prompting them to respond to photos or questions chosen in advance by their family members, such as, “What was the hardest thing you had to overcome as a child?”.

After gathering a maximum of a year’s worth of responses, the AI converts the raw transcript into a naturally flowing narrative that goes into a physical book complete with images and QR codes linking the text to the original recordings.

Greene told Fortune Thanksgiving presents a great opportunity for people to discover newly introduced memories or learn new twists on well worn stories from their relatives.

“One of the things I want for my daughter is the chance to sit next to her grandmother and hear her say ‘Believe it or not that’s me.’ Thanksgiving is a pretty good excuse to pull an old album off the shelf and make room for the two of them on the couch,” he stated.

According to recent reports, last year, Greene secured a $300,000 investment from billionaire Mark Cuban during an episode of Shark Tank in exchange for a 10% stake in his tech giant. He has raised a total of $4.3 million since launch.

Greene stated he understands some people’s skepticism of AI, because “A lot of what AI is proposing to the world doesn’t feel actually that good to our lives right now.”.

Widespread anxiety about AI replacing human workers as well as concerns over its environmental footprint have contributed to some people’s increasing skepticism toward the technology. A March study of more than 3,000 people by the nonprofit Jobs For the Future found that 38% of respondents noted AI was doing more harm than good, while less than half said the technology was a net positive.

Yet Greene hasn’t gotten as much pushback about the organization’s use of AI as he had expected because Remento is using the technology to provide its users with something deeply personal, he added.

In a recent development, “Investors want to invest in AI, because it’s an exciting place to be. But I think what we’re experiencing is people have problems and they want them solved, and they want consumer technology to be able to solve those problems,” he remarked.

In a recent development, kindred Tales, a rival platform cofounded by Nick Hern and his wife Rebecca Hern, has seen a similar trend with their customers. The tech giant has both AI and non-AI versions of its product.

While the non-AI version requires users to type out their responses to weekly prompts, the AI version helps by providing speech-to-text transcription and some light editing. It can also write a first draft of the interviewee’s story, if they want.

Before 2025, just over half of the company’s customers chose the AI version, but that number jumped to 80% after 2025.

“Customers increasingly see AI as a meaningful part of the storytelling experience, not just an extra,” Nick Hern told Fortune.

Part of the reason is that the manufacturer’s AI chatbot, called “Ali,” gives the interview process a conversational feel by teasing more out of customers with follow-up questions crafted to their responses.

Industry observers note that AI has helped Kern, who also works full time for Thomson Reuters, run the company as well. He remarked he has used the technology to help filter emails, as well as slowly replace freelancers that he previously hired to help him craft marketing and social content.

At a time when companies are spending billions to bring AI to every American, Greene, said, despite its flaws, AI has allowed Remento’s customers’, as well as himself, to record moments with family members that are invaluable.

“AI in our organization is being used to get people to do things that they’ve always wanted to do but haven’t been able to, and to make that experience as seamless and humanlike as possible,” he mentioned.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on April 25, 2026.

Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. Sources indicate that corma isn’t the only firm using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s latest startup Armadin, as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Flop Labs has confirmed a minor delay to the launch of its public testnet, pushing back from its previous goal of 15:00 (UTC+8) on November 24.

It's unclear what the reason for the delay is, although the team does expect to launch the testnet before 18:00 (UTC+8) the same day.

Industry observers note that possible reasons for the delay could include conducting final checks, calibrating nodes, validator onboarding, load testing, etc. (although Flop Labs has not confirmed any of these to be the reason for the delay).

It does not appear that Flop Labs has any plans to move the testnet launch to another day.

It has been revealed that flop Labs is building FLOP Network, a blockchain serving as a settlement layer for what it calls the "agentic economy". This would enable AI agents to make payments for computation (e.g. model inference) and memory services, and provide rewards to GPU miners that contribute their computational power to fulfill these requests.

Computation is verified via Flop Labs' "Proof of Useful Inference", which entails miners providing evidence that they've carried out the desired AI computation, and validators checking this evidence.

It has been revealed that why does this matter? FLOP Network would enable agents to make payments for computation, memory, etc. Flop Labs' main competitors include Akash Network and io.net (both of which facilitate access to compute/gpu resources in a decentralized manner), as well as Render Network (which started out facilitating decentralized graphics rendering but has since expanded into AI/compute more broadly).

While Flop Labs' competitors also facilitate access to compute, Flop Labs' main differentiating factor appears to be its focus on facilitating agent-to-agent commerce and computation-verification.

Recent findings suggest that flop Labs is led by Arthur Hayes, co-founder of crypto exchange BitMEX and current chief investment officer at Maelstrom. The rest of Flop Labs' team includes Sergey Vidyuk (ex-Deutsche Bank/BitMEX) as CTO, and Shu Duan (with experience in investment banking and crypto asset management) as chief strategy officer.

The testnet would be an opportunity to see if Flop Labs can successfully build out its envisioned agentic economy.

Breaking: DoorDash global food access head: Hunger doesn’t take a holiday. Putting food on the table will take all of us

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (630 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hunger gets harder to bear at the holidays, when everyone else seems to be gathering around a full table.
  • No single organization can close this gap.
  • At a time when everything seems to cost more, putting food on the table has become harder than ever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hunger gets harder to bear at the holidays, when everyone else seems to be gathering around a full table. With nearly 48 million Americans experiencing food insecurity in recent years, including 14 million children, millions of Americans will be facing a Thanksgiving table that has less on it.

No single organization can close this gap. It will take food banks, businesses, neighbors and public leaders all showing up.

At a time when everything seems to cost more, putting food on the table has become harder than ever. Hunger exists in every county, and increasingly often among those who never expected to need food assistance before. More than eight in ten people surveyed by Feeding America identified rising costs as the primary driver of food insecurity.

It has been revealed that the pressure is building for those in need. Recent changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the nation’s largest federal nutrition assistance program, have contributed to a significant decline in participation. According to the Food Research Action Center, approximately 5.5 million people have lost access to SNAP benefits since last year.

Recent findings suggest that food banks and pantries have always been the country’s backstop. But now, like everyone else in this economy, they are being asked to do more with less. Organizations are bracing demand rivalling or surpassing experienced during last fall’s government shutdown that created unprecedented disruption to SNAP. Some food banks are experiencing demand levels exceeding the COVID-19 pandemic.

It has been revealed that getting food to people can be just as challenging as securing it. Many of those served by food banks — including seniors, people with disabilities, or those without reliable transportation — cannot easily get to a distribution site on their own.

Tackling this challenge requires everyone contributing what they do best. For DoorDash, that’s logistics, and closing the gap between food and the people who need it.

Through Project DASH, DoorDash transports goods from food banks and pantries to doorsteps. Since 2018, 9 million deliveries of an estimated 150 million meals across the U.S. and Canada have arrived via DoorDash.

Sources indicate that this holiday season, we’re waiving fees for more than 300 Project DASH partners between Thanksgiving and Christmas, supporting delivery of an estimated 2 million meals. By removing that expense, food bank partners can strategy larger holiday distributions with confidence and reach more people.

In a recent development, many of our grocery partners are also doing everything they can to make the holidays more affordable for Americans who are struggling to get by, such as offering discounts for SNAP users to stretch their budgets further. The data is clear: Making it easier to use SNAP benefits can also have a significant impact in the fight against hunger. Since introducing SNAP payments on our platform in 2023, more than 4.5 million consumers have added their SNAP cards to DoorDash, and nearly a third of those we surveyed noted it has helped make them less likely to run out of food.

In a recent development, this is only one incremental step in a larger national conversation about hunger. No single company, program, or nonprofit can solve it alone. Food banks understand their neighbors and the needs of their communities, and businesses can bring their resources, technology, and expertise to bear.

Hunger is a neighbor-helping-neighbor matter. Americans of every background can agree that no one should go without a meal, especially at the holidays.

There is enough food for everyone in America. What’s missing is a way to get it to every table. With everyone at the table, we can build toward that together.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I was recently on a podcast and the host asked me what my lowest part of my career was,” Hank Green mused on a recent episode of his own podcast, Dear Hank & John.

That’s a tough question for anyone to answer, let alone someone who has spent about two decades regularly posting videos online for an increasingly broad audience.

“Really the low — the long low — was just watching as [the internet] went from being this lovely thing that a bunch of creatives were goofing around [on] to it being freaking everything, and mattering so much, and getting taken over by all tons of terrible vibes and algorithms selecting for outrage, and it being a huge degradation to the social order,” Green noted.

Industry observers note that that’s bleak, but Green is at least trying to lead by example in showing that we don’t have to accept that the good parts of the internet are gone forever. The notoriously entrepreneurial vlogbrother has spun up a newly introduced organization with Leslie Morgan: ClockwiseTV, a curated, ad-free educational video platform for children ages 8 to 12.

Sources indicate that “[Hank] came to me last September like, ‘I have had this idea for a really long time, and it stems from the fact that my child, who’s nine, always is asking me for five more minutes on whatever device he’s on,’” Morgan, who has spent 20 years working on the business side of the creator economy, told TechCrunch. “I was like, I have that same problem… ‘How do you contain time, but also give the child agency?’”.

Industry observers note that clockwise’s answer to that question seems to be this: At the start of each viewing session, the parent and child decide how long they can watch, and the platform will recommend videos that will adhere to that time frame. If a kid is in the midst of a 30-minute session and has already watched two 10-minute videos, they’re not going to be suggested a 20-minute video when they only have 10 minutes left.

The startup is addressing a pretty widespread concern among parents, who are worried about more than simply negotiating with their children about how long they can use the iPad. According to a 2025 study by the Pew Research Center, about 51% of parents of children 12 or younger say their kid watches YouTube every day, among other video apps.

YouTube has a dedicated app for children under 13, YouTube Kids, which offers a wide range of parental controls, but the app can reportedly still serve children a wealth of low-quality AI slop. Other apps that don’t have a kids’ version can be even worse.

Clockwise says it is also solving that problem by hand-curating a library of educational videos from creators like Odd Animal Specimens, Draw with Jazza, and Nerdforge, as well as channels Green had a hand in creating, like Crash Course Kids and SciShow Kids.

“When you go into the app, there’s a dozen choices [of videos] that you can choose from to start,” Morgan, the startup’s CEO, said. “There’s search functionality as well, so you can say, ‘Hey, I’m really interested in math today,’ so you can look up Stand-up Maths and look at what’s available in that time frame.”.

According to recent reports, some of these creators cater to people of all ages, but Clockwise notes its team manually reviews each video it uploads and edits it so that it’s ready for younger eyes. The team might remove anything from embedded product placement to what Morgan calls “spectacle power tool use.”.

“Simone Giertz, who’s a maker creator, tends to curse a lot. But a lot of that content is great for kids,” Morgan explains. “She makes a skateboard for her three-legged dog, and if she drops an f-bomb, we’re going to cut it out so that it’s suitable for children.”.

Sources indicate that clockwise pays these creators an upfront fee to use their videos, then shares 25% of revenue based on watch time. Clockwise charges parents $6.99 per month or $69.99 per year to access the platform, which it promises will remain free of ads.

Sources indicate that “Humans are checking [the videos] four times at least before it’s ever published into our app […] That will always stay,” Morgan mentioned. “We’re not interested in using AI to wash down our content.”.

So far, a few hundred parents have tested Clockwise with their children in beta. On Tuesday, the platform is opening to the public with apps made for iOS and Android smartphones and tablets.

The platform has not taken on any outside funding, and is funded by Green himself.

Recent findings suggest that “It was really important that he had full control,” Morgan said. “He wanted to invest his own wealth into this. That was also really important because it is something he just believes in so wholeheartedly, as do I.”.

webAI Releases TwIL-8B: A 5 GiB Open-Weight Reasoning Model With a 98.2 MATH-500 Score

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B.
  • A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500.
  • webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Recent findings suggest that webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

It has been revealed that the card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It states TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight customers want to hear.

In a recent development, on MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

The card is also more candid than most. It says TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

Industry observers note that here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

Gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

None of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

Read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

The AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card says AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Sources indicate that against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card shows the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a major generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 newly introduced tokens and a 40,960-token context.

In a recent development, anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card says all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

Industry observers note that the card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Sources indicate that overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

It has been revealed that the useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

#133481. From Mamdani to mass-scale empathy: Mast CEO Grant Canary’s unexpected take on climate action

📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Geekwire ↗ Open Full Page

From Mamdani to mass-scale empathy: Mast CEO Grant Canary’s unexpected take on climate action

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.
  • Since Grant Canary launched his firm a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.
  • The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:00 amNovember 23, 2026 at 2:28 pm.

Since Grant Canary launched his firm a decade ago, the technology he uses has shifted and pivoted but the goal has remained steadfast: restoring wild forestland.

The Seattle startup began as DroneSeed, which mapped forests devastated by fires, then flew large drones to re-tree the landscape. It went on to purchase three companies that collect and cultivate conifer seeds and grow saplings for planting, and rebranded as Mast Reforestation.

The manufacturer recently shifted again, adding a newly introduced line of operations: taking scorched timber and burying it in clay-lined vaults where it won’t rot and release carbon. Biomass burial clears the woody debris — the most expensive step in forest restoration post wildfire — while also generating essential revenue by selling carbon credits. Proceeds from the sales help landowners “get their forest back,” Canary said, which benefits everyone.

Just as Canary has pursued unexpected paths to forest restoration, the sustainability leader also has unconventional solutions and sources of inspiration for tackling climate change. Keep reading to learn more. His quotes have been edited for clarity and length.

When did you realize you had to work in sustainability?

Industry observers note that high school. I had a really fantastic teacher my senior year, and they got me focused on my philosophical underpinnings. I’m a utilitarian — greatest good for the greatest number of people, is how I would define that — and so my worldview formed around that time. And climate change is the problem that all other problems report to.

What’s your biggest worry when it comes to solving climate change?

Humans aren’t great at long-term projection. We’re much more responsive to short-term, and I am concerned that by the time that it is short-term, which is now, that there is not enough political will to understand the implications of climate change and how that affects all of the issues.

What gives you the most hope for the planet?

When I founded what would become Mast, there were not the technologies to replace the [fossil fuel] incumbents. That was 2016. The state of EVs versus internal combustion engine cars was not there yet. It’s getting there promptly. Solar was not necessarily the cheapest. Battery was still not there. Geothermal, we didn’t have that. Now we continue to have more and more of those tools to replace the incumbents. And by the way, the “incumbents” is the corporation, not the people working for those companies.

Industry observers note that I very much want all of the better products and technologies. Yes, they’re sustainable, but they’re also just better. I want to brain drain all of the oil and gas companies and put them to work in geothermal.

If you could invent one sustainability solution overnight, what would it be?

In “Ready Player Two” [a sequel to “Ready Player One,” which Steven Spielberg turned into a movie], there is a technology that allows you to step into other humans’ lived experience and feel — and not just in video form, but in the smells, in the emotions, in the feelings, and basically live out other people’s lived experience.

According to recent reports, that ability to make empathy mass scale would be a massive game changer in humans having more empathy for each other and understanding the challenges and problems that others are dealing with globally. That would be the technology that would advance things significantly.

What’s one habit you’ve changed personally because of environmental concerns?

In a recent development, my personal infrastructure. I’m lucky enough to have bought a house a few years ago and upgraded to a heat pump; Span [electrical] panels, which sets us up for vehicle-to-grid, solar, batteries, other things; an EV; and then less glamorous but equally vital: insulation, both in the siding and in the windows and blinds. I’m sort of on my journey. We already have an electric cooktop, it’s not the amazing kind, and we have gas hot water heaters, so those are next up — and solar and batteries.

Coffee with any sustainability leader, past or present — who do you pick?

I would change the question and say, who would I want to work for? There’s a ton to learn from someone by working for them, and I think my answer then is [New York City Mayor Zohran] Mamdani. Not a sustainability leader by default, but he has accomplished and built a political backing to do massive things that are ambitious, and from a sustainability lens, I would want to learn from that.

In the climate space, when we got started, the problem was [a need for more sustainable] tools. It has moved down the supply chain into execution, it’s go-to-market, and that means political will.

What’s the most overhyped climate solution right now?

AI. I use it. I enjoy it. I think it’s fun. But to say that it will solve the challenges of climate in the future are complete red herrings. AI is available to both sides. It is equally as effective at making gas extraction, oil extraction cheaper, faster, etc. as it is helping sustainable technologies get off the ground, and so I would say it is a neutral technology at best.

What’s an underrated solution that deserves more attention?

Nature as infrastructure. If people can’t get themselves to the place where they value forests for their aesthetics, for the health, for the community, for all of the other things, fine. Look at it on a spreadsheet and tell me how much it’s going to cost to replace several hundred thousand acres of forest with water treatment plants, water chiller plants, water purification plants, because that’s going to be a lot of tax dollars. And if we just let it burn, if we clear-cut it all to oblivion, that means that the city of Seattle’s water supply is not going to be as cold. It’s going to require a hell of a lot more purification, and there’s not going to be as much of it.

What impact do you hope your work has in 20 years?

My hope is that we’ve established the funding source for reforestation with a carbon market. The carbon market is what pulls nature as infrastructure into a valued asset. It’s not an esoteric nice-to-have from a philosophical perspective, it is a valued asset that puts it into the human system of economics in a much bigger way. A carbon market is as major an evolutionary step for humanity as the printing press, as banking, as generally accepted accounting principles.

A large firm had finished moving a group of business customers onto a fresh billing platform. The implementation team completed migration testing, reconciled the account data and handed the platform to billing operations, which would run the process day to day.

Industry observers note that operations accepted the migrated accounts, the required defects were closed, and the implementation work moved to “complete” status. The project team then shifted to the next group of customers.

Three weeks later, billing specialists began finding a recurring problem in a small set of migrated accounts. The records matched the approved migration rules, but certain combinations of account settings forced specialists to correct fields manually before an invoice could be released.

Each correction was manageable, but the pattern became expensive only after the same work kept appearing in normal billing activity.

The difference became clearer at the next billing cycle.

The affected accounts didn’t fail in the same way every time. One required a manual tax treatment, another needed a contract setting corrected, and another triggered an exception only after a billing adjustment.

Each case looked like “ordinary operating cleanup” until the team compared them and found the migration pattern underneath. That comparison took time because the work was being recorded where it occurred.

None of those activities were recorded as a reopened implementation issue while the project remained closed.

In a recent development, the cost showed up first in operating time. Billing specialists who should have been reviewing current invoices were opening migrated accounts, comparing settings and correcting fields before invoices could move.

Industry observers note that team leads added exception checks to the billing cycle, and finance partners joined troubleshooting calls to understand why the same account pattern kept reappearing. Customer-service teams then had to answer questions when invoice timing slipped for affected accounts.

Recent findings suggest that the extra work sat inside operations. It didn’t reopen the implementation project, and it didn’t change the completion status already recorded for the migration.

Industry observers note that the billing team also had to protect normal work while dealing with the exceptions. Meanwhile, experienced specialists spent part of each cycle correcting migrated accounts, which left less time for current billing issues that had nothing to do with the migration.

It has been revealed that as the pattern continued, managers started moving work between people to keep invoices flowing. The platform had been delivered, but the receiving team was now carrying a recurring cost that hadn’t existed before the change.

In a recent development, this is where the “Broken Handoffs” execution leak appears. The receiving team got the system, the documentation and the agreed support path, and the handoff itself worked as designed.

Recent findings suggest that those measures answered different questions. One captured whether the agreed work crossed the boundary successfully, while the other captured what it took to make that work function after the boundary.

Once the project closed, the operating cost had no direct route back into the measure that had already recorded the implementation as complete. The consequence stayed visible, but it lived in a different record.

The sensible response was to strengthen acceptance before the next group of customers. The firm did three things:.

Those changes helped. More configuration problems were caught before transfer, and operations had a stronger basis for accepting the work.

It has been revealed that the acceptance test still judged the deliverable at the moment of handoff. The recurring manual effort only became visible after enough migrated accounts passed through normal billing for the pattern to emerge.

A stronger test can reduce what crosses the boundary, but it still closes the project before downstream work has had time to reveal every consequence.

For the next group of customers, the stronger checks caught several configuration issues before transfer. Operations accepted the migrated accounts, the implementation work closed, and billing moved into the normal cycle with fewer exceptions than before.

A different pattern surfaced later.

A subset of accounts required manual correction only after a billing adjustment changed how two fields interacted. The migration had passed the stronger acceptance test because the matter didn’t appear until those accounts went through live billing activity.

It has been revealed that billing specialists again became the first people to see the consequence. They reopened affected accounts, compared the new exceptions with the earlier corrections and traced which cases required manual handling before invoices could move.

The implementation record still highlighted a “completed migration” while the added work accumulated inside the billing cycle.

The manufacturer also kept the implementation team available during a stabilization period. That gave operations a route back when the account pattern became clear.

Support path? It worked, and specialists traced the configuration logic, changed the migration rule for the next group of customers and helped operations clean up the affected accounts.

Industry observers note that the technical issue was fixed; however, the earlier operating cost remained where it had been counted. Billing had already spent time on corrections, finance had already absorbed additional review work, and customer service had already handled the questions created by delayed invoices.

Post-launch support corrected the problem after transfer, but it didn’t change the fact that the implementation had already been recorded as complete before the cost appeared.

A finished project can keep generating work after its own measures say the work is over. The receiving team carries the effect in operating time, service activity or rework while the sending team’s completion record remains unchanged.

A pattern like this becomes especially hard to see when both records are accurate. An implementation team can show that the agreed migration work passed its tests and was accepted. Operations can show that the live process now requires additional effort.

In a recent development, no one has to misreport anything. The separation sits in where each result is counted.

Recent findings suggest that that’s why the mechanism survives good project management, stronger acceptance and responsive support. The organization has improved how work crosses the boundary without reconnecting where completion is counted to where the later consequence appears.

A project isn’t finished when the work closes in one system while the cost of making it work continues to accumulate in another.

Recent findings suggest that as AI threatens to wipe out jobs, millions of people are ditching the 9-to-5 to build something of their own. And American Express is backing them with £1 million (about $1.3 million) in support to grow their small business—no strings attached.The $209 billion financial services giant is handing out £10,000 (about $13,000) grants to 100 independent U.K. businesses, in partnership with Be the Business, a U.K. organisation that helps small businesses boost their productivity.“We know that even a relatively modest investment can make a meaningful difference,” Hannah Lewis, country manager at American Express U.K., said, while adding that founders can use the cash towards “revamping their premises, reaching more customers or bringing something upcoming to their community.”.

In turn, helping them grow could help their local communities too. According to the scheme, one of the main objectives is “to help small businesses contribute to vibrant destinations, active high streets and socially connected local communities.”.

Amex’s own research found that 75% of British consumers believe small businesses positively impact their local communities, and around two-thirds would be more likely to shop with a business that employs local people.

But there’s a catch: the cash can’t go toward just anything, and 5% is held back until winners prove how they spent it.

It has been revealed that to apply, you’ll need to run an independent, for-profit business with a valid Organization Registration Number, incorporated on or before Dec. 1, 2025.

Industry observers note that you also need at least one employee on top of the owners or directors, and no more than 49 full-time equivalents. And you must operate from a permanent physical location in the U.K. that’s open to customers.

That rules a lot out. Online-only and home-based businesses, franchises, and anyone not registered with Companies House can’t apply.

Sources indicate that but, of course, the cash comes with conditions. Winners get 95% (£9,500) once they’ve signed a grant agreement and submitted an approved budget and delivery initiative. The last £500 only comes after they file a final impact report and proof of how they spent it.

Sources indicate that the money must also go on a specific project, like shopfront improvements, accessibility upgrades, equipment, e-commerce, digital marketing, product development or community events. It can’t cover day-to-day costs such as wages, rent, or stock. Applications will be judged on business impact, community impact, and project quality and feasibility.

Amex isn’t the only company throwing money at people who want to be their own boss.

Earlier this year, Zoom gave away $150,000 to five solopreneurs in the U.S. “This isn’t about building billion-dollar companies,” Zoom’s chief marketing officer Kim Storin told Fortune. “It’s about building sustainable, profitable businesses that support a life.”.

Multimillionaire entrepreneur Tim Armoo similarly launched the Legon Fund earlier this year, where he committed £5 million (around $6.7 million) of his own cash to fund AI startups founded by minority entrepreneurs.

Recent findings suggest that it comes as more than 33 million Americans are self-employed, with 82% of small businesses operating without a single employee, according to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Meanwhile, in the U.K., there are around 1.2 million startups, with 832,000 fresh manufacturer incorporations registered in 2025 alone. And that number just keeps growing.

LinkedIn CEO Daniel Shapero told Fortune that “founder” is now one of the fastest-growing job titles on the platform, up 70% year on year.

It has been revealed that as Armoo said, it’s never been easier to start your own business. “So now, you have no excuse, because you can learn—ChatGPT and Claude are virtually free—and if you’ve got something that’s working, here’s the money to get more customers for it.”.
