Crypto wallet provider Trezor has issued a security warning to cryptocurrency people following a recent theft report: "Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website.".

In a recent development, according to Onchain Lens, a user reported losing over $600,000 across TRON and Solana while using an iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1. Both the Trezor Safe 7 and the Exodus wallet were reportedly affected. The victim had been using a Trezor Safe 7 for nearly two months.

Sources indicate that according to the victim, the Trezor wallet arrived sealed, with no visible tampering; the recovery phrase was generated on the Trezor screen and not on the iPhone; the seed was written on paper and never stored digitally. The victim used Trezor Suite on an iPhone 17 Pro Max via Bluetooth and also had the Exodus wallet on the same iPhone.

According to recent reports, the device was running iOS 27.2.1, and the victim never approved the unauthorized transactions. The Trezor wallets for TRON and Solana shared one recovery phrase.

The user stated $580,000 was stolen from Trezor on TRON and that an unauthorized transaction moved 49,999 USDT on Nov. 21, 2026. The transaction used the default owner permission, making the signing authority central to the investigation.

Another $23,400 was drained from Trezor on Solana, and the victim says they never approved that transfer using the hardware device. The iPhone remains the main focus, as both Trezor Suite and Exodus were reportedly used on the same iPhone 17 Pro Max running iOS 27.2.1, and both were affected.

Trezor is designed to keep private keys inside the hardware device. However, compromising the phone alone should not normally provide access to Trezor's private keys, and the mechanism behind both thefts remains largely unknown.

On November 9, 2026, Apple issued iOS 27.2.1, which patched several security holes (including some related to Bluetooth). The victim was reportedly running this version when the theft occurred. Thus, there is currently no evidence connecting those vulnerabilities to these transactions. Possible causes outlined included compromised recovery credentials, unauthorized signing, or a device or software security failure.

It has been revealed that trezor responded to this disclosure, saying that Trezor wallets don’t get drained out of nowhere and that there are presently no reports of funds being stolen remotely from any device. It noted that similar cases usually trace back to a compromised wallet backup.

Sources indicate that @OnchainLens @binance @Bybit_Official UPDATE: This device came directly from Trezor and demonstrates no sign of an implant. We’re still investigating what happened. So far there’s no confirmed loss of funds from implants and no implant found in any Trezor Safe 7. Never type your wallet backup into a phone, app or website.

In a further update, Trezor confirmed that the device affected came directly from the firm and showed no sign of an implant. The wallet provider added that it continues to investigate what happened.

This appears to be a standalone case, as Trezor reiterated that, so far, no confirmed loss of funds from implants has been reported, and no implant has been found in any Trezor Safe 7. It also reiterated an important security warning: people should never enter their wallet backups into a phone, application, or website.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A large business unit was entering its annual planning cycle with three upcoming priorities competing for specialist capacity. The leadership team had already reduced the list once, and the remaining proposals had strong business cases, clear owners and estimated resource needs.

According to recent reports, the planning baseline also indicated an older regulatory-remediation program that would continue into the upcoming year. Nobody had forgotten it. The work was visible, funded and already staffed because the program had missed its original completion date.

During the planning session, one executive asked whether the remediation program would release its specialists early enough for the new priorities to start as planned. The program lead mentioned the current end date still held unless the final regulatory review produced additional work. The room accepted that date and returned to ranking the new priorities, treating the remediation capacity as already committed until then.

What the planning discussion didn’t do was force the remediation work to compete again with the three newly introduced priorities. It sat in the baseline as committed work, while leaders debated how to allocate what they believed was the remaining capacity.

By the end of the session, the team had made disciplined choices:.

The overcommitment was already there.

Industry observers note that the problem became visible in the first weeks of execution. One of the approved priorities needed several of the same risk, legal and data specialists who were still closing the remediation program.

Recent findings suggest that the planning model counted those people as partially available because the older work was expected to wind down early in the year. Instead, a final set of regulatory findings required more analysis, and a small group of specialists stayed fully engaged.

According to recent reports, the new priority still had its approved funding, executive sponsor and start date. The people needed to move it weren’t actually free.

The old work was visible, but its claim on the fresh year’s capacity had been treated as fixed background rather than as a choice.

According to recent reports, managers began stretching the same specialists across both commitments. The new priority’s first milestone slipped as specialist reviews that should have happened early were pushed behind remediation work. Meetings multiplied, decisions slowed, and work that looked fully staffed on paper started moving in fragments.

The pressure spread beyond those specialists. Project leads started moving milestones to fit the people they could get, finance held back some spending because dependent work couldn’t start, and senior leaders spent more time resolving clashes between commitments they believed had already been reconciled during planning.

The interesting thing was that the approved proposal hadn’t changed, but the amount of work that could move at the same time already had.

The new initiative hadn’t been badly prioritized at all. The leadership team had already removed a lower-ranked proposal, but part of the capacity used in the ranking exercise simply hadn’t been available to begin with.

This is where the “Hidden Problems” execution leak appears.

The planning process had surfaced the remediation program, its budget and its expected completion date, yet the fresh work was still being ranked against an overstated view of what remained available.

It has been revealed that A baseline records what’s already in motion, but it doesn’t force old work to justify its capacity against new work. Once carryover is treated as given, only the new initiatives are asked to compete.

That distinction matters because visibility can create false confidence.

Leaders can see every major piece of work on one page and still never face the question of whether an old commitment deserves to keep the people and budget it carried across the year boundary.

Sources indicate that listing carryover isn’t the same as choosing it again. The planning process therefore becomes disciplined about one side of the load while leaving the other side untouched.

When execution starts slowly, leadership tightens prioritization. Leaders ask for fewer initiatives, sharper business cases and clearer ranking, then delay or reject upcoming proposals that can’t justify scarce capacity.

Those actions improve the choices among newly introduced priorities; however, they don’t reopen the older commitments already sitting in the baseline. That was the pattern in this business unit.

Leadership had reduced the upcoming-priority list before approving the proposal, and when capacity pressure appeared, the first response was to ask whether one of the new initiatives should move more slowly.

The remediation program wasn’t part of that debate because it had been approved in the prior year, and finishing it was treated as an “obligation” rather than as a competing use of scarce capacity.

The organization was re-ranking upcoming work while the carryover never faced the same test.

A stronger planning process adds a formal carryover line. That certainly improves visibility, but it doesn’t change the underlying mechanism when carryover remains exempt from comparison.

The remediation work can appear clearly in the plan, with its budget, owner and expected completion date, and still never face the one central question: Is finishing this work now more valuable than starting the upcoming priority that needs the same people?

In this business unit, the remediation program remained on every planning view. Its existence was never hidden. What did stay hidden was the effect of treating its capacity claim as “non-negotiable” while the upcoming priorities competed for whatever was left.

The plan could be complete as an inventory and incomplete as a capacity decision.

Every item appeared somewhere, but not every item had to earn its place in the same contest for scarce people and budget.

By the time the conflict became obvious, leaders were dealing with a problem the planning process had already created. The remediation work couldn’t simply stop, and the upcoming priority had already been approved.

The same scarce specialists now sat between two legitimate commitments, each with consequences for delay. Leaders were forced to make the tradeoff during execution instead of during planning, when they still had more room to change the portfolio.

When that conflict reached the next leadership review, the discussion was no longer about which work deserved to start. It was about which already-approved commitment would lose access to people both sides now depended on.

Sources indicate that the plan didn’t fail because leaders chose the wrong upcoming priorities. Not at all. The planning choice had been postponed until both commitments were already in motion.

  • Industry observers note that “I thought, oh my gosh, what am I going to be peddling cigarettes?” Patrick told the “How Leaders Lead” podcast in a recent episode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1998, Artemis Patrick turned down a job at a relatively small perfume brand that had just been acquired by the luxury giant LVMH. That manufacturer was Sephora, and 26 years later, she became its North America CEO. Patrick stepped into the top job for the global beauty retailer’s North America division in April 2024, earning a shoutout in its parent company’s half-year earnings call in July for “good performance.”But Patrick’s journey to the top of the cosmetics empire started with a detour into cigarettes.

Industry observers note that patrick was studying for her MBA at San Francisco State University when a friend introduced her to the LVMH brand, which was hiring for entry-level planning roles. Patrick initially went in to interview for a role at the duty-free giant DFS in the only category that was hiring: tobacco.

Industry observers note that “I thought, oh my gosh, what am I going to be peddling cigarettes?” Patrick told the “How Leaders Lead” podcast in a recent episode. “This is crazy. So I [asked] if they had anything else, and she said, well there is this tech giant called Sephora—LVMH just acquired it—and it sells fragrance.”.

Sources indicate that “Same salary, same building, because at the time Sephora was sharing the office floor with DFS. And I remarked, I mean, obviously I’ll take the beauty job. She said there’s only one catch: You have to wear black white, or gray.”.

“And I remarked, I’ll take the cigarette job.”.

Sources indicate that patrick, who emigrated to the U.S. from Iran at the age of 7, said her decision to take the DFS role rather than the beauty job wasn’t necessarily down to independence but rather to personal finances. After all, Patrick was a student, and her wardrobe was full of patterned dresses—she couldn’t afford to repurchase multiple monochromatic looks.

DFS turned out to be an “incredible opportunity” that took Patrick around the world and promptly propelled her from the cigarette category into wine. But in 2006, Sephora came calling again courtesy of a referral from Carolyn Bojanowski, now Sephora’s executive vice president for merchandising.

Patrick interviewed with the same HR representative she had turned down years before, and the corporate dress code of black, white, and gray (“concept colors,” as they were referred to at the time) was still in place.

Recent findings suggest that “They’d added red to the concept at that point,” Patrick recalls. “It was actually another, I think, six or seven years before we added color.”.

Patrick’s path to Sephora and then up its ranks wasn’t linear—after DFS she worked at Restoration Hardware and Peet’s Coffee & Tea—and noted this diversity of experience is now precisely what she looks for when building her own teams.

Industry observers note that “I feel that my job is to remove obstacles and to make sure that they get to do what we hired them to do,” added Patrick. “So I definitely believe in building diverse teams, and I do feel that my job as a leader is to protect them from the noise and deal with the things that I should be dealing with.”.

Why hiring neurodivergent talent isn’t enough, and what leaders should do instead

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Companies are increasingly recognizing the value of neurodivergent talent, but hiring is only part of the picture.
  • Jonathan Mok, a Hong Kong-based neurodiversity advocate, speaker, and leadership trainer, has seen that gap from both sides.
  • Jonathan Mok, neurodiversity advocate, speaker, and leadership trainer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Companies are increasingly recognizing the value of neurodivergent talent, but hiring is only part of the picture. Many neuroinclusion strategies still rely on employees to disclose their diagnoses and request workplace adjustments themselves, an approach that assumes they feel safe doing so. According to a 2026 survey by the nonprofit Understood.org, about 70% of neurodivergent employees in the U.S. worry that disclosing their neurodivergence could negatively affect them at work. When employees stay silent, employers may never learn which barriers need addressing.

Jonathan Mok, a Hong Kong-based neurodiversity advocate, speaker, and leadership trainer, has seen that gap from both sides. He was diagnosed with ADHD and autism at 37, after years of working in education in Hong Kong. Today, he trains corporate teams across Asia on neuroinclusion and coaches executives who have received late diagnoses. His own experience suggests that even when employees do disclose, formal support does not always translate into belonging.

Jonathan Mok, neurodiversity advocate, speaker, and leadership trainer.

According to recent reports, after his diagnosis, a workplace medical committee recommended that Mok should not feel obliged to attend department social gatherings. When his boss invited the team to a New Year lunch and he raised his hand to join, colleagues kept telling him nobody was forcing him to go. They meant well, but a measure intended to protect him left him feeling excluded. “I wanted to go. My boss was paying for lunch,” Mok recalls. “But the message I kept hearing was that I didn’t really belong there.”.

Despite receiving formal accommodations, Mok continued to face challenges at work, and he resigned in 2020. His experience reflects a wider pattern. In a 2025 report by Boston Consulting Group, supported by SG Enable, 62% of neurodivergent employees surveyed in Singapore said their neurodivergence had been misunderstood as a poor attitude. While 99% believed reasonable accommodations would help, only 33% said these were available at their workplace, and just 24% considered them adequate.

In a recent development, the findings point to a disconnect between recognizing neurodivergent talent and creating the conditions for it to thrive. Gartner predicted in 2023 that by 2027, a quarter of Fortune 500 companies would actively recruit neurodivergent talent to improve business performance. Recruitment, however, is only the first step. Inclusion also depends on whether employees feel they belong, can speak up without fear of judgment, and receive support that works in practice.

Recent findings suggest that mok believes that an emphasis on meritocracy can lead some employers to assume that anyone capable enough to be hired does not need to disclose anything. Employees, in turn, try to fit in until they no longer can. He adds that organizations often focus on deficits and rely heavily on medical guidance rather than on what individuals actually want or need. In his view, support should not depend on employees asking for it; it should be built into how the organization operates.

He also challenges the idea that organizations must be ready to hire neurodivergent employees before taking any steps toward inclusion. One cosmetics retailer found that quiet shopping hours did little to ease the sensory demands of a busy store. After consulting Mok, a colleague, and store staff, it introduced ribbon-marked baskets that let customers signal a preference for minimal interaction without explaining their needs. Because retail turnover is high, the accompanying staff training was kept simple enough to pass on to newly introduced employees.

Mok points to a neurodivergent internship program at the Hong Kong office of an international insurer as a more comprehensive example. Rather than treating recruitment as the endpoint, the company paired the program with manager training and structured onboarding, helping teams build the skills to support neurodivergent colleagues. It also works with a local nonprofit organization to source talent and provide training.

To help organizations turn good intentions into action, Mok uses a 4P framework covering People, Place, Policy, and Program. It is designed as an ongoing approach rather than a one-time training session. Under People, he encourages organizations to recognize inclusive managers, create safe channels for raising concerns, and highlight neurodivergent role models. Under Place, he recommends sensory-friendly workspaces and normalizing tools that allow people to work in ways that suit them.

Sources indicate that policy involves clear procedures around disclosure, workplace adjustments, and job expectations, so that employees and managers know what support is available. Many managers, Mok notes, only look for guidance after a problem arises and then have to dig through documents that can run 50 or 60 pages. The program focuses on long-term planning, consultation, and partnerships with community organizations, including neurodivergent individuals and their families, so that initiatives address real needs rather than assumptions.

For companies operating across Asia, Mok stresses the importance of understanding how culture, law, and local knowledge shape neurodiversity in each market. Even within the region, conditions such as autism and ADHD are recognized differently, as the contrast between Hong Kong and mainland China shows. Such differences can complicate standardized inclusion policies. He also believes that meaningful progress is possible for organizations of every size, not only multinational corporations.

Industry observers note that for Mok, the next stage of neuroinclusion means looking past whether organizations are willing to hire neurodivergent people and asking whether their cultures, policies, and leadership allow those employees to stay and succeed. “The next diversity metric should not be hires,” he claims. “It should be stays.” A seat at the Fresh Year lunch, offered without hesitation, may say more about an organization’s inclusion than any recruitment target.

Industry News: Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1231 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second.
  • For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises.
  • Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

In a recent development, according to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

Those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

Denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

It has been revealed that the sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

It has been revealed that timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

This removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

Industry observers note that app developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

Sources indicate that node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

This is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

The affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

Contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams plan to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec claims it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

In a recent development, the coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

Denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Science Corporation, the medical technology startup founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the firm stated in a blog post.

Investors in the latest round valued the company at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.

Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage fresh technologies to understand and interact with the brain.

Science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for fresh conditions.

Hodak confirmed that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

It has been revealed that with the funding, the manufacturer aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S.

Still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The manufacturer is currently designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

In periods of competing blocks, Solana validators spend CPU and timing resources replaying blocks that will never make it into the canonical chain once another competing block from the same slot has been finalized.

Sources indicate that this PR proposes changes to validator software to help prevent work from being done. It also decouples functionality and gives control to Votor in requesting slot cancellation without modifying BankForks.

Sources indicate that overall, this is a reasonable technical improvement and has a good engineering motivation. Further technical comments and review would be helpful to understand if there are potential race conditions or issues with reliability of replay and consensus. This could be split into two PRs to make it easier to test and review.

There are two main proposed changes:.

Make sure that the replay thread doesn't block on the scheduler finishing processing blocks.

Add slot cancellation, where Votor can tell replay which blocks to stop trying to process.

There was an earlier PR (PR #16454) which attempted to solve a similar problem, but that PR included some complexity around being able to pause and resume block processing.

Recent findings suggest that this PR attempts to solve a similar problem in a simpler way by adding slot cancellation. It allows validators to stop replaying blocks that will never make it into the canonical chain once another block from the same slot has been finalized.

Industry observers note that this is an efficiency-focused change to validator software. It's not intended to have a particular effect on transaction throughput or SOL price. For Solana to continue to perform well, it's important not only to continue to increase TPS but also continue to find ways to make sure that validators aren't doing unnecessary work.

According to recent reports, for everyday owners, it's unlikely there would be noticeable effects from this change. Sending/receiving SOL, using a DEX, using DeFi more broadly, and using any other Solana-powered website/app should all continue to function as normal. It's possible that users could see some benefits from this change in the form of Solana being more performant in the face of heavy compute loads.

#133470. I Paid My Team a Bonus for Doing More — and the Work Got Worse. Here’s What It Taught Me.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1092 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

I Paid My Team a Bonus for Doing More — and the Work Got Worse. Here’s What It Taught Me.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1092 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • According to recent reports, the bonus was simple.
  • Recent findings suggest that after it started, creative quality dropped.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

According to recent reports, the bonus was simple. Hit a set number of completed videos and earn extra cash on top of your salary. I wanted more productivity, and a clear target seemed like the fairest way to ask for it.

Recent findings suggest that after it started, creative quality dropped. At least a quarter of our clients began to complain, and our cancellation rate hit 13%.

The target mentioned completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those shows up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the plan asked for.

Industry observers note that I paid extra for the thing I measured and lost the thing I valued. The clients noticed before I did.

For a while, we were clueless about what was happening. Then we dug into the revision requests. The revision rounds behind the complaints could easily have been avoided in the first edit.

We traced it further. Editors were bypassing parts of the process to save time. Where a video clearly needed motion graphics, they used basic B-roll instead. They also put less effort into building a stronger hook.

When we tracked mistakes by team and by editor, the same people were making the same mistakes on repeat. Those were the editors producing the most videos. Newly introduced editors made repeat mistakes too, but they produced few videos, so that was a different problem.

Recent findings suggest that that changed how I read the bonus. My read is that it paid people to skip the steps that protect quality.

Industry observers note that I wasn’t the first owner to run into this. In a field experiment in Chinese factories, economists paid workers a bonus for output. Quantity rose, and quality fell sharply — and the effect was much stronger for workers on a flat wage. My editors are on fixed salaries, so I was in exactly that group.

Recent findings suggest that A second study, published in Management Science, tested 224 retail stores. Regular performance review conversations raised profits by about 7%. A profit bonus alone produced no significant gain. Paying the bonus on top of the reviews erased the benefit of the reviews, and the authors’ surveys suggest the bonus changed the nature of the conversations.

Bonuses aren’t always the wrong tool. A research review by Dirk Sliwka for IZA World of Labor notes that they can work when the key tasks are easy to measure, and workers can change their output, as with installing windshields. A good edit isn’t easy to measure. None of this research comes from creative work, so I treat it as a pattern and not as proof for my business.

We stopped chasing volume. Editors who were doing good work got raises, and everyone else got a clear path to follow. Use the same steps, avoid revision rounds, and you qualify for a raise. A raise replaced the bonus.

In a recent development, the results came rapidly. Within a month, our cancellation rate was back to single digits. For the next few months, we delivered better, and client retention went up. Our cancellation rate is now about 3%, which is normal. Clients pause or leave when they stop wanting to create content or have health or travel reasons. When we track why clients cancel, quality-related reasons are under 1.8%.

According to recent reports, the difference is what each pays for. A volume bonus pays for finishing. A raise tied to fewer revisions pays for getting it right the first time, and it doesn’t disappear next month.

We’re also piloting a second model with three editors. They have a low base salary, and their pay grows with the clients they keep. Lose a client, and the commission drops. Keep one, and it grows, and a high-paying client can mean steady, high commission. Pay follows retention instead of volume, which makes each editor responsible for keeping their clients.

Sources indicate that the early signal is small. The three editors are taking ownership of their clients because keeping them keeps their commission high. I’m seeing slightly better results so far. I won’t pretend that’s proof. Three people is a pilot, not a verdict.

Recent findings suggest that while the pilot runs, we’re writing SOPs that define what quality work really means and how to track it. We also built a two-layer QC process, one AI layer and one human layer, so mistakes get caught before the client sees them.

The hard part hasn’t been the formula. It’s been the people. Most of the team still wants fixed income for peace of mind, and I understand why. A low base with a bigger upside asks someone to take on risk they never signed up for. A few editors are willing to try but want certainty about what they’ll earn. I don’t have a clean answer yet.

Recent findings suggest that before you add a bonus, here are the questions I would ask now: What am I counting, and what matters that I am not counting? Am I tracking rework next to output? It was the only way we found who was skipping steps. Can the person actually change the number? And what will they do if the only way to hit it is to cut a corner?

If you change how people are paid, pilot it with volunteers and expect resistance. A pay change is a change to the deal.

After it started, creative quality dropped. At least a quarter of our clients began to complain, and our cancellation rate hit 13%.

It has been revealed that the target said completed videos, so that is what it measured. Creative quality is harder to count. A cut that lands with the audience, a pause that gives a line room to breathe, a graphic that fits the story — none of those shows up in a tally. When one thing is counted, and the other isn’t, people look after the counted thing. That isn’t laziness. It’s what the proposal asked for.

#133469. Breaking: Amazon is buying Decart’s AI chip software for a reported $7.5B and bringing its founders aboard

Breaking: Amazon is buying Decart’s AI chip software for a reported $7.5B and bringing its founders aboard

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (671 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.
  • Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.
  • According to recent reports, amazon didn’t disclose financial terms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 23, 2026 at 8:25 amNovember 23, 2026 at 8:27 am.

Amazon confirmed Monday morning that it will acquire Decart’s AI optimization technology, known as the Decart Optimization Stack, and bring on the 3-year-old startup’s founders and team of AI researchers and engineers.

According to recent reports, amazon didn’t disclose financial terms. Amazon agreed to pay about $7.5 billion for the assets, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The deal is tied to performance targets over five years, Globes reported.

Industry observers note that the deal could boost Amazon’s push to compete with Nvidia, which sells most of the chips used for training and running AI models today. Amazon makes its own AI chips, called Trainium, and has signaled prepares to start selling them directly to other companies, beyond its own AWS data centers.

“We believe we’re going to have a very significant business selling chips externally,” CEO Andy Jassy stated on the manufacturer’s earnings call last month.

Amazon declared the deal the same day Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, ending a leadership shakeup at the chipmaker that put CFO Colette Kress in the interim role.

Decart’s software is designed to get more performance out of each chip, one of the main selling points Amazon needs to win those external customers. Microsoft is building its own Maia chips, mainly for its own AI services, and Google has its TPUs.

Recent findings suggest that decart’s software has also run on chips from Nvidia and Google. Amazon didn’t say whether that will continue.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” mentioned Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing, in the blog post announcing the acquisition.

Recent findings suggest that decart’s three co-founders are joining Amazon: CEO Dean Leitersdorf, his brother Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev. Amazon isn’t buying Decart’s AI models, Bloomberg reported. Those include Lucy, which edits live video in real time, and Oasis, which generates interactive virtual worlds.

The deal runs through Annapurna Labs, Amazon’s chip unit, and Decart’s technology will be used to improve performance on Amazon’s Trainium and Inferentia AI chips, according to Globes. The Israeli business publication reported that Annapurna co-founder Nafea Bshara led the negotiations for Amazon.

The founders, who own about 64% of Decart, have committed to stay at Amazon for five years and could receive about $4.8 billion collectively, Globes reported.

In a recent development, amazon bought Annapurna, also founded in Israel, in 2015 for a reported $350 million. Its engineers went on to design Trainium and Amazon’s other custom chips.

Recent findings suggest that amazon and Decart have worked together since 2025. Decart was among the first customers on Trainium3, and Amazon said last December that Decart was running real-time video four times faster on Trainium at half the cost of GPUs.

According to recent reports, the deal follows Amazon’s release last month of TorchNeuron, a tool that runs common AI code on Trainium with minimal changes. Both moves target the software advantage that has kept developers on Nvidia hardware, as GeekWire explained when the talks surfaced in October.

Decart drew interest from other massive buyers before Amazon. Anthropic was in talks to acquire it for about $6 billion, Bloomberg reported in August, before it walked away in September. Nvidia held earlier acquisition talks, according to CTech, and invested in Decart’s $300 million funding round in May.

Sources indicate that “From day one, our mission has been to redefine the boundaries of what AI can do and to make it dramatically more efficient along the way,” Dean Leitersdorf stated in Amazon’s announcement. “Joining Amazon gives our team the scale, the customers, and the infrastructure to pursue that mission faster than we could on our own.”.

The deal is subject to regulatory clearance. Amazon didn’t say what happens to Decart’s AI models or to its existing customers, such as eBay, which is also an investor in the startup.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although XRP has begun to cool from the sudden price recovery witnessed at the beginning of the week that allowed it to reclaim the $1 price level, payment activity across its network has remained high.

After multiple days of extreme caution from traders, the latest on-chain data from XRPScan reveals a sharp resurgence in payment volume on the XRP Ledger.

The data shows that the total volume of XRP transferred between accounts on the XRP Ledger surpassed a massive 997.2 million XRP on November 23rd.

Further data indicates that this marks an increase of about 370.1% in XRP payment volume over the last 24 hours; this means that the amount of XRP transferred between accounts has soared significantly after the major drop in activity seen the previous day.

The rapid spike in volume has drawn attention as it far exceeds the network's 30-day average payment volume of 791.8 million XRP.

While the surge has coincided with a sharp rebound in the price of XRP, it appears that transaction activity has picked up considerably as the market regains confidence.

It is key to note that the surge in XRP payment volume has come after XRP witnessed a parabolic price move, showing a daily increase of over 10% after reclaiming its $1 price level.

However, it appears that the rally has cooled as XRP has briefly fallen back into the red, retesting $0.9 once again.

Although its price movement has become weak again, on-chain data indicates that its network activity remains strong as holders continue to move the token across accounts.

Pedestal AI raises $4.7 million to agentify the supply chain

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Delivery supply chains are the lifeblood of contemporary businesses — and a new startup is betting that purpose-built AI agents can make them run a lot more smoothly.
  • Recent findings suggest that on Tuesday, Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding.
  • The seed round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delivery supply chains are the lifeblood of contemporary businesses — and a new startup is betting that purpose-built AI agents can make them run a lot more smoothly.

Recent findings suggest that on Tuesday, Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding. The tech giant’s goal is to use agentic AI to make supply chains faster and more reliable — a proposal that’s already brought them together with Fortune 500 companies and some of the largest shipping firms in the world.

The seed round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage. Pedestal notes the funding will be used to expand its product and engineering time, grow the marketing organization, and support additional deployments.

In practice, much of Pedestal’s work is about removing friction from the shipping process — with agentic technology used as a means to that end. In one case, the manufacturer reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents to take on some of the work that drivers were supposed to do. The agentic system they built would call customers 30 minutes before a delivery and collect any special instructions; if the call didn’t go through, a text would be sent from a separate system. Along the way, the deployment collected a wealth of data about friction points in the process, which could be used to optimize the system even further.

CEO Raj Aggarwal says contemporary AI systems are particularly useful for dealing with that data. “The challenge is that the data is messy and it’s constantly changing,” Aggarwal told TechCrunch. “It’s disparate because it sits in so many legacy systems. That’s what makes it hard.”.

Supply chain AI has become a particularly hot space in recent months as alumni from autonomous driving teams look to launch their own startups. The supply chain startup Atomic, launched by a team of Tesla alumni, came out of stealth in 2025 with an emphasis on streamlining inventory. Another venture called Loop was launched by Uber alums to focus on predictive analytics.

Recent findings suggest that as Aggarwal sees it, deliveries are particularly well-suited to training reinforcement learning systems. Because of their high volumes and easily measured outcomes, it’s easy to fine-tune contemporary AI systems toward what’s working and away from what isn’t.

Perhaps most importantly, it’s the kind of problem that can have an immediate effect on a client’s bottom line, making it easy to justify the expense.

“If you can get it right,” he told TechCrunch, “you can have really substantial impact.”.

Reddit’s stock has taken a battering this year, but its COO says it’s barely started banking ‘over a decade of karma’ from devoted users

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reddit boasts engagement metrics that would be the envy of many other online platforms: Over 80% of its monetization comes from loyal, logged-in owners, who spend eight times as much time on the site in their fifth year as they did in their first.And yet, Reddit’s share price is down 62% for the year to date, as the platform grapples with an internet increasingly shaped by AI.In its Q3 earnings call in October, Reddit’s CEO, Steve Huffman, mentioned Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode were leading to a decline in search referrals to the site, the lifeblood of many social and media-adjacent businesses.
  • In a recent development, chief Operating Officer Jen Wong told Fortune in an exclusive interview that some factors were lost in translation.
  • Industry observers note that in their first year on Reddit, customers tend to spend five minutes a day on the app or website.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reddit boasts engagement metrics that would be the envy of many other online platforms: Over 80% of its monetization comes from loyal, logged-in owners, who spend eight times as much time on the site in their fifth year as they did in their first.And yet, Reddit’s share price is down 62% for the year to date, as the platform grapples with an internet increasingly shaped by AI.In its Q3 earnings call in October, Reddit’s CEO, Steve Huffman, mentioned Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode were leading to a decline in search referrals to the site, the lifeblood of many social and media-adjacent businesses. The market did not like the implications, and the share price dropped from just shy of $130 apiece to a little under $91 overnight.

In a recent development, chief Operating Officer Jen Wong told Fortune in an exclusive interview that some factors were lost in translation. The shifting relationship between Reddit and search engines “requires a different kind of partnership,” she mentioned, rather than any separation. If anything, Wong believes Reddit is well-positioned to navigate the latest era of online information gathering.

Industry observers note that in their first year on Reddit, customers tend to spend five minutes a day on the app or website. By their fifth year, that figure rises to 40 minutes, Wong tells Fortune. The number of “communities” (topic-focused discussion groups) that users are in jumps from 10 in the first year to more than 100 by their fifth.

“Reddit is really interesting because we have customers who have over a decade of karma,” Wong said. “Reddit typically gets you as a young adult, and then you season over time in this incredible way. If you look at the chart, it’s very consistent.”.

Wong sees customers’ changing life stages reflected in the communities they join: “[They’ve] gone through life with Reddit. You started as a student, you got your first rental place, you got married, you had kids, and we see kind of your life’s journey.

“You just never age out of Reddit because all of those life stages are available to you on Reddit, and you’re always going through something that you have to traverse.”.

Navigating different life stages appears to be a key differentiator of the Reddit platform. In 2024, an article published in “Higher Education Research and Development” found that one in three students use Reddit for study help, ahead of TikTok at 14.9% and Instagram at 12.7%. YouTube leads the pack, with more than 90% of the 1,000 students surveyed using it for educational purposes.

According to recent reports, the site’s leadership wants to expand on that function. In early November, Reddit launched Reddit Reviews, organizing product feedback across multiple communities to provide overall ratings.

“Logged-in people season very, very well, which is another motivation for us to say we want more logged-in users, because we want the opportunity to teach you about all these other aspects of Reddit,” Wong adds, “Not just the information and retrieval part of Reddit, but the part of Reddit that is around the connection, the communities, and the conversation.”.

Industry observers note that every media platform needs to maintain or grow its audience. But Reddit has a unique problem: It has more than 100,000 “communities,” according to various reports, all of which have volunteer moderators. These moderators are unpaid and are not Reddit employees, instead choosing to spend their free time building their communities and ensuring the content is fit for its purpose.

But with ever-evolving channels and upcoming voices within them, demand for experienced moderators is high—in fact, Reddit even has a dedicated page where communities can recruit volunteer moderators.

In the recruitment group, individuals are either looking for or offering moderation skills for hours a day, on a daily basis. Posts include requests for moderators in specific time zones, often for about 3 hours a day.

But Wong says even if Reddit wanted to bring its moderators in-house and pay them, they probably wouldn’t take it. While moderators are interested in earning, she said, they didn’t want strings attached: “They really like their independence from us, to be able to say, ‘This is our community, we set the rules, and this is how we want to operate.’.

According to recent reports, “Our relationship with moderators, I think, has greatly improved. I’ve been with Reddit eight, almost nine years, and where at the beginning we were not investing as much as we could in creating moderator tools and making their lives better in terms of reducing some of the repetitive work, over the last few years we’ve done a much better job also applying AI to help them with a toolkit, so that they can spend the time on the things that they really care about.”.

In a recent development, but overall, Wong is bullish on Reddit’s long-term position in the age of AI. “Reddit is basically the taste layer of the internet. No model and no recommendation system can be good, I think, without a dash of Reddit in it, because you just don’t have the freshness of information. That adds value in so many places.”.

Breaking: Loopscale Pauses Protocol After kySOL Collateral Was Priced as zBTC in a 4,597 SOL Loan

📅 07 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1307 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC.
  • One token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins.
  • Industry observers note that loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC. The decimal mismatch behind it is the most instructive part of the incident, and a second attack path reveals how far the probing went.

One token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins. The arithmetic behind the mistake is simple.

Industry observers note that loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor. Its APIs were taking more than 30,000 malicious requests a day. Loopscale's pause announcement, as summarized on CoinMarketCap, says user deposits remain secure and affected vaults were restored. The team has not named the suspected attacker.

Recent findings suggest that the loan itself can be traced onchain. A November 1 transaction shows a wallet Loopscale identified drawing 4,597 SOL after depositing one kySOL, a restaked SOL token. The collateral deposit paired kySOL with a zBTC asset identifier, which backs up Loopscale's account that the collateral was valued as a different asset.

Sources indicate that an independent researcher's trace found that the attacker bought one kySOL for about 1.31 SOL and deposited it into Loopscale roughly 154 seconds later. The protocol priced it as ten zBTC. At the loan's implied SOL price, that kySOL was worth somewhere near $120, while ten zBTC would be worth about ten Bitcoin.

The numbers line up with a decimal mismatch. On Solana, each token's mint account stores its own decimal precision, as Solana's documentation on tokens explains. kySOL uses nine decimals, like SOL, while a Bitcoin-denominated token such as zBTC uses eight. One kySOL is 1,000,000,000 base units, and read at eight decimals, that same raw balance comes out to 10.0. The protocol never had to be fooled about the price of Bitcoin. It only had to read one token's raw amount on another token's decimal scale.

That arithmetic explains the reported valuation, but it is not a root-cause statement from Loopscale. The team's own description is broader: a misconfigured combination of asset-pricing parameters caused collateral to be valued as a different asset. The result was an undercollateralized loan of about $412,000.

The harder question is how the protocol accepted a mismatch at all. According to the researcher's analysis, the attacker picked a price entry for zBTC, labeled the collateral as an Orca position and deposited kySOL. Under the Orca collateral rule, the kySOL mint was allowed to differ from the zBTC identifier. Labeling it as a standard SPL token would have failed, since that rule demands the mint and identifier match.

That detail matters more than the decimals. Each rule looked sensible by itself, and the flaw lived in the combination: a price source, a collateral type label and a mint check that together let one token be priced as another. It also explains why Loopscale pointed to both its publicly inspectable program logic and its private transaction-building APIs. Thirty thousand requests a day reads like systematic probing for a combination the normal API would build or authorize.

According to recent reports, loopscale's November 6 enhancement named two attack paths. The second went after the USDC Genesis Vault. Per the protocol, an atomic transaction bundle sold a loan carrying an extreme interest rate into the vault, inflating its net asset value and setting up a disproportionate redemption of about $521,000. Loopscale says its systems halted that redemption within 30 seconds of the transaction being generated.

In a recent development, so the incident ended in two different outcomes. The SOL path produced a real undercollateralized loan, while the USDC path was an attempt the team states it stopped. Counting both as stolen would overstate the damage, and Loopscale maintains that depositors took no loss and that affected vaults were made whole.

Loopscale linked four addresses in its disclosure. The two Solana addresses are 247Lk5YNH9URfBBvxVUtDruz8GvGX8gKGuYHVCZThpiR and AzPh2dUV3duK9n8PWV6CxKMwWr9Rk7fxPNBZuv1CiwMr.

It has been revealed that the two EVM addresses are 0xb8959Aca4e4C796A3BaDA66833eAe60b1BC0bfb2 and 0xB7Ec7eF24FD73f3000C651CA9D0Fa45b61DcF854. Reports indicate the borrowed SOL was bridged out of the protocol, which fits the pairing of Solana and EVM addresses.

It has been revealed that the loan's later history is visible onchain as well. A November 3 liquidation of the same loan moved about 4,598.4 SOL from a separate wallet back to the lending strategy. The researcher's trace puts the figure at 4,598.434180621 wSOL against 4,597 SOL borrowed, a gap of roughly 1.43 SOL. The liquidator received the lone kySOL as collateral. The public record doesn't yet show who funded that liquidation, so Loopscale's post-mortem will need to explain how the vault was made whole.

The takeaways are narrow and practical. Decimal scales should come from the token's own mint data rather than a configured identifier, and a deposit should fail when the collateral's mint doesn't match the asset the pricing path assumes. Private transaction-building APIs deserve the same scrutiny as onchain code, because an attacker who can probe them tens of thousands of times a day can map out which combinations they will build.

Sources indicate that vault accounting needs limits too. An extreme interest rate that is legal in the program can still reprice a share if the vault treats the loan mark as authoritative, which is why the 30-second halt on the second path counted for so much.

It has been revealed that this looks less like a clever exploit than a missing sanity check. A deposit worth about $120 should never support a 4,597 SOL loan, and a simple ceiling on collateral value against the borrower's deposited units would have flagged it. Loopscale also lost $5.8 million in April 2025 to a pricing flaw before recovering the funds, so the next thing to watch is whether its post-mortem indicates pricing safeguards that match how often this class of bug has shown up.

What’s Next For Recruiting, Job Hunting And HR? More AI, Of Course

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (779 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines.
  • Recent findings suggest that so far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows.
  • To get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, AI agents and humanoid robots may dominate the funding headlines. But even so, investors haven’t lost interest in startups focused on finding, filling and managing jobs for actual humans.

Recent findings suggest that so far this year, venture backers have poured close to $4 billion into an assortment of global companies focused on recruiting, finding jobs and streamlining processes associated with HR and payroll management, Crunchbase data shows. Not surprisingly, the vast majority are also incorporating a heavy dose of AI.

To get a sense where capital is flowing, we used Crunchbase data to analyze investment to employment-related categories for the past few years. Broadly, findings show 2026 funding on track to meet or slightly exceed year-ago levels, albeit with reduced deal count.

It has been revealed that much of this year’s investment has gone to a small group of companies. To illustrate, below we put together a list of 14 of the largest fundraisers.

As you can see, it’s a varied list, with a commonly shared theme of bringing more automation to hiring, HR and payroll tasks.

According to recent reports, by far the largest funding recipient is Mercor, a startup that pairs human experts with developers of AI models and tools. The 4-year-old company raised $750 million in a Series D round this month at a whopping $20 billion valuation.

San Francisco-based Mercor is betting that as companies build AI agents to take on more work tasks, demand for subject matter experts to guide these efforts will grow. While frontier labs have been its primary buyers for the past few years, Mercor claims it expects enterprises will soon be its major customers.

The next two largest fundraisers on our list for this year are focused on automating more employer tasks. Paris-based Skello secured $220 million this summer for its AI-enabled software platform for HR teams. And HiBob, a New York-based platform for HR and payroll, picked up $166 million in a Salesforce1-led financing.

Sources indicate that of course, investors aren’t only looking at startups automating work tasks or training AI agents to do so. They’re also backing companies focused on the old-fashioned business of matching workers and employers.

In this sector, one of the larger rounds this year went to San Francisco-based Juicebox, an AI tool for recruiters to find talented candidates. The 4-year-old firm picked up an $80 million Series B at an $850 million valuation.

Agentic hiring is also a thing. Metaview, a San Francisco-based startup that offers an agentic recruiting platform optimized, in its words, to “get the right butts in seats,” secured $60 million in a September Series C financing. Around the same time, London’s Jack & Jill AI, which offers AI agents for finding careers and for hiring, closed on $40 million in Series A funding.

Another agentic hiring platform, San Francisco’s Paraform, announced a $40 million round this spring, pitching itself as an offering for an age in which employers are making fewer hires overall but still need highly skilled people for highly paid jobs.

So what kind of employment future do startup funding trends paint for human jobseekers?

Not a good one. As a human who has spent decades writing about sector-specific startup funding, this is probably the most depressing data dive into investment trends for an industry that I have ever done.

Overall, the bulk of big rounds are going to one of three categories: using humans to help train their potential AI replacements, automating work tasks around supporting people in the workplace, and getting AI to help hire the right people for the dwindling pool of available positions.

According to recent reports, typically, I’m rooting for startups to succeed. And honestly, there’s not an individual manufacturer highlighted here that I’m specifically hoping will fail. But nonetheless, the broad vision of an increasingly AI-dominated workplace does bring with it a sense of trepidation.

They also stock sugar packets, teas, mini creamers, plastic stirrers and paper cups. It’s too much. Offer fewer coffees so you order less. With a Roth, there are no minimum distributions, and you can take the money out whenever you want, provided it meets certain requirements like a first-time home purchase, higher education or unreimbursed medical expenses.

Make sure your company has an HSA and contribute the max. It will reduce your tax expense and allow you to save money for future healthcare expenses.

Sources indicate that nvidia’s equity in private companies continues to grow: It revealed its stakes are now worth $65.5 billion on Tuesday, up from the $22 billion reported in January. The increase includes both fresh investments and significant markups of existing portfolio companies.

The tech giant invested $16 billion into equities in the past quarter alone, it noted, and $58 billion in the past nine months of its fiscal year. This amount includes buying shares in public and private companies, yet it indicates how the chipmaker made massive bets over the course of the year, especially compared to last year; in November 2025, the company reported spending $5 billion buying equity in the first nine months of that fiscal year.

But it’s unclear if this growth will continue under the interim CEO and Jensen Huang’s successor.

Nvidia stated in late 2023 that the goal of its corporate investing is to expand the AI ecosystem by backing startups it considers to be “game changers and market makers.”  Over the nearly three years that followed, the chipmaker has invested in nearly 350 startups, according to PitchBook. The companies Nvidia backed include Anthropic and OpenAI; neolabs like Thinking Machines and Reflection; neoclouds, like Lambda, Nscale, and Crusoe; as well as other companies developing AI infrastructure, robotics startups, and applications.

It’s also become a big financier of the data center build-out, reporting $118 billion in guarantees with $105 billion of that the backstop it supplied for OpenAI’s $500 billion data center in Ohio.

It has been revealed that the company made those commitments by allocating a meaningful portion of its excess cash flows. In Tuesday’s earnings call, Kress noted Nvidia would continue providing financing assistance to strong customers and that “as the market matures and additional sources of capital become available,” the company would be “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”.

But the question for the VC ecosystem is whether the tech giant will continue to back startups at anywhere near the same level without Huang at the helm.

Industry observers note that huang’s rampant dealmaking has reportedly been a source of concern for Kress. Investors have told TechCrunch that they anticipate she will take a more conservative approach to startup investing, becoming more selective with latest investments and writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio companies.

“We intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders during this last quarter and going forward,” Kress mentioned on the earnings call on Tuesday. Just how strategic startups will be under her leadership, and under the future permanent CEO, remains to be seen. But for now, VCs are bracing for a meaningful pullback in capital.

  • In a recent development, but at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club showed that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Grace Kaste on Nov 23, 2026 at 3:29 pmNovember 23, 2026 at 3:29 pm.

Industry observers note that recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering. Jobs seem to be disappearing every day, while coursework can be done by chatbots.

In a recent development, but at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club showed that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create. If anything, it’s allowing them to build things they wouldn’t have been able to before.

“We’re seeing projects that normal college students would not be expected to make,” club co-president Leonard Paya noted. “As AI becomes more advanced, you can see how fast they scale up their knowledge and execute on things that are truly amazing.”.

CSEED, founded a few years ago and already one of UW’s largest clubs, supports aspiring software designers and engineers. It’s funded by the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, as well as venture capital firms such as AI House, Madrona and Pack Ventures. Its members have gone on to join startup incubators including Y Combinator, Z Fellows and Founders Inc.

Sources indicate that twice a year, CSEED accepts applications for its Buildspace cohort, a program for students with hardware, software or design pitches. Over six weeks, the cohort meets up for build sessions, and they also receive mentorship, supplies and AI credits. Demo Day on Nov. 17 at the UW’s Gates Center marked the conclusion of the sixth Buildspace cohort, with 30 inventions presented to 150 audience members.

It has been revealed that “We’ve brought together curious and ambitious students from all backgrounds,” vice president Amy Lu noted. “CSEED gives them the community to turn their ideas into reality.”.

One of the most technically advanced ideas presented was DubDash, a fully autonomous robot for delivering food orders from the dining hall to dorms.

Industry observers note that “The best part of this is that these people were all freshmen who hadn’t yet taken robotics classes,” Paya stated. “Who would have thought that four freshmen could make a fully fledged robot in six weeks?”.

According to junior and Buildspace co-director Talal Kheiry, that’s a testament to AI. Buildspace members receive AI credits, which Kheiry mentioned have changed everything.

“AI helps guide them through the gritty parts of the project, so they can just focus on the creative parts without worrying about the technical stuff,” Kheiry stated.

Industry observers note that other inventions offered a glimpse into what’s on students’ minds these days. From notification-silencing focus apps to social connectors and mental health education platforms, nearly half of them had to do with curbing the effects of social media.

According to recent reports, “Social media isn’t social anymore,” Junaid Akhtar told the audience as he and his three team members presented. “It’s just a place to see media. Our goal is to make social media bring people together again.”.

It has been revealed that his team’s presentation was the audience’s favorite: a satirical pitch for a platform they call FeedPicks, which creates live ranked prediction markets of friends’ social media feeds. Their demo won an award for “best energy” at the end of the night.

It has been revealed that other inventions sought to get customers off their screens altogether. Joe Chae, a freshman at the Allen School, presented Pidgin, a Tinder-style app that helps users who want to practice each other’s languages to meet up in real life.

It has been revealed that “I came to UW hoping to meet some Korean international students here and learn to speak Korean with my relatives, but I didn’t meet anyone,” Chae said. “So I thought, what if I made an app that could help me find someone who speaks Korean natively and wants to learn English?”.

It has been revealed that also focused on the real world was Sasha Bogatirev’s Hadden Cybernetics. Bogatirev built a wearable gaming console that takes in information from a user’s environment and turns it into a game.

“The person has to pay attention to their surroundings,” Bogatirev remarked. “The idea is to prompt the imagination as much as possible for someone to experience another world.”.

In a recent development, his prototype used the ESP32-S3 microcontroller to render the visuals onto wearable glasses. An nRF chip on the wristband takes in scripted gestures, which he trained to turn a player’s gestures into shields, lightning strikes and fireballs. Next, he plans to add haptics using hardware supplied by CSEED.

Andrew Edwards also built a video game accessory: cStar, which is an open source, low-cost console that can play a game on any TV screen by loading it onto an SD card and popping it into a 3D-printed box. Inside that box is a microcontroller like you’d find inside a stopwatch or a microwave, unlike the highly complicated circuitry used by an Xbox or PlayStation.

“We were able to squeeze HDMI video out of the microcontroller, which allows us to show 2D and 3D graphics on a home television set,” Edwards noted. “Since the games are based on standard SD cards, a curious programmer can just write software on the computer, stick it onto an SD card, put it in the console and you’re ready to play.”.

Other notable inventions presented at Demo Day:.

Recent findings suggest that this cohort was their largest and most competitive yet. Next up, under the guidance of club advisor and Allen School professor Kurtis Heimerl, CSEED is looking to expand. They’ve started hosting build sessions every Saturday that are open to non-students.

Recent findings suggest that to do that, they’ll need to fundraise. According to CSEED co-president Benya Vahdat, they’ve already used up their Allen School allotment for the year, and they’re now in the process of raising money from donors. They recently incorporated as CSEED Foundation and received nonprofit status in Washington state.

“We want to grow this mentality of building, and maybe expand across campuses not just in Washington but across the country,” Vahdat said. “Maybe even globally.”.
